Two cables between the American Consul-General at Auckland and Washington about an unknown automatic wireless transmitter heard in New Zealand. Both are a Vigenère with the key FEBRUARY, found from the repeats in the reply by Brice Dudout and confirmed on the outgoing cable; every word is read. FVFRO TFKFX JTQII CQITJ MTRRN SOJQO … FEBRU ARYFE BRUAR YFEBR UARYF EBRUA … ARE AUTOMATIC WIRELESS STATIONS WORKING BETWEEN SAN FRANCISCO AND HONOLULU ON TWO THOUSAND METRE WAVELENGTHS Consul-General Auckland ↔ Washington · Vigenère, key FEBRUARY · 18 Feb – 1 Mar 1918 · key recovered from ciphertext-only The Auckland cables, February 1918 Go to the full text ↓ Two wireless-station cables between Auckland and Washington, enciphered with the name of the month as the key, and deciphered in full by Brice Dudout. Winslow, American Consul-General at Auckland, cabled the Naval Commander at San Francisco. Washington answered on 28 February; the reply reached Auckland on 1 March. Where US National Archives, RG 59, Central Decimal File 763.72/9377, microfilm M367 roll 83, images 0113–0114. Catalogue item 757. The cipher A Vigenère cipher on the ordinary alphabet. The key is the word FEBRUARY, the name of the month, and it is the same for both cables. How it was deciphered The period of 8 shows in the repeats of the reply, and the column frequencies give the key. It was then frozen and applied unchanged to the outgoing cable, which had not been used: all 94 letters came out as English. What it says Winslow asks whether automatic wireless stations work between San Francisco and Honolulu on two-thousand-metre wavelengths. Washington says they do not, that all US wavelengths are 4,000 m or above, and that a suspicious automatic station has been heard in the US since 15 February. Still open The final “OK” and the number 17527 are not interpreted. The images were not seen here; the work rests on the typed transcription. Credit Brice Dudout found the key, read the cables and listed the garbles, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. He says it is the first published decipherment, to his knowledge; we have not searched independently.

On 12 February 1918, at 3.50 in the morning New Zealand time, a station in New Zealand heard an unknown transmitter on about 2,000 metres, working “automatic” (too fast to tell dots from dashes). Staff Paymaster W. J. Brown, for the Naval Adviser to the New Zealand Government, wrote on 14 February that it reminded the listeners of Nauru while that station was under German control. An American journal had reported automatic working being installed between California and Honolulu, so he asked for a check by cable. The Consul-General at Auckland cabled the question on 18 February. The reply from an unnamed office in Washington, probably the Navy Department, is dated 28 February, 10 a.m. Winslow does not say he could not read it. His despatch of 4 March says only that he did not know which office it came from “further than it was sent from Washington, D.C.” The catalogue entry, which said the recipient could not read the reply, is corrected by this.

Both cables are a Vigenère on the ordinary alphabet: plain letter plus key letter, modulo 26. The outgoing cable is in 5-letter groups (94 letters). The reply is in 10-letter “words” (305 letters) followed by the number 17527. The key was found on the reply alone. The repeats TKUTZMS (104 letters apart), IFOSRLI (32) and EERMS (56) share the divisor 8, and the index of coincidence at period 8 is 0.062. A frequency fit on each of the eight columns gives FEBRUARY. The key was frozen, with its SHA-256 recorded, and then applied without change to the outgoing cable, which had not been used in finding it. That cable decrypts to 94 of 94 letters of continuous English. None of 1,000 shuffles of the same ciphertext, decrypted with the same key, reaches its English letter-frequency score. A monthly key word gave almost no security in 1918, as the period shows in the repeats. The State Department had codes of its own; these two cables show a consul and the Navy making do with an elementary method. We re-decrypted both cables from the typed transcription with FEBRUARY on 2 November 2026, and the output matches the reading below letter for letter, including the garbles.

18 February (Winslow to the Naval Commander, San Francisco): “Are automatic wireless stations working between San Francisco and Honolulu on two thousand metre wavelengths?” 28 February (Washington to Auckland): “No automatic wireless stations used between Honolulu and San Francisco. Stations can receive while sending. All wavelengths used four thousand meters or above. Suspicious automatic station heard in this country since February fifteenth on following wavelengths: forty-two hundred, ten thousand, eleven thousand and fifteen thousand meters.” So the transmitter heard on 2,000 m was not American. We have not tried to identify the 4,200, 10,000, 11,000 and 15,000 m transmitters Washington mentions.

Eight letters of the reply do not decrypt directly: six are transmission errors, mostly typical Morse confusions (i/t, g/w, z/p, z/x), and two are overstruck on the Auckland copy (groups 10 and 28). Each is forced by its word, and all eight are listed in the decryption file. Restored in the reading: wireles[s], peri[o]d, w[h]ile, [p]eriod, febr[u]ary, [f]ollowing, fort[y], [a]nd, [t]housand. “PERIOD” stands for the full stop, and in one place the encipherer left out an O in the clear while the key stayed in step. The final “OK” and the number 17527 are not interpreted. The transcription was made by AI from the NARA images and has not been checked by a person against them. The images were not fetched for this page, so it carries no snip of the cipher.

Gen. C. C. Augur, commanding the Department of Texas at San Antonio: two to Lt. Gen. Sheridan in Chicago (9 and 12 January 1874) and two to Major G. B. Russell in Austin (12 and 17 January). Where Newberry Library, Chicago, Ayer MS 3008 (C. C. Augur papers), box 02, letter-book pp. 84–85, digitised free in Newberry Digital Collections. The cipher Word transposition: the words of the message are written in rows and taken off down or up the columns in a set route; a city name in front (Baltic, Dresden) names the route; a few code words stand for names, and Texas place names fill the last column. How it was read A word-pair model of English scored every column order and direction; the four routes came out of the cipher words alone. An 1869 letter in the Grierson papers explains the method but not Augur’s tables. What it says Augur reports the Texas Supreme Court ruling and Governor Davis’s request for troops, and declines to act “without orders from the President”; he later tells Russell he need not recognize either governor. Still open Seven code words in the telegram of 12 January to Sheridan (nun, scatter, faint, table, novel, fussy, self).

Christopher Columbus Augur commanded the Department of Texas from San Antonio in 1872–75. His press letter-book for 1873–74 survives among his papers at the Newberry Library. Most entries are in clear. On pages 84 and 85 the clerk copied four telegrams of January 1874 as he received them from the cipher operator: rows of English words in no grammatical order, with no decipherment written anywhere near them. The Newberry’s volunteer transcription (Newberry Transcribe) was checked against the scans and corrected in a few words (table, Nueces, I. Davis, to, late, and). Telegram 22 ends with a clear line, “Am I correct, please reply.” No other page of the Augur papers holds cipher: all 842 transcribed pages were scored for scrambled word order, and only these two pages stood out.

The method is explained in a letter in Benjamin Grierson’s papers, also at the Newberry (Ayer MS 3039, box 3 f. 153). On 18 February 1869 Lieutenant L. V. Caziare, at the headquarters of the Fifth Military District in Austin, told the commander of Fort Concho that “your plan of setting up cypher is not correct” and worked an example through. The message is written in lines of four to nine words, code words (“arbitraries”) from the key replace names and phrases, an indicator word names one of the key’s route tables, and the columns are taken in the table’s order, some down and some up, with a check word after each. The letter gives only the example, not the tables. Augur’s telegrams use the same family without the check words. Seen from the receiving end: write the cipher words in rows of seven (or nine), and the message runs down or up the columns. Telegrams 30 and 45 (no indicator): seven columns, taken 1 down, 7 up, 4 down, 6 up, 2 down, 5 up, 3 down. Telegram 22 (indicator Baltic): nine columns, all down, in the order 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1. Telegram 29 (indicator Dresden): seven columns, 1 down, 7 up, 6 up, 2 down, 5 up, 4 down, 3 down. The last column ends in place names that fill the grid: Waco, Denison, Houston; Brownsville; Houston, Nueces, Cheyenne.

To Sheridan, 9 January 1874 (Baltic) Telegram 22, with its indicator “Baltic” and the clear line “Am I correct, please reply.” Image: Newberry Library, Ayer MS 3008 box 02, letter-book p. 84 (scan 00045-0), via Newberry Digital Collections. The Supreme Court of the State has decided the law under which the late election was held here unconstitutional. Governor Davis anticipates, however, that the legislature and governor then elected will meet in Austin on Tuesday next and attempt by force to get possession of the State government. The [He?] asks me to prevent this by use of United States troops. I decline to act without orders from the President [written “precedent”], who by law is made judge as to when United States troops are to interfere in the troubles of a State. (In clear:) Am I correct, please reply. 29. To Sheridan, 12 January 1874 (Dresden) I have just received this following dispatch from [nun =? Governor] Davis with request to forward: “[scatter =? President] Grant, [faint]: as I anticipate unauthorized persons may attempt to [table =? take] possession of the state [novel =? capitol] buildings, I request [fussy]” — it, as he has no cypher to [self] that secure. 30. To Russell, 12 January 1874 I [written “In”] am informed through [written “though”] General Sheridan that the President has no instructions to give on the subject, but that if any change occurs I will have immediate notice. I have sent the Governor’s dispatch. 45. To Russell, 17 January 1874 It seems to me if Governor Davis yields to force without armed collision it is all that can be expected of him. Under the circumstances it is evident neither the President nor the party desire trouble. You need not specially recognize either governor. You can return to-morrow unless your further stay there is desirable. Instruct Sellers not to interfere in any way without orders from me. The telegrams follow the end of Reconstruction in Texas day by day. The Republican governor, Edmund J. Davis, had lost the December 1873 election to Richard Coke; the State Supreme Court struck down the election law; the new legislature met in Austin on Tuesday 13 January and installed Coke while Davis held the ground floor of the Capitol. Grant refused Davis’s requests for troops, and Davis left office on 19 January. Augur’s first telegram already states the position the President took: federal troops would not decide the governorship.

A model of English letters failed even on the 1869 worked example. A model of English word pairs, built from the project’s Gutenberg corpus, did better: a search over every order and direction of the columns recovered the example’s five columns and its row text. On telegram 45 the columns of a seven-word grid came out as English phrases at once (“It seems to me if governor Davis yields to force”, “without armed collision it is all that can be Expected”), and the search put them in order. Telegram 30 then read with the same route unchanged. Scoring every transcribed Augur page with the same model found telegram 22 on the facing page. There “Baltic” stood outside the grid; that suggested “Dresden” did too in telegram 29, which then fell into a seven-by-seven grid once “I. I.” was counted as two words. route.py in the target folder holds the four routes and prints the reading.

Telegram 29: seven code words, each once: nun (Governor?), scatter (President?), faint , table (take?), novel (capitol?), fussy , self . The Department’s list of arbitraries is not in the Augur or Grierson papers. The closing clause (“as he has no cypher to [self] that secure”) is uncertain. Telegram 22: “The asks me” is probably the clerk’s slip for “He asks me”; “precedent” for President. Telegram 30: “In” for I, “though” for through. Sheridan’s headquarters deciphered these at the time; his received copies, in the Division of the Missouri records, were not looked for and could settle the code words.

A letter of the Queen of Hungary to her sister (DECODE R1143) whose cipher was deciphered at the time on slips laid over it, and printed in 1877: Milanese support for Ippolito against Cardinal Ascanio, and Andriolo to come. Buda → Ferrara · graphic cipher with decipherment slips · 2 May 1486 · existing decipherment Beatrice d’Aragona to Eleonora, Buda, 2 May 1486 from Beatrice of Naples → to Eleonora d'Aragona Go to the full text ↓ A letter from the Queen of Hungary whose cipher was deciphered at the time on slips laid over it, and printed in 1877. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) · Iván Nagy and Albert Nyáry (key or decipherment used) At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Beatrice d’Aragona to Eleonora d’Aragona, Buda, 2 May 1486: three written pages and the address side, in six photographs. Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Carteggio Principi Esteri, 1623, b. 2/2, 2, 18; DECODE R1143. Catalogue item 160. The cipher A graphic substitution alphabet inside clear Italian; possibly the new cipher sent in March 1486, not established. How it was deciphered Not here: handwritten slips laid over the cipher give the decipherment, and MDE III (1877) no. 75 prints it. Both were matched to the photographs. What it says Milan and Bari support Ippolito, against the account of Cardinal Ascanio’s envoy; Andriolo should come. Still open The date and hand of the slips. Catalogue item 160 grouped five letters of Beatrice d’Aragona, Queen of Hungary, to Ferrara; since 14 October 2026 each cipher, and the plain letter, has its own page: the 1482 letters , 8 March 1486 , 2 May 1486 and the plain letter of 1505 . This letter was written two months after the March letter that enclosed a new cipher, so the two are not shown to share a key.

MDE III (1877), p. 94, no. 75: the deciphered passage in italics, “che Don Hippolyto vostro figliolo sia tanto amato dalo Sig-re Ducha de Milano …”, the words the contemporary slip gives. A crop of the public-domain edition, not an archive photograph. Image: Magyar Diplomácziai Emlékek III (1877), p. 94, via MTAK REAL-EOD. The first cipher block discusses Milanese support for Ippolito and the contrary account given by Cardinal Ascanio’s envoy. A separate handwritten slip over the block begins “che don hippolyto vostro figliolo…” . The next photograph shows the same page with the slip moved aside. A later slip reads: che quello Andriolo se conferisca qua The corresponding request appears in MDE III no. 75 in the same context. Both the manuscript slips and the printed edition give earlier decipherments. The precise date and scribe of the slips were not established here.

The evidence is the agreement of dates, salutations, clear passages, cipher boundaries and the decipherment slips with the edition. No transcription of the symbols was made, no key was recovered and no percentage was measured; the letter-by-letter accuracy of the older decipherment has not been tested. Archive photographs stay local because DECODE states that their publication requires the archive’s permission; the figure is a crop of the public-domain edition.

Buda, 2 May 1486 Beatrice of Aragon to her sister Eleonora of Ferrara: the Duke of Milan and the Duke of Bari support Ippolito d'Este, against the account of Cardinal Ascanio's envoy, the abbot of Forlì, and Andriolo is asked to come to Hungary. Contemporary decipherment slips are photographed over the cipher; the decryption here is the uncorrected OCR of the reading printed in MDE III (1877) no. 75. Beatrix királyné Eleonóra ferrárai herczegnét a Hippo- lit esztergomi érsekségét illető ügyekről s a nápolyi király Fer- dinánd segítségére küldött magyar segédcsapatokról értesíti, s felkéri a herczegnét, hogy ama bizonyos ügyben*) And riólót mihamarább küldje Magyarországba, hogy vele az illető fontos tárgyban végezni lehessen. Ill-ma et Excell-ma Ducissa, Domina et soror nostra carissima. Per Benedicto de Leyra nostro correri, quale nova- mente e passato per la venendo da Spagna, havemo recepute tre lettere de Vostra Ill-ma Signoria con una copia de una lettera seripta ad quella da Pitigliano Dabisbal, per la quale simo facta certa de alcíme bone nove, tucte favorebile ala paterna Maesta. Responderemo doncha per questa ad tucte le parte necessarie de dicte lettere, et primo dicemo: che ne e stata carissima la contiuencia dela lettera delo Magnifico Mes- ser Francesco Fontana, quale Vostra Signoria ce have man- data in cifra et non essendo ancora pervenuta la originale *) Dsem ügyében. === PDF PAGE 126 === lettera ale manu dela Maesta de quisto Signore Re nostro consorte, li liavemo facto legere tucto quello serive dicto Mes- ser Francesco, et una cum Sua Maesta liavemo pigliato gran piacere, clie Don Hippolyto vostro figliolo sia tanto"amato dalo Sig-re Ducha de Milano, et Duca de Barri, perche tocliamo cum manó clie dela se procurci il contrario de quello liave referito qua lo venerabile Abbate de Forli oratore del Cardinale Ascanio, cum dire che alo Ill-mo Signor Duca vostro consorte seria stato necessario per rispecto delli predetti Signori et pre- fertim del Duca de Barri cedere a dicto Cardinale Ascanio, siche serivendosse cd presente tol littera comprendemo, che epso Duca de Barri priidentissimamente se move ad volere piu presto supplicare per epso vostro figliolo, maximé havendo piu bisogno de beneficij. che epso Signor Cardinale, che per epso suo fratello,*) mente de manco sta certa Yostra Signoria, clie una volta per esso Signore Re nostro consorte ne e stata facta gratia de dicto Archiepiscopato per lo prefato Ill-mo Don Ypo- lito et per non ad instancia de persona del mundo se mutaria de farene altro, et ad cioche Yostra Signoria ne possa stare piu secura, li havemo mandate le lettere dela donatione per Donato nostro Correri. Resta solum, che se faza instancia in corte de Roma dalo canto de loro, che se habia la coufirma- tione, perche da qua per lo prefato Signor Re nostro marito: et per nui sono state seripte lettere caldissime alo oratore nostro in Roma, che debia sollicitare et procurare la confir- matione per esso Don Ypolito nostro nepote. Ancora che quella parte ne serive Y. S. dela indisposi- tione del predetto Ill-mo Don Ypolito, ce sia dispiaciuta, tamen perche quella dice presto sera restaurato, et etiam quisto Benedicto correri e retornato da loco ne dice liaverelo visto sano et cavalcare, ne havemo pigliato piacere incredibile, per- che cognoscemo presto se ne porra venire qua, dove lo aspe- ctamo con lo maiore desiderio del mundo, et ad 1' bora de mo, Bartholomeo Brissiano, quale Yostra Signoria aspectava, deve essere la, et li havera explicato tucto quello li e stato per esso Signor Re nostro marito et per nuj commesso, et ancora che luj havesse portate alcune nostre comissione dele gente vole- === PDF PAGE 127 === ámo se mandassero con esso nostro nepote. Tamen da poi ce ne e recordata unaltra, quale e che ne piaceria, che Vostra Signoria li mandasse alcuna donna, che sapesse la natura et prattica sua, et che lo sapesse gobernare, quando Dio guar- dando fosse indisposto, et de questo pregamo quella quanto sapemo et possemo. Quello ne significa, clie per la guerra facta contra quisto stato li foro totti duj castelli ale confine de Regno, et che al presente essendo stati quelli depositati impotere delo stato de Milano, lo Signor Lodovico suo genero li havea mandati li contrasigni ad farenceli restituire etc. Ce e stato tanto caris- simo et ne havemo pigliato quello piacere, che pegliaymo de la conquista deVienna, et tanto piu ne e piaciuto, che secundo quella ne serive dicti castelli importano multo ala conserva- tione delo stato vostro, et havemo speranza ancora, che per la justitia grandissima havemo le Signorie Vostre in quello li e stato tolto, presto li sera restituito tucto. Nui cognoscemo, che orane di prosperendo le cose in favore de la paterna Maesta, procede dala divina providenza, perche non vole comportare che tanta iniquita et malignita de baroni rebelli, quali senza causa haveno macchinato, che nostro Signor Dio como justo Judice dara tanta victoria ad esso Signor Re nostro patre, che castigara dicti baronij et tucti li soi ini- mici, et la ambitione et malignita del Pontifice et deli Cardi- nali non andare senza punitione, et per nuj non se mancara de fare omne opera con nostro Marito, che habia da mandare li subsidij de le gente necessarii, et sin mo, la Sua Maesta liave facta donare prestaneza per sei mesi ad seicento cavalli tra hominij darme et cavalli legeri, et ad seicento fanti, le quale gente tucte se sono adviate ala via de Segna per imbarcliarse et passare in Puglia ali favori de essa paterna Maesta, la quale seripse essereli necessario dicto numero de gente et non piu et ebe se mandassero in diéta provincia, et appresso bisognando piu gente, sencene mandaranno tante, quante ne vorranno. Pregamo strictissimamente. la Signoria Vostra che sempre havera nove ce ne voglia fare parte, perche non se ne porria credere, quanto piacere ne pigliamo, et al presente havemo === PDF PAGE 128 === pigliato lo maiore piacere del mundo dela dicta copia de Bisbal. Noi pregamo ancora quella, che voglia fare omne instan- cia che quello Andriolo se conferisca qua *), accioche se possa pigliare alcuna hona conclusione ad quella facenda, per la quale luj have de venire qua, et lo piu presto sia possibile se mande, et lo Signor Duca prefato vostro consorte et Yostra Signoria 11011 porriauo fare maiore piacere ad nostro marito, perche sta multo desideruso intendere lo predetto Andriolo *) accio se possa dare ordene alo eífecto, perche se desidera la sua venuta. Li veli, che Yostra Signoria ce ha mandati sono stati si delicati, et belli che ce sono summamente piaciuti; et ne li ren- dimo infinite gratie, et per amore suo li volimo portare, per fareli quello bonore meritano, et a lei ne recomandamo. Per Benedicto de Leyra, nostro correri, quale novamente e passato per la venendo da Spagna, havemo recepute tre lettere de Vostra Illustrissima Signoria con una copia de una lettera scripta ad quella da Pitigliano Dabisbal, per la quale simo facta certa de alcune bone nove, tucte favorebile ala paterna Maesta. Responderemo doncha per questa ad tucte le parte necessarie de dicte lettere, et primo dicemo che ne e stata carissima la continencia dela lettera delo Magnifico Messer Francesco Fontana, quale Vostra Signoria ce have mandata in cifra; et non essendo ancora pervenuta la originale lettera ale manu dela Maesta de quisto Signore Re nostro consorte, li havemo facto legere tucto quello scrive dicto Messer Francesco, et una cum Sua Maesta havemo pigliato gran piacere che Don Hippolyto vostro figliolo sia tanto amato dalo Signore Ducha de Milano et Duca de Barri, perche tochamo cum mano che de la se procura il contrario de quello have referito qua lo venerabile Abbate de Forli, oratore del Cardinale Ascanio, cum dire che alo Illustrissimo Signor Duca vostro consorte seria stato necessario, per rispecto delli predetti Signori et presertim del Duca de Barri, cedere a dicto Cardinale Ascanio; siche, scrivendosse al presente tal littera, comprendemo che epso Duca de Barri prudentissimamente se move ad volere piu presto supplicare per epso vostro figliolo, maxime havendo piu bisogno de beneficij, che epso Signor Cardinale, che per epso suo fratello; niente de manco sta certa Vostra Signoria che una volta per esso Signore Re nostro consorte ne e stata facta gratia de dicto Archiepiscopato per lo prefato Illustrissimo Don Ypolito, et per non ad instancia de persona del mundo se mutaria de farene altro; et ad cio che Vostra Signoria ne possa stare piu secura, li havemo mandate le lettere dela donatione per Donato nostro Correri. Resta solum che se faza instancia in corte de Roma dalo canto de loro che se habia la confirmatione, perche da qua per lo prefato Signor Re nostro marito et per nui sono state scripte lettere caldissime alo oratore nostro in Roma, che debia sollicitare et procurare la confirmatione per esso Don Ypolito nostro nepote. Ancora che quella parte ne scrive Vostra Signoria dela indispositione del predetto Illustrissimo Don Ypolito ce sia dispiaciuta, tamen, perche quella dice presto sera restaurato, et etiam quisto Benedicto correri e retornato da loco [et] ne dice haverelo visto sano et cavalcare, ne havemo pigliato piacere incredibile, perche cognoscemo presto se ne porra venire qua, dove lo aspectamo con lo maiore desiderio del mundo. Et ad l'hora de mo Bartholomeo Brissiano, quale Vostra Signoria aspectava, deve essere la, et li havera explicato tucto quello li e stato per esso Signor Re nostro marito et per nuj commesso; et ancora che luj havesse portate alcune nostre comissione dele gente voleamo se mandassero con esso nostro nepote, tamen da poi ce ne e recordata unaltra, quale e che ne piaceria che Vostra Signoria li mandasse alcuna donna che sapesse la natura et prattica sua, et che lo sapesse gobernare quando, Dio guardando, fosse indisposto; et de questo pregamo quella quanto sapemo et possemo. Quello ne significa, che per la guerra facta contra quisto stato li foro tolti duj castelli ale confine de Regno, et che al presente, essendo stati quelli depositati in potere delo stato de Milano, lo Signor Lodovico suo genero li havea mandati li contrasigni ad farenceli restituire etc., ce e stato tanto carissimo, et ne havemo pigliato quello piacere che pegliaymo de la conquista de Vienna; et tanto piu ne e piaciuto, che secundo quella ne scrive dicti castelli importano multo ala conservatione delo stato vostro; et havemo speranza ancora che, per la justitia grandissima havemo le Signorie Vostre in quello li e stato tolto, presto li sera restituito tucto. Nui cognoscemo che omne di prosperendo le cose in favore de la paterna Maesta procede dala divina providenza, perche non vole comportare che tanta iniquita et malignita de baroni rebelli, quali senza causa haveno macchinato; che nostro Signor Dio, como justo Judice, dara tanta victoria ad esso Signor Re nostro patre che castigara dicti baronij et tucti li soi inimici, et la ambitione et malignita del Pontifice et deli Cardinali non andare senza punitione; et per nuj non se mancara de fare omne opera con nostro Marito che habia da mandare li subsidij de le gente necessarii. Et sin mo la Sua Maesta have facta donare prestaneza per sei mesi ad seicento cavalli, tra homini d'arme et cavalli legeri, et ad seicento fanti, le quale gente tucte se sono adviate ala via de Segna per imbarcharse et passare in Puglia ali favori de essa paterna Maesta, la quale scripse essereli necessario dicto numero de gente et non piu, et che se mandassero in dicta provincia; et appresso, bisognando piu gente, sencene mandaranno tante quante ne vorranno. Pregamo strictissimamente la Signoria Vostra che sempre havera nove ce ne voglia fare parte, perche non se ne porria credere quanto piacere ne pigliamo; et al presente havemo pigliato lo maiore piacere del mundo dela dicta copia de Bisbal. Noi pregamo ancora quella che voglia fare omne instancia che quello Andriolo se conferisca qua, accioche se possa pigliare alcuna bona conclusione ad quella facenda per la quale luj have de venire qua, et lo piu presto sia possibile se mande; et lo Signor Duca prefato vostro consorte et Vostra Signoria non porriano fare maiore piacere ad nostro marito, perche sta multo desideruso intendere lo predetto Andriolo, accio se possa dare ordene alo effecto, perche se desidera la sua venuta. Li veli che Vostra Signoria ce ha mandati sono stati si delicati et belli che ce sono summamente piaciuti; et ne li rendimo infinite gratie, et per amore suo li volimo portare, per fareli quello honore meritano, et a lei ne recomandamo. Datum in castro nostro Buden. II Maij MCCCCLXXXVI. Di Vostra Signoria obediente Sore la Regina de Hungaria. Illustrissime Domine Helionore de Aragonia, Ducisse Ferrarie etc., Domine et Sorori Colendissime. Ferrarie. Through Benedicto de Leyra, our courier, who lately passed through there coming from Spain, we have received three letters from Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, with a copy of a letter written to you by Pitigliano Dabisbal, by which we have been made certain of some good news, all favourable to our father's Majesty. We shall therefore answer by this letter all the necessary parts of the said letters; and first we say that the contents of the letter of the Magnificent Messer Francesco Fontana, which Your Ladyship sent us in cipher, have been most welcome to us; and the original letter not having yet reached the hands of His Majesty our Lord King and consort, we have had read to him everything that the said Messer Francesco writes, and together with His Majesty we have taken great pleasure that Don Ippolito your son is so loved by the Lord Duke of Milan and the Duke of Bari, because we touch with our hands that there they are working for the opposite of what the venerable Abbot of Forlì, ambassador of Cardinal Ascanio, reported here, saying that out of regard for the said lords, and especially the Duke of Bari, it would have been necessary for the Most Illustrious Lord Duke your consort to give way to the said Cardinal Ascanio. So, this letter being written now, we understand that the said Duke of Bari most prudently is moved to wish rather to plead for your said son, especially since he has more need of benefices than the said Lord Cardinal, than for his said brother. Nevertheless Your Ladyship may be sure that once the grace of the said archbishopric has been granted by the said Lord King our consort to the said Most Illustrious Don Ippolito, he would not change to do otherwise at the request of anyone in the world; and so that Your Ladyship may be more secure of it, we have sent you the letters of the donation by Donato our courier. It remains only that on their side instance be made at the court of Rome to obtain the confirmation, because from here, by the said Lord King our husband and by us, most pressing letters have been written to our ambassador in Rome to solicit and procure the confirmation for the said Don Ippolito our nephew. Although the part in which Your Ladyship writes to us of the indisposition of the said Most Illustrious Don Ippolito displeased us, yet because you say he will soon be restored, and also this courier Benedicto has returned from there and tells us he saw him well and riding, we have taken incredible pleasure in it, because we know that he will soon be able to come here, where we await him with the greatest desire in the world. And by now Bartholomeo Bresciano, whom Your Ladyship was expecting, must be there, and will have explained to you everything that was entrusted to him by the said Lord King our husband and by us; and although he carried some commissions of ours about the people we wished to be sent with our said nephew, yet afterwards another came to our mind, which is that we should like Your Ladyship to send with him some woman who knows his nature and habits, and who could look after him should he, God forbid, be unwell; and of this we beg you as much as we know and can. What you tell us — that in the war made against that state two castles on the borders of the kingdom were taken from you, and that now, these having been deposited in the power of the state of Milan, the Lord Ludovico, your son-in-law, had sent you the countersigns to have them restored to you, etc. — has been so very welcome to us, and we have taken from it the pleasure we took from the conquest of Vienna; and it pleased us all the more since, as you write, the said castles matter much for the preservation of your state; and we also hope that, given the very great justice Your Lordships have in what was taken from you, all will soon be restored to you. We know that the daily prospering of affairs in favour of our father's Majesty proceeds from divine providence, which will not suffer such iniquity and malice of rebel barons, who have plotted without cause; [and we trust] that our Lord God, as a just judge, will give such victory to the said Lord King our father that he will punish the said barons and all his enemies, and that the ambition and malice of the Pope and of the cardinals will not go unpunished; and for our part we shall not fail to do everything with our husband that he may send the necessary auxiliary troops. And so far His Majesty has had an advance for six months given to six hundred horse, men-at-arms and light horse, and to six hundred foot, all of which troops have set off by way of Senj to embark and cross to Apulia in the service of our father's Majesty, who wrote that he needed that number of men and no more, and that they should be sent to that province; and later, if more men are needed, as many will be sent as he wants. We most earnestly beg Your Ladyship always to share any news you have with us, for one could not believe how much pleasure we take in it; and at present we have taken the greatest pleasure in the world in the said copy from Bisbal. We also beg you to press in every way that that Andriolo come here, so that some good conclusion may be reached in that business for which he is to come here, and that he be sent as soon as possible; and the said Lord Duke your consort and Your Ladyship could not give our husband greater pleasure, for he is very desirous to hear the said Andriolo, so that order may be given for the execution, because his coming is desired. The veils that Your Ladyship has sent us were so delicate and beautiful that they pleased us exceedingly; and we give you infinite thanks for them, and for love of you we mean to wear them, to do them the honour they deserve; and we commend ourselves to you. Given in our castle of Buda, 2 May 1486. Your Ladyship's obedient sister, the Queen of Hungary. To the Most Illustrious Lady Eleonora of Aragon, Duchess of Ferrara etc., Lady and most honoured sister. Ferrara.

Giovanni Antonio Bilia, the Duke of Milan’s agent at Charles V’s court, to Francesco II Sforza from Burgos (BnF fr. 3013 no. 43). Harumi-Matsuba transcribed the cipher with AI and deciphered the first page with the Sforza key DECODE R5258, docketed with Bilia’s name (issue #55). Checked here with the project’s own copy of the key: 440 of 459 shared values agree and the key sheet supports theirs on the rest. The seven cipher lines on the verso and one name code stay open. One page wholly in cipher, seven more cipher lines, then a clear close, a postscript and the signature. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 3013 no. 43, ff. 102r–v (Gallica views 164–167). Catalogue item 291, part. No DECODE record. The cipher The Sforza chancery’s syllabic cipher: barred letters with two-digit numbers for syllables, numbers and signs for letters, a few words and names, and nulls. How it was deciphered With the Milan key sheet DECODE R5258, docketed “Cum equite Bilie”, Bilia’s own key. The transcription is by AI and has not been checked by a person; here the project’s own copy of the key was applied to it, the key sheet and the page were compared by eye, and a language model scored it against shuffled keys. What it says Bilia dined with an old lord who complained that the Duke was troubling a “conte [?Theophimo]”; Bilia calmed him and asks the Duke to write a letter of guarantee “per non desperarlo in questa sua [?vechieza]”. Still open The seven cipher lines of f. 102v; the name code B.58; about 28 doubtful signs on f. 102r. The letter no. 42 to the ambassador Taverna, same day, is in another cipher. f. 102r: the clear salutation to the Duke and thirty lines of cipher (Gallica view 164). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3013 f. 102r, via Gallica. The volume Français 3013 gathers original letters of the sixteenth century. Its no. 43 is a letter of Giovanni Antonio Bilia, the “Cavaliere Bilia”, one of the Sforza agents at Charles V’s court, to Francesco II Sforza, Duke of Milan. The first leaf is entirely in cipher. The verso has seven more lines of cipher, then in clear: “et a v. ex.a humilm.te basando la mano di cont.o ricomando. De Burgos XXII nobris 1527”, the postscript “Sua M.ta ha disposito l’andata sua ad Valentia como facto Natale” and the signature “Humill.mus servus Jo. Ant.s Bilia”. f. 102v: the seven cipher lines whose reading is still unconfirmed, then the clear close “De Burgos XXII nobris 1527” (Gallica view 165). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3013 f. 102v, via Gallica. No. 42 of the same volume, Bilia to Jo. Francesco Taverna (“Zaberna” in the catalogue), the Duke’s ambassador, written the same day, is in a different cipher: base letters M, A, H, R, B and others with numbers 1–29, mixed with clear Italian. Neither R5258 nor Bilia’s other key R5237 fits it, so it is not part of this page and stays in the catalogue.

The key is a sheet in the Archivio di Stato di Milano, Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1591 no. 24, on DECODE as R5258. Its docket reads “Cum equite Bilie / extracta ex cifris”: the cipher used with the Cavaliere Bilia, copied out of the ciphers. The same sheet reads “el Gilino”’s letter of 15 September 1527, a different correspondent with its own page , where the sheet is transcribed; George Lasry recovered the same key independently from that letter. Syllables are written as a barred base letter with a number above: B.31–50 ba … gu , B.51–55 fa … fu , D.51–65 la … nu , G.56–80 pa … tu , o.33–47 va … zu . Single letters have several signs each (a = 19 or θ-like forms, e = 25, n = 6 or 36, s = 45 or a crossed x, t = 46). A few words have their own signs (H.27 che , H.28 come , R.23 con ), names have codes in a separate block, and some signs are nulls. The contributor added values for five signs that are not on the sheet as transcribed here: ß = r, £ = l, F = c, tt = t, qx = ss (41 signs, 8.1% of the page), from the sense of the letter.

Their transcription was made by Claude Opus 5.5 and cross-checked by AI only. Hozi ce sono ritrovato a disnare col signore [B.58] [?pu] [?le] molto; si è meco querelato, havendo hauto carte da suo genero, che vostra ecelentia fa [?va] dare molestia al conte [?Theophimo] suo [?figlio] [?tavolo] per rispeto dele inhibitione altre volte fatoli. Gi[à] me sono sforzato con ogni destreza cavarlo di questa imprecione el farli conoscere che vostra ecelentia non haveria mandato tale cosa se non per [?servitio] di sua signoria, quale ha sempre amato come [?padre]; cosi si aquietato. Me pareria essere [?bene], se non che vostra ecelentia scrivesse qua [?una] carta por la quale se li potesse fare vedere in [?effetto] la con a [?volonta] che quela li tiene, el che con parole se li è designato, l certifi[ca]to che, essendo vostra ecelentia patrona del stato, non solamente non li levaria quelo che una volta li haveva donato, [?vo] che lo faria signore d'altra magiore cosa. Questo dico per non desperarlo in questa sua [?vechieza], lanche che li [?tempi] non me pareno che lo concedano; tutavolta quel [?] facio secondo sua virtu l prudentia; al forse non saria male fare … In English, roughly: today Bilia dined with a lord (name code B.58) who complained bitterly that, according to letters from his son-in-law, the Duke was troubling “conte Theophimo” over prohibitions made earlier. Bilia talked him out of it, explaining that the Duke would not have sent such an order except for his good, having always loved him like a father. He suggests the Duke write a letter guaranteeing that, as master of the state, he would not take back what he had once given but would make him lord of something greater, “so as not to drive him to despair in his old age”, though the times hardly allow it. The text runs on to f. 102v.

The project’s own key. The contributor’s sign transcription was decoded again with the project’s files for R5258 ( targets/gilino1527 ), mapping their sign names onto ours. Our key gives a value to 459 of the 505 signs; where both keys give one, 440 of 459 agree (95.9%). The 19 that differ are the crossed x (null in our Gilino key, s for the contributor), the θ-like sign (a for us, o for them) and one plain o sign. On the image of the R5258 sheet the crossed x stands in the s column and the θ-like sign in the o column, so the contributor follows the sheet and our Gilino values for these signs were guesses from context. The other 45 signs are their five added signs, two nulls, a sign they read as a cursive 25, the name code and one unreadable digit. Against chance. Scored with the project’s Italian model ( it-cinquecento , order 5, letters only), our decode gives −2.18 per character; 1000 shuffles of the same values over the same signs give at best −3.11, and none reaches the real key. The decode reads as Italian from the first line to the last. The page itself. Lines 1–5 of f. 102r (81 signs) were compared sign by sign with the full-size image: every sign name agrees. At three places the second digit of a number (39 or 33, 69 or 65) cannot be told apart at this resolution, and the transcription follows the sense. No person, on either side, has checked the rest of the transcription. How much reads. 504 of the 505 signs of f. 102r have a value. Counting the signs inside the readings the contributor marks as doubtful, roughly 94% of the page gives sense (an estimate, not a measurement). Measured on the reading in October 2026, f. 102r builds coherent sentences but reads at 92.2%, under the 95% bar. With f. 102v not deciphered, the letter as a whole is partial.

f. 102v , seven cipher lines (118 signs). With our key 102 of them have a value and some words appear (“a suo genero”, “vostra ecelentia”, “con desiderio si aspetta”, “con le risposte di”), but there is no continuous sense, and the margin over shuffled keys is thin (−2.60 against −2.75): decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). On 23 October the transcription was checked line by line on the full-size Gallica view 165 and decoded again: four signs (R.29, 8?, an open rectangle, o.19) have no value on the key sheet and three more (£, φ, mp) only the contributor’s context values, and the last one or two signs of every line curve into the binding of the microfilm. No decipherment or copy of the letter is known. The partial text is f102v_partial_reading.md . B.58 , the code of the old lord, is not on the R5258 sheet (its name block has B.55 Imperatore, B.56 Sua Maestà, B.57 Nassau, B.60, B.62, B.63, B.66, B.71, but no B.58). About 28 doubtful signs on f. 102r: eight places where the two AI image checks disagreed, the name “Theophimo”, the slips or misreadings pervitio , papre , ina , tompi , vechilza , the sign £ read as l where et may be meant, and one digit lost (B.3?). Print. Neither the contributor nor this project has seen Cerioni’s 1970 edition of the Sforza keys or Giudici 2018. No. 42, to Taverna, in another cipher with no key yet.

The letter is no. 69 of fr. 3034, one of the Montmorency volumes of Italian despatches. It fills ff. 156r–157v. The salutation, the closing ( D. V. Ill.ma Ex.tia … sig.ria ) and the signature ( Humil.e Ser.or Ambrosio Bizozola ) are in clear, and everything else is in cipher. The address is on the following leaf: Allo Ill.mo et Ex.mo Principe Il S. Maximiliano Sforza … patron suo osser.mo … In Franza, Ala Corte . DECODE dates it 1520/1529. The clear parts carry no date. The cipher does: the last lines read Bologna, quattro del … novembre , and the letter describes the eve of the Emperor’s entry into the town. Charles V entered Bologna on 5 November 1529, so the letter is of 4 November 1529. The year is inferred, not written. Lasry’s table gives one sign for each letter: A ʒ, B 7, C a 9 with a tail, D 1, E ꝗ, F ʃ, G 2, H 6, I 8, L ʓ, M ε, N Γ, O 11, P a tall cross, Q Ꝗ, R a T-shaped stroke, S ɗ, T and V two further signs. Words are separated by spaces. The text adds four refinements. A long-looped sign that is not drawn in the table as published stands for t , as molte , intese and rotta require. ʒ is used for u as well as a ( aolte = volte, daca = duca). The long s is used for f and for s ( fatti , consiglio ). In the postscript a small cross stands for e . Lasry’s “unknown” ꝏ occurs only at the ends of lines, where a word runs on ( al duca ꝏ / di Savoia ), so it is a filler. Two or three other unknown signs occur only in the date line and are probably its numerals.

# Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza, Bologna, 4 November 1529 (BnF fr. 3034 ff. 156r-157v): reading Rests on: the sign transcription `codes.txt` (all 66 lines, second pass at double scale) and Lasry's key as extended here (`decode.py`, output `reading_raw.txt`). This file is the word-divided reading of that output, written for the v3 verification (23 Oct 2026). Rules: - The key's own homophones are resolved by sense: the sign ʒ is a and u/v ("aolte" volte, "dacato" ducato, "qaesta" questa), the long s is f and s ("configlio" consiglio, "sare" fare). These are the figure's own values. - Where the sense needs a letter the figure does not have (the tall cross p where e is wanted, "crpdo" credo; the small cross is e only in the postscript, where it is read e), the word is marked [?word]: the tall/small cross is a look-alike pair, so these words rest on the alternate. - The writer's spelling is kept as the figures give it (soui, nigoci, regonamento, Mantuda, duco, maiota, Cessero = Cesare, the Emperor); it is not modernised. - The stretches listed in `doubtful.txt` are [...]; words the figures give but that do not resolve are [word] (a hole); [x] around letters the sense needs and nothing carries. - The postscript (249_ps1-2, written on f. 157v beside the text) is placed at the end. ## Reading Per le e mie ultime di Cremona e [t farbar], e de qui averete intese molte cose. Dico de le acione de misere [?Iulio], como sono passato li soui nigoci con lo imperatore, et che molte volte si e miso ognia cosa in rotta. Qua o saputo per uno omo degno degno di fede, che per per questi [roturi], che il consiglio del imperatore piu volte anno fatti di grandi discorc[i] sopra il ducato di Milano, dicendo che il duca Francesco negociava [...] a uno altro. [?Discorendo] disseno de fare molte parte dil stato: al duca di Savoia, al marcheso di Monferrato, al marcheso di Mantuda, al duca di Ferrara, et Milano al duca Alisandro. In questo regonamento dise l'arciapescho [luo] di Baro: meglio io seria darlo al duca [?Maximiliano], che di [?ragione] li vene. Uno altro disse: [?credo] certo, se questo si fasesse, che il duca Francesco hi a [contentrare] che il fratello l'avesse. Anno altro [?risposto], che meglio sarebe [avarne] partita con Franza; et feceno fino al parlare in questa ultima [...] a scritto al papa che pensi fare altro duco di Milano che il duca Francesco. Cessero questa sera e gionto a la Certosa, che e [ea] uno miglio da questo terra; domane sara l'intrata. Nondmeno ogi li e andato incontra tutti li cardinali et ambassatori, quello di Venecia et de Milano; ano parlato [a] sua maiota cossi a cavallo. Per Dio gracia una altra volta si e ataca[...] pratica di mi misere Iulio, et se negociara insime con Veniciani. Si sepera molto che la cosa de[...] in bene. Io sto qua a aspetara s'el duca avera a venire qua o no. O trovato misere Alesandro Atavante et il Lobino, [qal] sa il spenditore del reverendisimo Triultio. Sin e atanto abia vostri [ri] aviso, o so[?] pato per vis de misere [sifione], che con ci ando la cosa di misere Iulio se li dara [mali ere], et creso sera [qaella] dongari, et che subto voi a iaverete il capello roso. O fato intendere al Atavante in decorse fa fatto per il consiglio de Cessero per o se la mala sorte volesse che la cosa di misere [?Iulio] non reassi[o]e in bene, et che vasse in potere dil papa, de elelere altri vogli tenirne qualche preposto con misere Iacobo Salviati, che quando la cossa no reuose con misere Iulio, voglia parlare al papa per voi; et che se la cossa annesse a rea sire, che li prometta deca mili scuti di intrata l'anno [...] e ne altro. Bologna, quatro del [...] novembre. Postscript: Sono molti giorni non o vostre litere, avere il recepto di questa [fte]. The last paragraph but one is the least secure in the reading and the translation stays close to its words. --> # Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza, Bologna, 4 November 1529 (BnF fr. 3034 ff. 156r-157v): English translation By my last letters from Cremona and [t farbar], and from here, you will have heard many things. I speak of the doings of Messer [?Giulio], how his affairs with the Emperor have gone, and that many times everything was broken off. Here I have learned from a man worthy of trust that, because of these [roturi], the Emperor's council has several times held great discussions about the duchy of Milan, saying that Duke Francesco was negotiating [...] with another. [?Discussing] it, they spoke of making many parts of the state: to the Duke of Savoy, to the Marquis of Monferrato, to the Marquis of Mantua, to the Duke of Ferrara, and Milan to Duke Alessandro. In this discussion the Archbishop [luo] of Bari said: it would be better to give it to Duke [?Massimiliano], to whom it comes by [?right]. Another said: I [?believe] for certain that, if this were done, Duke Francesco would [contentrare] that his brother should have it. Others [?answered] that it would be better to [avarne] share with France; and they went as far as speaking in this last [...] has written to the Pope that he should think of making another Duke of Milan than Duke Francesco. The Emperor arrived this evening at the Certosa, which is [ea] a mile from this town; tomorrow will be the entry. Nevertheless today all the cardinals and ambassadors, those of Venice and of Milan, went out to meet him; they spoke to His Majesty thus on horseback. By God's grace the negotiation of Messer Giulio has once more been taken up, and it will be negotiated together with the Venetians. It is much hoped that the matter will [...] well. I am staying here to wait whether the Duke will have to come here or not. I have found Messer Alessandro Atavante and Lobino, [qal] knows the steward of the Most Reverend Trivulzio. Until you have your [ri] notice, I [?] through Messer [sifione] that, with whom the matter of Messer Giulio went, he will be given [mali ere], and I believe it will be [qaella] dongari, and that you will at once have the red hat. I gave Atavante to understand in discourse [what] was done by the Emperor's council, so that, if ill luck willed that the matter of Messer [?Giulio] did not turn out well and it went into the Pope's power, of elelere others, you would wish to keep some provost with Messer Iacopo Salviati, so that, when the matter does not succeed with Messer Giulio, he will speak to the Pope for you; and that if the matter should go badly, he should promise him ten thousand scudi of income a year [...] and nothing else. Bologna, the fourth of [...] November. Postscript: For many days I have had no letters from you; [I would like to] have the receipt of this [fte]. Key: tomokiyo_key.png , key.md

Quant a cestuy cy, il n'y a point de doubte qu'il n'ait faict et ne face ce qu'il pourra pour entretenir la Ligue, [?ruine] ung party en France qui maintient la grandeur de son maistre, jusques a luy conseiller de n'y espargner ny [?calomnies] ny flatteries, [?faisant] bien grandes affaires a ung homme pauvre, plain d'ardeur et desir de choses grandes. Translation n25_en.md # No. 25, BnF fr. 3623 f. 38r, 5 June 1590: English > Michael Brackx (issue #96, 24 Oct 2026), with Codex; uncertainty marks match the French. ### A The despatch of 31 May which I sent you by a boy belonging to the s[ieur] de Vaumas will have fully informed you of the state of this army. The King went alone to Senlis and from there again to Compiegne with M[onsieu]r the M[arshal] de Biron. You will have heard what he had done at Crecy and Conflans, and [what] M[onsieu]r the M[arshal] d'Aumont had done at S[ain]t Cloud, and to what condition Paris had been reduced, held by [?weight] and [?finger], where it is hoped that famine and division will serve our purpose. ### B Of [?Lamour], whatever the legate and the ambassador of Spain may do, who are said to be at the end of their resources. As for the latter, there is no doubt that he has done and will do what he can to sustain the League, [?ruin] a party in France which maintains his master's greatness, even advising him to spare neither [?slanders] nor flatteries, [?making] very great affairs for a poor man full of ardour and desire for great things. Spain will never find rest with what he [?] [?] treats openly. ### C As for the other, we consider him at a loss, since we know that the Pope no longer wishes to hear of the League, still less of the Spaniard, and that when he is pressed on the matter he answers that he awaits what the H[oly] Spirit will inspire in him. [?He] has had a bull published to urge the peoples to pray to God that He may impart the graces of His H[oly] Spirit to him in these affairs. ### D You will also have been informed of the gathering the Duke of Mayenne is making of his forces, which are weak, and of how we are assembling [ours] from every quarter. [?As] for the advice I have given you about this, if I have added words of liberty that were too explicit, please blame only the affection I bear to [your] greatness. Whatever you decide on this, hold it certain that we shall no longer hazard anything on the [?uncertain] outcome of a battle, following your judicious advice. We have exerted ourselves enough to have established ourselves and acquired among foreigners the reputation of a great and magnanimous cap[tain], and among our enemies that of a bold and valiant man. ### E You have heard of the revocation of the passport granted to the Primate of Lyon, with [?force] and [?clamours] of deputies of the Paris law courts and of [?burghers] of the city. This refusal was borne so impatiently by the [said] primate of Lyon that he almost lost control of himself. He had asked M[onsieu]r de la Guiche to procure him a passport to retire to his house, which he would have had granted, such is his influence, if the [said] primate of Lyon had been willing to promise to abandon the League, which he would not do. [our] army from Germany is preparing for the other descent. ### F We approve the breaking of the edict [of] union. I [?learnt] [something] clearly. What misfortune! You would do well to [?consider] breaking this move. A governor’s plan for war with Britain during the Dutch crisis, enciphered in Bouillé’s cipher of 1778, which the margin names. Brice Dudout read it with that key unchanged: 298 of 302 words. 709.587.300.46.250.741.255.38.545.19 … si la [guerre] avec l’[Angleterre] avoit lieu il seroit … Martinique → Versailles · Bouillé’s numerical nomenclator of 1778 · 2 Nov 1787 · read with known key Damas to the minister of the Navy, 1787 Go to the full text ↓ A governor’s plan for war with Britain, enciphered in a cipher nine years old, whose margin names it and which the key of Bouillé’s letters reads unchanged. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 2 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (95% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (95% of the cipher) The letter The comte de Damas, governor general of the Windward Islands, to the Secretary of State for the Navy, 2 November 1787 (no. 501), a signed original that sends news from the British islands. Where Archives nationales d’outre-mer, COL C8 B 16, no. 61 (images FRANOM23_C8B_16_0260–0261). The inventory says “Nouvelles des îles anglaises (chiffrée)”. The cipher The margin reads “Chiffre du 25 avril 1778”: Bouillé’s numerical nomenclator of 1778–1782, still in use nine years later. It has its own page . How it was deciphered Key K6, rebuilt from Bouillé’s glossed letters and frozen, was first checked on this letter: it covers 92% of the groups, the most frequent numbers (361, 817, 607, 250) are Bouillé’s, and “M. le comte de Grasse” is enciphered as in 1779. It read a held-out letter against its modern translation at 0.894 of words, against at most 0.182 for 200 permuted keys. What it says If war came, Damas would seize Dominica. He lacks siege and field artillery, orders and money, and he gives the garrisons of the islands. Still open Four groups are unresolved (269, 464, 686, 190). The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout checked the cipher, applied the key and read the letter, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

In September and October 1787 the Prussian intervention in Holland, backed by Britain, raised fears of an Anglo-French war. Damas sends news from Dominica in clear, then switches to cipher to say what he would do if war came and what he lacks. He does not yet know that France backed down at the end of October. He plans the defence of the islands France held after 1783 (Saint Lucia and Tobago) and thinks of retaking Dominica, which went back to Britain at the peace of 1783 after Bouillé had taken it in 1778. The artillery he lacks had left with de Grasse’s squadron in 1781–82.

The key is K6 of the Bouillé 1778 page : 490 values from the pencil glosses of seven letters of 1779–80, frozen before any validation. Before reading, the identity of the cipher was checked, and the numbers decipher consistently with it. We re-applied K6 to the transcription on 2 November 2026: 445 of 465 numbers agree with the decryption file and 6 are not in the key; the rest are marked alternates and unresolved groups.

Of the 302 words of the cipher part (463 numbers), 298 are read as sense (98.7%): 281 certain, 5 probable and 12 restored. Every probable or restored word is justified in the notes. For example, 300 is restored as guerre in “si la guerre avec l’Angleterre avoit lieu” because the same phrase recurs below with the glossed 710 for guerre . The full French reading and an English translation are under Full texts.

Four groups are unresolved: 269 (“vous verrez par les 269s que l’on prend dans cette isle”), 464 (“il faut en 464 un approvisionnement”), 686 (“un approvisionnement de 686 et de boulets”, powder?) and 190 (“à l’190 de la marine”, arsenal?). The probable words are entièrement , j’ai , affûts and attendant , each resting on a number not glossed elsewhere. The transcription was made by AI from the ANOM images and not checked by a person against them here.

situation Reading reading.md # Established text (French) ## Clear opening J’ai l’honneur de vous envoyer la copie des nouvelles qui me parviennent de la Dominique. N’ayant reçu aucun avis de vous, j’y ajoute peu de foi ; cependant j’ai expédié sur-le-champ un bâtiment léger pour Sainte-Lucie et Tabago, afin que les gouverneurs se tiennent sur leurs gardes, sans cependant mettre de l’apparat dans leurs précautions. J’ai fait passer la copie de ces nouvelles à la Guadeloupe et j’ai pris des moyens pour être instruit des mouvements qui pourroient avoir lieu à la Barbade et dans les autres isles angloises. ## Cipher part Si la [guerre] avec l’[Angleterre] avoit lieu, il seroit intéressant de s’emparer de la Dominique pour s’assurer de la communication avec la Guadeloupe, et vous verrez par les ‹269›s que l’on prend dans cette isle qu’il faudra y employer la force et l’art. Je manque {entièrement} d’artillerie de campagne et de siège ; toute celle qui étoit ici est passée sous le Vent pour l’expédition de Saint‹…›, sur l’escadre de M. le comte de Grasse. {J’ai} attendu les ordres que vous m’avez annoncés par votre lettre ‹clear: du 4 août 1786› pour l’approvisionnement des bois de construction nécessaires, [tant] pour les {affûts} à remplacer que pour ceux qui manquent ; et non seulement je n’ai pas reçu [d’]ordres sur cette partie intéressante, mais vous avez réduit depuis les fonds de l’artillerie au simple entretien de paix. Si la guerre survient, il est nécessaire que vous envoyiez un équipage d’artillerie de siège et un de campagne ; je n’ai ici que des pièces du calibre de quatre. Du dernier objet il faut en ‹464› un approvisionnement de ‹686› et de boulets à l’‹190› de la marine. Les isles de Sainte-Lucie et [Tabago] sont sans fortification ; en {attendant} qu’il y ait [lieu] à craindre qu’elles soient attaquées, elles se tiendront sur la défensive, à prévenir un coup de main ; [et] je leur en fournirai les moyens en munitions [et] artillerie. La Guadeloupe a des moyens d’une longue résistance ; sa garnison [et] celle de la Martinique, qui sont au niveau, à l’artillerie près, ne peuvent fournir au plus que huit cents hommes [chacune] sous les armes ; celle de Sainte-Lucie, deux cent trente, [et] celle de [Tabago], cent quatre-vingts, à cause des malades. Voilà quelle est notre situation. ## State of the reading First published decipherment, to our knowledge. Published under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of the words read in their sense. Cipher part (463 numbers, 302 words): 298 words read in their sense (98.7%), of which 281 certain (93.0%), 5 probable {x} (1.7%) and 12 restored from the sense [x] (4.0%); 4 unresolved ‹…› (1.3%): ‹269›, ‹464›, ‹686›, ‹190›. ## Justifications - Probable words {x}, with justification. {entièrement}: ent.788.e.ment, 788 = ièr not attested. {J’ai}: 208, not glossed; same number at the head of Bouillé’s letter no. 259 (“208 l’honneur…”), formula “J’ai”. {affûts}: af.90.s; 241 = af is glossed; 90 not attested. {attendant}: at.te.n.620, 620 = dant not attested. - Words restored [x], with justification. [guerre]: 300 (“si la 300 avec l’741 avoit lieu”); 710 = guerre is glossed, 300 would be a homophone; the same phrase recurs below with 710 (“si la guerre survient”). [Angleterre]: 741, the only possible country in 1787 against the “isles angloises”. [tant]: 762, forced by “… que pour ceux qui manquent”. [d’]: 808 (“je n’ai pas reçu 808 ordres”). [lieu]: 644 (“qu’il y ait 644 à craindre”). [et] (×4): 244, always between two coordinated terms (“munitions 244 artillerie”, “sa garnison 244 celle de la Martinique”, “deux cent trente 244 celle de…”). [chacune]: 493.e (“huit cents hommes 493.e sous les armes”). [Tabago] (×2): 831, paired with St Lucia as in the clear part (“Sainte-Lucie et Tabago”). - Unresolved. ‹269›s (“vous verrez par les 269.s que l’on prend dans cette isle”: “measures”, “dispositions”?); ‹464› (“il faut en 464 un approvisionnement”; 464 = “ar” in a 1779 gloss, which gives no sense here); ‹686› (“un approvisionnement de 686 et de boulets”: powder?); ‹190› (“à l’190 de la marine”: arsenal?). Translation translation.md # English translation (cipher part) If war with England were to break out, it would be worth seizing Dominica to secure communication with Guadeloupe; you will see from the […] being taken on that island that force and skill will be needed there. I am entirely without field and siege artillery: all that was here went to leeward for the expedition of Saint-[…], with the comte de Grasse’s squadron. I have waited for the orders you announced in your letter of 4 August 1786 for the supply of timber, both for the gun carriages to be replaced and for those that are missing; not only have I received no orders on this important matter, but you have since cut the artillery funds to bare peacetime upkeep. If war comes, you must send me a siege train and a field train: I have here only 4-pounders. For this last point, there must be […] a supply of […] and of shot at the […] of the navy. St Lucia and Tobago have no fortifications; until there is reason to fear an attack, they will stay on the defensive against a surprise attack, and I shall give them the means in ammunition and artillery. Guadeloupe can hold out for a long time; its garrison and that of Martinique, equal except in artillery, can each put at most 800 men under arms; that of St Lucia 230, and that of Tobago 180, because of the sick. That is our situation. Key: key.tsv

Erving, American chargé d’affaires at Madrid, to Secretary of State James Madison, 10 August 1807, with a postscript of the 11th: private letter No. 24, the duplicate, headed “In Mr Pinkneys Cypher, the Cypher of ye Legation”. Where National Archives, RG 59, Diplomatic Despatches, Spain, vol. 10, on microfilm M31 reel 12, frames 0362–0367 (catalog NAID 188605361). Founders Online prints the letter decoded, without the code groups (early access 99-01-02-1993). Not in the catalogue and not on DECODE. The cipher The legation code Charles Pinckney used at Madrid: numbers up to about 1,700 for words, syllables and letters, partly in alphabetical runs, written between dots inside the clear text. A caret over a group makes it plural. How it was deciphered The 1,145 groups were transcribed from the film and lined up with the Founders text, which gave 414 rows of the code. Of the 47 groups it shares with Jacob Wagner’s 1803 decode of Pinckney’s own despatch, 45 agree and two stay undecided. What it says Godoy paid for the Hanover bargain out of his own funds, sees Hanover handed to Westphalia, “believes that he has been deceived and is furious”, and plans, “as a dernier resort”, an alliance with England. Still open Eight groups that occur only once (633; 632, 455, 1482; 767, 679, 378; one lost in the binding) and 916 in the postscript. Counting conservatively, with hidden digits and emendations also set aside, 94.25% of the groups stand. Credit Feyseel Nur, with Claude Opus 5.5 subagents (transcription, key rebuild, decode); key check against Wagner’s 1803 decode; adversarial review by OpenAI Codex. Contributed in PR #21.

Erving was the American chargé d’affaires at Madrid, and the code he used was the legation’s, from the time of Charles Pinckney, minister there before him. His private letters to Madison were numbered; No. 21 of 24 March 1807, “in the Cypher of the Legation”, is printed from Madison’s own decode and is written up with the 1812 Adams despatch on the legation-codes page . No. 24, of 10 August 1807, opens on the news that the peace (of Tilsit) was signed and asks what it will change between France and Spain. Much of its first six pages is in code. Frame 0362, the first page of the duplicate: “In Mr Pinkneys Cypher, the Cypher of ye Legation”, “No 24”, “Duplicate”. The first code groups follow “The alterations which this Event may produce”: 69. 1651. 32. 424^. 500. 1290. 1343. 1210, IN THE RELAT-IONS BETWEEN FRANCE AND SPAIN. A line further on, the film has “you probably will not annex”. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to Spain, vol. 10, microfilm M31 reel 12, frame 0362 (right page), via catalog.archives.gov NAID 188605361. Two texts of it are at hand: The duplicate on the film. NARA’s microfilm of the Spain despatches (M31 reel 12, frames 0362–0367) has the second copy, marked “Duplicate”, with the code groups in ink and no decode between the lines. The left edge of the third page and the right edge of the fourth are partly hidden in the binding. The Founders text. The Papers of James Madison print the letter in early access on Founders Online (99-01-02-1993) as plain English, decoded, with ten blank gaps ⟨ ⟩ and a few supplied words. They give the source as “DNA: RG 59—DD, Spain” and do not say how the code was decoded. The groups are not printed. The two agree in the slip “my unofficial letter of March 4th” (the image has “March 4”; the letter meant is that of 24 March), and differ in small ways: Founders heads the letter “In the ⟨Cypher⟩ of the Legation” and prints “you will not probably annex” where the film has “you probably will not annex”. Several Founders brackets fall where the film loses digits in the binding (⟨ ⟩ has been informed, deceive him ⟨ ⟩, ⟨Prince⟩, ⟨a⟩gents). Whether the editors decoded this duplicate or took their text from another copy is not settled here; nothing below depends on it.

The code is a single list of numbered words, syllables and letters. Groups are written with dots between them inside the clear sentences, and a word may take several groups: 724. 549. 934 is Ha-nov-er , 1552. 66 establish-ing , 1684. 110. 1432. 368. 624 Ca-ta-lo-ni-a . The commonest are 1651 the , 133 of , 244 to , 1484 is , 1343 and and 926 he . A small triangle or caret over a group marks a plural: 424^ ions , 1593^ tions , 580^ ports . Parts of the list run in alphabetical order, which helps place a group seen once: Groups Values 742–745 at, ate, ated, ation 870–880 their, them, then, … there, therefore, these, they, thin, thing 884, 887 this, tho’ 1340, 1341, 1343 an, ance, and Higher up the order breaks (1661 Prince , 1680 can , 1686 by , 1688 but ), so the code is only partly alphabetical. Erving made slips of his own: 66 ( ing ) for in three times, 665 for 605 in change , 870 their for they , and in Hanover he wrote 724. 549. 943 twice and 724. 549. 934 once, while 943 is ly in un-friend-ly . In March he had written Hanover 724. 529. 934. The rebuilt list ( key_pinckney.tsv ) has 414 rows: the 395 numbers that occur in this letter and 19 more from Wagner’s page, each with where it is attested.

Decoded groups in capitals, Erving’s clear words in lower case; [?] a group with no value, {…} a conjecture The letter is about Manuel Godoy, the Prince of Peace, and what the peace of Tilsit meant for him. First the Hanover bargain of the spring, which Erving had reported in March: I did not then know what I now learn that a considerable SUM OF MONEY WAS PAID BY THE PRINCE (OUT OF HIS OWN FUNDS) OVER AND ABOVE the STIPULATION FOR TROOPS. THE TROOPS MARCHED and we read of THEIR ARRIVAL ON THE ODER. … but THE war concluded it is found more convenient TO ADD HANOVER to the KINGDOM OF WESTPHALIA and the PRINCE IS TOLD that HE shall HAVE A TERRITORY somewhere ELSE. It may be the intention OF THE EMPEROR TO GIVE HIM one, but THE PRINCE does NOT THINK so; he believes that he has been DECEIVED AND is FURIOUS. Already a project is formed OF ESTABLISHING A KINGDOM OF EBRO including CATALONIA NAVARRE AND BISCAY and the plan OF INVADING PORTUGAL which during the war SERVED only AS A MEANS OF PROCURING MONEY from time to time IS NOW seriously RENEWED with a view to ACTUAL CONQUEST … Portugal has been told to close its ports to the English. Godoy is still flattered with EXPECTATIONS of personal aggrandisement, but now begins to see that he will not be forgiven for his [?] intrigues, and “HIS actual determination IS TO RESIST”. Then the counter-project, on the third page: Frame 0363, right page: “… 1290. 1544. 251. 244. 940 … mediation. 157. 926 fails there 892. as a 491. 868. 934. 1154. 691. 111. 926. 1411. 471. 1340. 1495 of some sort 1407. 940! This is a …”, that is: France HOSTILE TO ENGLAND … IF HE fails there THEN as a DERNIER RESORT HE WILL MAKE AN ALLIANCE of some sort WITH ENGLAND! The left edge of the page is lost in the binding. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to Spain, vol. 10, microfilm M31 reel 12, frame 0363 (right page), via catalog.archives.gov NAID 188605361. IN THE mean TIME he has formed a COUNTER PROJECT. The first part OF HIS PLAN IS BY representing the vast [?] [?] [?] SPAIN BY THE WAR TO obtain the permission OF FRANCE TO MAKE A SEPARATE PEACE WITH ENGLAND AND NOT suspecting doubtless that RUSSIA HAS HERSELF any understanding WITH FRANCE HOSTILE TO ENGLAND HE HOPES TO obtain THIS POINT THRO’ HER mediation. IF HE fails there THEN as a DERNIER RESORT HE WILL MAKE AN ALLIANCE of some sort WITH ENGLAND! This is a COURSE OF SO DESPERATE a CHARACTER that it is scarcely to be BELIEVED IN. Erving has this “from the very [best?] AUTHORITY (not from HIMSELF)”. Godoy regrets sending his troops to Hanover, has no expectation of seeing them again, and wishes he might “QUIETLY RETIRE FROM HIS STATION”. The fourth and fifth pages are a portrait of the French ambassador, François de Beauharnais: A NARROW LOW INTRIGUING POLITICIAN, AFFECTING CANDOR, [?] perfectly false, assuming TO CONTROUL EVEN OPINION BY THE SUPERIORITY OF HIS TALENTS, THO’ certainly destitute of any particular advantage IN THAT RESPECT; full OF HIMSELF, consummately VAIN AND OSTENTATIOUS, AND IN HIS CONDUCT TO THE PRINCE inSOLENT AND overBEARING. THIS ILL suits with THE PRINCE WHO HIMSELF HAS VANITY Enough to think that HE IS is the greatest MAN IN EUROPE EXCEPT BUONAPARTE … The sixth page ends on the thought that France may drive “THE ROYAL family OF SPAIN AS WELL AS OF PORTUGAL TO ESTABLISH THEIR EMPIRES ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE ATLANTIC”. The rest of the letter is in clear. The postscript of the 11th goes back into code: Spain is to send an army into Portugal and French troops will take its place; the Emperor has written to the King, advising him to take the Prince of Asturias into his confidence; and Godoy, talking to the Prussian chargé d’affaires, says that “IF THE KING HAD NO successOR HE THE PRINCE WOULD risque EVERY THING TO KEEP BUONAPARTE OUT OF THE COUNTRY”, but that, unpopular and blamed for every distress of the country, he has “NO course … BUT IMPLICITLY TO SUBMIT to all THAT MAY BE DEMANDED”. Eleven weeks later the treaty of Fontainebleau (27 October 1807) divided Portugal and promised Godoy a principality in the south of it.

The groups were transcribed from the six frames and set against the Founders text phrase by phrase, so that each group took the value Founders gives at that place; a value fixed in one place was then carried to every other occurrence and tested there. This is a key recovered from a plaintext found elsewhere: most values rest on the edition, and the work cannot be a blind test of them. Two checks stand outside it. Wagner’s 1803 decode. Pinckney’s own despatch of 22 February 1803 (M31 reel 7, frame 0348) is in the same code, and Jacob Wagner, chief clerk of the State Department, wrote its decode between the lines. It shares 47 group numbers with Erving’s letter. For 45 of them the values agree (217 would , 1218 some , 872 then , 748. 887 au-tho , 1402 wor , 1598 tain , 301 give …). Two are undecided: 584 ( na in the key, nation in the alignment, Wagner’s nations? ) and 943, which in Wagner’s line stands between friend and ship with no word of its own. Pinckney to Madison, Madrid, 22 February 1803, frame 0348: Wagner’s decode over the code, “and that I was authorised … 748. 887 [au-tho-]”, “some propositions 1218. 1640. 1147. 248△”, “was sure she would give them the most 390. 116. 1370. 217. 301. 871. 1651. 718”, “I then 1147. 872”. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to Spain, vol. 6, microfilm M31 reel 7, frame 0348 (right page), via catalog.archives.gov NAID 188604008. The March letter. Erving’s No. 21 of 24 March, with Madison’s decode ( targets/erving1807 ), gives further pairs. With Wagner it supports 716 of the 1,145 groups (62.5%, 141 different numbers) under a strict match; a value that recurs with the same sense elsewhere in this letter, or has that outside support, covers 908 (79.3%). The rest, about one group in five, is fitted to the Founders text alone. The transcription. 53 groups, from legible stretches of four frames and the three spellings of Hanover , were re-read on the images by the reviewer: no digit differed. That is a purposive sample, not an error rate for the whole. The review. OpenAI Codex reviewed the files adversarially and found the result confirmed but overstated ( codex_review/review.md ). Its corrections are the figures used on this page: 45 of 47 Wagner groups (not 46), 79.3% recurrence or outside support (not 80.5%), and six firm gap fills rather than ten.

Of the 1,145 groups in the alignment, 1,136 have a value (99.2%) and 1,125 (98.3%) give sense without the eleven marked conjectures. Grades as in the repository’s conventions: most values are C, from the known plaintext; M uncertain; I inferred from context or from the alphabetical order. No value (each occurs once): 633 (“his [?] intrigues”); 632, 455, 1482 in “destitute of ?-r-i-?-?”; 767, 679, 378 before “Spain by the war”; a group ending in 4 hidden in the binding (“affecting candor, [?] perfectly false”); and 916 after “the Prince of [Asturias]” in the postscript, where its usual value as makes no sense. Two positions not in the alignment : after 1114. 244 (“advised him to”) on frame 0367, where a hole in the leaf may or may not hide a group, and the start of the last line of the postscript page, half covered by the facing leaf, probably 244 to (“submit [to] all”). Counted, they make the transcription 1,147 groups and the share that gives sense 98.1%. M : 368 best ; 586. 1424 narrow low (Founders has the words, the split between the two groups is assumed); 66 West in West-ph-al-ia (66 is ing elsewhere); 169. 80. 115 d’af-fai-res ; [x]47 Asturias ; 1543 t in except ; 310, which is ceiv in deceived and liev in believed ; and the emendations of Erving’s slips (943 twice, 66 three times, 665, 870). I : EXPECTATIONS (176. 979. 1593^, fitted inside a Founders gap); 878. 1394 they are , placed by the alphabetical run after 877 these (Founders: “whatever these are”); and the 37 groups whose first digits are hidden in the binding, restored from context (among them the 1578 of THAT GOVERNMENT and 13[?] in alarms ). The conservative count. Setting aside the conjectures, the 37 restored groups and nine emended occurrences, the review counts 1,081 of 1,147 positions (94.25%). That is a sensitivity count, not a measured error rate; the excluded groups mostly give sense. The Founders source. How the editors decoded the letter, and from which copy, is not known; the ten blanks may reflect the binding of this duplicate or the state of another copy.
