Two cipher passages from the young Ferdinand to his father John II (BNE MSS/20211/64 and /73), each in its own homophonic alphabet. Both keys were rebuilt from the interlinear notes of a second hand, the 1474 one aligned on the clear paragraph at the foot of the page. Ferdinand brings 800 horse for the relief of Perpignan, and a year later asks that Mossèn Santcliment be sent to Naples about his sister Juana’s marriage. Contributed by Michael Brackx; two signs of the 1473 line 5 and two doubtful words of 1474 stay open. … e porque agora me puede mandar lo que acerca su servicio tengo de fazer … acorde de lo certificar de la gente que comigo trayo Hostalric and Zaragoza → John II of Aragon · two homophonic letter substitutions set inside clear Spanish and Catalan · 1473 and 1474 · key recovered from adjacent plaintext Ferdinand to John II, 1473 and 1474 from Ferdinand the Catholic → to John II of Aragon Go to the full text ↓ Two cipher passages from the young Ferdinand to his father, the first on the troops he is raising to relieve Perpignan and the second on his sister Juana’s marriage at Naples, read from the notes and the clear lines on the same pages. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 30 October 2026 · updated 2 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (97% of the cipher) Contributed by Michael Brackx (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (97% of the cipher) The letters Two letters from Ferdinand, king of Sicily and heir of Aragon, to his father John II: Hostalric, 5 June 1473, and Zaragoza, 3 November 1474. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20211/64 (BNE Digital bdh0000186643) and MSS/20211/73 (bdh0000186628); catalogue item 857. A third cipher letter of 1470 (/56) is transcribed only. The cipher Two different homophonic substitutions of letters, with several signs for each vowel, one place sign (Barcelona) in 1473, and a null and a sign for qu in 1474; the cipher is set inside the clear text. How it was deciphered A second hand wrote words and single letters over the signs. The 1473 key was rebuilt from them and extended by sense; the 1474 key was taken from them and then aligned on the clear paragraph at the foot of the page, which is the plaintext. What it says 1473: Ferdinand brings more than 500 horse from Aragon, Castile and Valencia, 800 in all with 100 men-at-arms, for the relief of Perpignan. 1474: he is astonished that the infanta Juana’s marriage has not been broken off and asks that Mossèn Santcliment go to Naples. Credit Transcription, both keys and both readings by Michael Brackx, working with Claude Code (pull request #195). Still open Two signs in the 1473 line 5; two look-alike signs whose values rest on sense; rompido and promendo in 1474; the 1470 letter.

MSS/20211/64 is a letter from Ferdinand, then king of Sicily, to his father John II, written at Hostalric on 5 June 1473. John II was besieged at Perpignan by the French, and the cipher passage, nine lines of the recto, reports the troops Ferdinand is bringing: his continos (the paid household guard of the Castilian crown) and men from Castile, more than five hundred horse from Aragon, and the Valencians, some already at Barcelona and the rest within the week, eight hundred horse in all with a hundred men-at-arms. MSS/20211/73 was written at Zaragoza on 3 November 1474. Its cipher passage has eleven lines. Ferdinand has learned that the marriage of the infanta Juana, his half-sister, “no se es rompido” as negotiated, and he is astonished; he asks that, if anyone is sent to Naples on the matter, it be Mossèn Santcliment, so that his own affairs are handled with the others. Juana married Ferrante I of Naples in 1476–77. A third cipher letter of Ferdinand to John II, MSS/20211/56 (Dueñas, 12 November 1470), is in a different system with a faint pencil decipherment; it is transcribed and not attacked. Galende Díaz (1994) lists /56 and /73 as ciphered letters of Ferdinand to John II, with no key; /64 is not in his list. The search made for this reading found no edition or decipherment of /64 or /73, but it missed two sources, found afterwards and not used. DECODE has marked both letters Decrypted since 2019 (R1183, R1177), with no document listed on the record, so that status may reflect only the interlinear notes. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s 2018 article reconstructs ciphers Ferdinand used in his 1470s letters to John II; it has not been read here, so whether it covers these two letters, and whether its keys agree, is open. This may not be a first reading.

A homophonic substitution of letters, 39 kinds of sign as transcribed and about 30 with a value, set inside the clear text. The vowels and c have several signs each; one place sign, a long s joined to an i with a cross-bar, stands for Barcelona; there is no other nomenclator sign. Signs that looked alike were separated at 12× magnification: 3 is h and 3- is y , T is r in 8 of 8 places and TT is s in 13 of 13. The key was rebuilt from the second hand’s interlinear notes ( certificar dela gente , trayo , continos , de castilla , de aragon , mas de quinientos , de cavallo , comigo and others, with single letters on ruled guidelines over the signs) and extended by sense. The decoder prints both values where a sign has two, and the raw decode is in the repository untouched; the reading below normalises it. … e porque agora me puede mandar lo que acerca su servicio tengo de fazer, acorde de lo certificar de la gente que comigo trayo, que ahora entre los [?mios] continuos e los que de Castilla c[…]o viene, e los de Aragón, más de quinientos de cavallo. E los valencianos son ya; algunos dellos llegados en Barcelona, e todos los otros hi serán por toda esta semana que viene; en manera que todos [?juntos], estimo, fan los que comigo irán ochocientos de cavallo, en que havrá ciento hombres de armas. Vea V. S. la forma que devo tener …

A homophonic substitution of its own, not the 1473 alphabet: bar signs, dotted signs, a null (an undotted A ) and a sign for qu . The sign 4 gives a , r and c , probably three look-alike signs. The 1473 key does not read /73 or /56. The key was recovered in two steps. A key of 19 signs read from the interlinear letters alone decoded no res menos se , matrimoni… infanta mi hermana no se , mossen s… , and the same words begin the clear paragraph at the foot of the recto. align1474.py then aligned the 310 signs with the paragraph’s 325 letters and re-estimated the key. Because the paragraph is the plaintext, this is a key recovered from adjacent plaintext, not an independent break, and polyphony of 20% of read tokens means the validation test does not apply. No res menos, senyor, yo he sabido como el matrimonio de la infanta mi hermana no se es [?rompido], segunt stava praticado e concertado, de que me so admirado. Y pues assi es, supplico humilmente a vuestra alteza le remede de lo que me [?promendo], que si aya hombre alguno a Napols por estos fechos, que vaya mossen Santcliment, porque yendo ell, mis fechos se facan a bueltas de los otros, e assi se seguira grant benefficio.

1473, line 5. Two signs ( H C ) after de Castilla : C occurs only here and the sense wants con migo or similar. Open. 1473, two look-alike signs. The sigma-like 6 is a in four words but i/j in mios and juntos , and the plain p stands for c , o and once a . Thirteen values were chosen by sense. The 1085-pixel scan does not separate the forms; a better image would. 1474, rompido and promendo . The first cipher sign of rompido is c elsewhere, while the clear text and the interlinear letter both give r ; promendo is so written in both texts and its sense is not settled. The place sign near a Napols and the signs met once or twice are too few to fix. Reading status. The reading checker finds half the sentences of the 1473 passage and 43% of the 1474 passage clean; the 1474 shortfall is probably the Catalan-Aragonese spellings ( senyor , fechos , facan ) against a Spanish model. A reader has gone through both readings as sentences, but neither has been checked against the image by a person. Other letters. Ferdinand’s other letters to John II in the same BNE series (/57, /80, /82, /99, /105, /120, /123) have not been checked for cipher in either alphabet.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Hostalric, 5 June 1473 (MSS/20211/64) read in part Ferdinand reports the troops he brings for the relief of Perpignan: his continos and the men from Castile, more than 500 horse from Aragon, the Valencians (some already at Barcelona), 800 horse in all with 100 men-at-arms. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (97% here); the holes are marked in the reading. Where Printed in figures in Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat , t. II (1819), p. 283; the editor could not translate it. The cipher The 367-group petit chiffre of the governors of Pignerol, the small companion of the 1691 Grand Chiffre. How it was read Louvois’ letter to d’Herleville of 6 September 1690, printed with its translation in t. I, shares 72 groups. Aligning one stretch recovered 167 of the 179 groups in use. What it says Feuquières is ready, expects no serious defence of Veillane, and will attack at two points while keeping the dragoons out of the castle. Still open Twelve singleton groups and the opening and closing nulls; the text was not checked against the original at Vincennes. Credit Bazeries deciphered it in 1893 and never published the text.

Antoine de Pas, marquis de Feuquières, took over the governorship of Pignerol at the end of the 1690 campaign from the marquis d’Herleville. In January 1691 he pressed Catinat, commanding in Piedmont from Suze, to let him surprise Veillane (Avigliana), a Savoyard post half way between Suze and Turin: five hundred Germans of Lorraine and the Croix-Blanche in the castle, four companies of Macel’s dragoons in the town. Catinat consented on condition of directing the attack himself, sent his “Mémoire pour l’entreprise de Veillane” on 19 January (rendezvous at the head of the ponds, the roads by Gumiane and Javan or by Trane, four days’ bread, tools, grenades, twenty horses to be asked of Feuquières for the cannon), and the two agreed by letter to march on the evening of the 26th and strike at daybreak on the 27th. The attack failed and the two blamed each other for the rest of their lives. This despatch is Feuquières’ side of the arrangement. Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat , t. II (1819), p. 283: the despatch as printed (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, bsb10720287). Three figures were corrected against the page images. Image: Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat, t. II (1819), p. 283, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek bsb10720287 scan 317, via the MDZ. The key came from volume I of the same edition. Among Louvois’ letters on the contributions of Piedmont the editor printed one to d’Herleville, “gouverneur de Pignerol, sur Mondovi”, dated Versailles 6 September 1690, whose body is in figures (183 groups, none above 366), followed by a traduction . The two Grand Chiffre letters to Catinat of the same days, also printed with translations, decode with Bazeries’ table and show that these translations are the clerks’ free renderings, not word-for-word decipherments. T. I p. 141: the end of the d’Herleville cipher and the beginning of its translation. The cipher has si vous croyez , Mondevis , razer ; the translation modernises to si vous jugez , Mondovi , raser . Image: Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat, t. I (1819), p. 141, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek bsb10720286, via the MDZ.

One code, two letters. 72 of the d’Herleville letter’s 91 groups occur in the Feuquières letter; both have 46 % of their tokens on groups below 100; twenty bigrams and the trigram 25 355 42 ( de Mon-de [vis]) are common to both. The union is 179 groups over 601 tokens, within Bazeries’ figure of 367 for the petit chiffre of 1691. Design, from the Grand Chiffre. Bazeries says the small cipher “ne différait du grand que par son nombre de groupes”, and so it proves: letters with two to four homophones each (i/j and u/v counted as one letter), consonant-vowel syllables, a stock of word stems ( de , que , les , pour , tout , mesme , comme , lettre , honneur , le roy , Monsieur , M. de Catinat , scavoi[r] ), and nulls doubling as full stops. Numbers and place names are spelled: dix , vingt-quatre , quatre-vingts , ve-il-la-ne , ia-va-n , Saint-Ambroise . No order. Neither block is alphabetical; the numbering is a two-part list, as in the Grand Chiffre.

Every automatic route failed, and the failures are documented in the repository: a beam aligner for exact known plaintext (which recovers 60 of 69 units on synthetic encodings) finds no consistent alignment of the d’Herleville cipher with its printed translation, because the translation paraphrases and because u and v are one letter; annealers scored on a French 7-gram model with the Grand Chiffre inventory, on the translation’s own 5-grams, or with a partial key fixed all return fluent nonsense, as they do on a matched synthetic control. The key was then built by hand. The last 31 groups of the d’Herleville letter can be divided in only one way into Grand-Chiffre-style units for comment aura réussi vostre entreprise sur le chasteau de Villefranche in which every repeated group carries the same unit (91 = t twice, 184 = au twice, 135 = ra twice, 21 = s twice, 56 = le twice, 101 = c twice). Carried into the Feuquières letter those units gave heures du matin , du vingt-quatre , m’escrire , duplicata ; each word fixed further groups; the thrice-repeated 301 151 310 became Veillane ; 150 = ve gave enleveront , trouve , doivent ; 243 = ns gave dragons , chemins , maisons ; the clause faire passer à … gave Saint-Ambroise , the village between Avigliana and Rivoli. English translation Feuquières to Catinat, Pignerol, 25 January 1691. I receive, Sir, at ten in the morning the letter you do me the honour of writing on the twenty-fourth, with the duplicate. You will have seen [by] the return of the courier that I tell you […] to carry out your orders. [By] this you will know that I am quite ready, [and] that no one thinks […] the […] that you [wish?] to begin them. [At] Veillane, persuaded that they will carry off the [post] at the noise of the attack on Veillane, the few men there are and the ways of getting in all must make one believe that they will not come to defend it seriously. I do not at all know by what way to pass the eighty troopers you ask [of us] to Saint-Ambroise; the roads for getting there from the Javan side cut across […]. Approaching Veillane one finds two roads, one of which leads you to the faubourg of the Three Crowns, the other to the houses […] and along the pond. I shall attack [at] two points, and above all […] shall take care that the dragoons cannot escape me. […] Louvois to d’Herleville, Versailles, 6 September 1690. […] I am writing to M. de Catinat that the King permitted you to demand the contribution of the country of Mondovì, and that if you believe it suits the King’s service to exempt them from it, even to allow the inhabitants of the said country to raze the citadel of the said Mondovì, to do so. — I shall await with impatience the arrival of the next post to learn how your enterprise against the castle of Villafranca will have succeeded. “Troopers” renders maistres , the period word for a mounted soldier; enlever le poste , to carry off a post, is the technical term for surprising and taking a garrison; Villefranche is Villafranca Piemonte, which d’Herleville took from Pignerol on 2 September 1690. The Feuquières letter answers Catinat’s letter of the 24th, not the memoir of the 19th directly, and it is written the day before the march. The eighty maistres (troopers) are Catinat’s request, to be posted at Sant’Ambrogio on the Turin side to cut off the garrison’s relief and retreat; Feuquières does not see how to get them there unseen, because the roads from Javan cross the approach. His two roads into Avigliana (one to the faubourg, one to the houses along the pond) are Catinat’s “se saisir des Capucins et du faubourg” and “la teste des estangs”. The last sentence states the aim of the operation as Feuquières later described it in his Mémoires : “ce régiment de dragons qu’on vouloit enlever dans la ville” must not be allowed to retire into the castle. On the 27th it did, because the two columns did not arrive together.

Twelve groups have no value (9, 19, 54, 122, 132, 194, 257, 271, 292, 333, 353 and the opening and closing groups taken as nulls). All occur once or twice; nothing in either letter fixes them. Des Trois Couronnes is the reading that fits 237 322 46 280 153 78 113 51 310 200 (des t-ro-is co-u-ro-n-ne-s) after fauxbourg ; a faubourg or inn of that name at Avigliana has not been verified. 241 reads vous in three places ( que je vous dis , l’un vous conduit ) but gives que vous vous demandez in the fourth; nous is possible. Two clerk’s slips are treated as such: ordi-au-i-re for ordinaire and du-i-t for dudit in the d’Herleville letter. The originals are in the Archives du dépôt de la guerre at Vincennes (vol. 1079 holds Catinat’s report of 29 January on the same affair); Bazeries’ own decipherment, if it survives, is in his papers there. Neither has been seen.

Translation translation_en.md # English translation of both letters, copied verbatim from NOTES.md (section 'English translation'). ## English translation > **Feuquières to Catinat, Pignerol, 25 January 1691.** I receive, Sir, at ten in the morning the letter you do me the > honour of writing on the twenty-fourth, with the duplicate. You will have seen [by] the return of the courier that I > tell you [...] to carry out your orders. [By] this you will know that I am quite ready, [and] that no one thinks [...] > the [...] that you [wish?] to begin them. [At] Veillane, persuaded that they will carry off the [post] at the noise > of the attack on Veillane, the few men there are and the ways of getting in all must make one believe that they will > not come to defend it seriously. I do not at all know by what way to pass the eighty troopers you ask [of us] to > Saint-Ambroise; the roads for getting there from the Javan side cut across [...]. Approaching Veillane one finds two > roads, one of which leads you to the faubourg of the Three Crowns, the other to the houses [...] and along the pond. > I shall attack [at] two points, and above all [...] shall take care that the dragoons cannot escape me. [...] > **Louvois to d'Herleville, Versailles, 6 September 1690.** [...] I am writing to M. de Catinat that the King > permitted you to demand the contribution of the country of Mondovì, and that if you believe it suits the King's > service to exempt them from it, even to allow the inhabitants of the said country to raze the citadel of the said > Mondovì, to do so. — I shall await with impatience the arrival of the next post to learn how your enterprise > against the castle of Villafranca will have succeeded. *Maistres* = mounted soldiers; *enlever le poste* = to surprise and take a garrison; Villefranche = Villafranca Piemonte, taken by d'Herleville from Pignerol on 2 September 1690. De Parigi li XX d'ottobre 1568. Io ho ricevuto la lettera dell'Alteza vostra, la quale veramente mi è ben stata di grande honore et consolatione, et inteso il favore che li è piaciuto fare al capitano Gio. Battista Ronchi, di che humilmente gli ne baccio le mani. Ho anco ricevuto con detta sua lettera quella del cardinale di Lorena, et l'ho data in mano propria a Sua Signoria Illustrissima quale m'ha fatto questa risposta, che non sapeva che la Maestà della Regina havesse fatto tale promessa a Vostra Alteza, che se l'havesse saputo gli l'havrebbe detto, ma che glie ne parlarebbe, et quello che Sua Maestà li dicesse me lo referirebbe. Non trovò comodità, come Sua Signoria Illustrissima dice, la prima volta di far questo officio, ma la seconda m'ha mandato a dire per il mio secretario che ha mostrato et letta la lettera tutta a longo al Re et alla Regina, et li hanno detto che havranno matura consideratione su tutto, et che li dritti et ragioni sarano sì ben guardati che si havra occasione di contentamento, che non mi pare che siano se non parole generali, et non si sa per ancor che le loro Maestà n'habbino fatto far scusa alcuna con il Signor Duca per lettere, come mi pare che dovria portare la natura d'un negocio simile, perchè almeno si vedesse in scrittura ciò che dicono non volerli fare preiudicio. Mostrai detta lettera di Vostra Alteza a messer Annibale, et conferii con lui il tutto secondo ch'ella mi comanda, il quale trova ancor lui strano che non siano conservate le sue ragioni tanto ample et chiare al Signor Duca eccellentissimo. Io ho inviato a Sua Eccellenza tutte le lettere che Vostra Alteza m'ha mandate, et similmente quelle del secretario Vergennino?. L'Alteza vostra potra forsi intendere che il Signor Duca si è fatto un poco di male nel braccio destro, et perchè molte volte corre voce maggiore di quello che sono i fatti, affinche l'Alteza vostra sappi che non è cosa d'importanza, le mando qui incluso copia della lettera che in questo proposito m'ha fatto scrivere il Signor Duca, che è quanto ho da scriverle per risposta di dette lettere de vii d'ottobre, alla quale reverentemente bacio le mani. Io ho inteso in questo punto da una persona degna di fede et homo di qualita che la Regina di Spagna è morta di parto, né alcuno per ancora arriva[to a] dare questa nova alle loro Maesta. A group refers to one entry of a numbered list: N underlined : the whole entry (58 = cour , 53 = Vienne , 162 = Elgin ). N,p,q,… : letters p, q, … of the entry, in that order (12 = certain : 12,1,3,2,4 = cret ). k/N (small number at the top left): the entry without its first k letters (127 = attachement : 4/127 = chement ). N (k (small number at the top right): the entry without its last k letters (24 = quelque : 24 (3 = quel ). Marks combine (84 = excellence : 2/84 (3 = celle ). Large parts of the list run alphabetically (10 Angleterre , 11 Berlin , 12 certain , 13 difficile , 14 engager , 15 France … 22 Orange , 23 Prusse , 24 quelque ); above 100 it holds common words and phrases (102 le cabinet , 107 le roi , 132 je compte , 133 on dit ). The same word can be spelled from many entries, so one plaintext has many encipherments.

The first paragraph is not in Colenbrander’s edition; it is decrypted here with the completed word list: La conférence que j’ai annoncée comme devant avoir lieu le huit entre Haugwitz et Elgin s’est effectivement tenue, et Lord Elgin m’a déjà communiqué le résultat, dont je [vais?] rendre compte, tandis que le comte Haugwitz me dit avant-hier au bal du Roi qu’il viendroit un de ces jours chez moi pour me parler sur cet objet. The conference I announced as due to take place on the 8th between Haugwitz and Elgin was indeed held, and Lord Elgin has already told me its outcome, of which I [shall] give account, while Count Haugwitz told me the day before yesterday at the King’s ball that he would come to me one of these days to speak to me about it. The rest of the letter agrees with the print, with small differences (the cipher has “sur cela” where the print has “à cette demande”, and “avoit” for “jouissait de”): Et il a fait à Elgin la communication de l’idée dont nous étions convenus ensemble, de faire une démarche en France pour déterminer cette puissance à consentir à rétablir les affaires dans la République sur l’ancien pied, ajoutant que vu le degré d’influence qu’il pensoit avoir à Paris il espéroit qu’une semblable proposition ne seroit point infructueuse … Lord Elgin lui dit n’être pas à même de pouvoir lui répondre … et qu’avant de prendre des nouvelles instructions à cet égard il désiroit savoir si au cas qu’une ouverture faite par le Roi à Paris fût infructueuse, le Roi la soutiendroit par les armes … Je convins avec Milord Elgin que quand Haugwitz me parlera sur cette matière et me rendra compte de sa conversation avec lui, je tâcherai de l’engager à faire une démarche en France sans avoir l’assurance qu’il désire avoir concernant nos colonies, puisqu’elle ne sauroit jamais nuire, et que si elle étoit de quelque fruit l’utilité seroit considérable, en quoi je me flatte de rencontrer les intentions de mon père, étant encore à remarquer que si le premier pas se fait, il est peut-être possible d’amener le second. The full text is in r2239_reading.txt in the repository. Prussia would sound out France on restoring the Stadholderate; Britain wanted Prussian arms behind it and would not promise the Dutch colonies in advance; the Prince meant to push Haugwitz to try anyway.

R2237’s cipher groups were aligned by hand with the clerk’s decipherment, group by group, and each group turned into constraints on its entry (a letter at a position, or a length). A small script ( wordtable.py ) holds the constraints, reports conflicts and decodes any group file. The rules were worked out from the first lines (90 = même gives 2/90 = me and 1/90 = eme ). An attempt to let a search split the plaintext among the groups failed, because a whole-word group can absorb any string; the alignment was done by hand. R2239 was transcribed from the DECODE photographs into the same notation. The R2237 entries decoded 59% of its groups, and context inference 70%. Colenbrander’s volume II was then searched on the Huygens Institute site. Its no. 752 matches R2239 from the second sentence on, and aligning it fixed the entries that only R2239 uses (208 défavorables , 209 désireroient , 219 instructions , 115 abondance , 202 avantageux , 79 cabale …). Those entries decrypt the unprinted opening.

“dont je [vais] rendre compte”: entry 244 occurs only here, as 244 (5 ; the word is a guess (I). The rest of the opening is graded H: every group decodes, and the entries used there are confirmed by other occurrences. The body is H where cipher and print agree. A few groups in the transcription decode wrongly because a mark was misread (e.g. the entry 87 groups where the print has “les”); the print settles those words. Addressee: DECODE gives William V (the letter is in his papers); Colenbrander prints the text as to Prince Frederik. The phrase “les intentions de mon père” fits a letter to the brother. The line at the foot of R2237 p. 7 after “la proposition” is not decrypted.

Decryption r2239_reading.txt DECODE R2239 — the Hereditary Prince to Prince Frederik (filed with William V's papers), Berlin, 12 March 1796. Reading of 21 Sept 2026. Paragraph 1 (to "sur cet objet") is not in print: read from the cipher alone. From "Et il a fait à Elgin" on, the cipher reading agrees with Colenbrander, Gedenkstukken II no. 752 (pp. 910-911), which was used as a crib; wording is the cipher's where the two differ (noted in brackets). [?] = entry 244, occurring once, not fixed. Berlin 12. Mars 1796. La conférence que j'ai annoncée comme devant avoir lieu le huit entre Haugwitz et Elgin s'est effectivement tenue, et Lord Elgin m'a déjà communiqué le résultat, dont je [vais?] rendre compte, tandis que le comte Haugwitz me dit avant-hier au bal du Roi qu'il viendroit un de ces jours chez moi pour me parler sur cet objet. Et il a fait à Elgin la communication de l'idée dont nous étions convenus ensemble, de faire une démarche en France pour déterminer cette puissance à consentir à rétablir les affaires dans la République sur l'ancien pied, ajoutant que vu le degré d'influence qu'il pensoit avoir à Paris il espéroit qu'une semblable proposition ne seroit point infructueuse, mais que comme la première demande à laquelle il s'attendoit de la part de la France seroit si dans ce cas l'Angleterre rendroit les colonies à la République, il désiroit avoir des assurances préalables pour pouvoir d'autant mieux traiter cette affaire en France. Lord Elgin lui dit n'être pas à même de pouvoir lui répondre [directe]ment sur cela [print: à cette demande], et qu'avant de prendre des nouvelles instructions à cet égard il désiroit savoir si au cas qu'une ouverture faite par le Roi à Paris fût infructueuse, le Roi la soutiendroit par les armes; qu'il croyoit devoir faire cette demande parce qu'elle est dans l'esprit de ses instructions, vu qu'en Angleterre on ne suppose pas la possibilité de pouvoir obtenir quelque chose à moins de soutenir sa demande par les armes, et qu'à cet égard du moins une démonstration [seroit] nécessaire, dont d'après ses derniers ordres il pouvoit assurer que les dépenses seroient amplement restituées à la Prusse; qu'au reste si effectivement le Roi avoit [print: jouissait d'] une influence assez prépondérante à Paris pour pouvoir y opérer par la négociation simple le rétablissement des affaires d'Hollande, l'assurance préalable de la restitution des colonies étoit superflue, et qu'il seroit tems d'en faire la demande en Angleterre après que la France se seroit expliquée. Haugwitz répliqua que le but étoit uniquement d'entamer une négociation sans avoir recours à la voye des armes, puisque dans les circonstances présentes le Roi ne pourroit en aucun cas prendre les armes pour le rétablissement des affaires [en Hollande], sur quoi Elgin assura ne pouvoir demander des ordres contraires à l'esprit de ses dernières instructions, mais il recommanda cependant à Haugwitz de faire des démarches en France en notre faveur, le but principal de l'Angleterre étant la restauration de la République, et si cette puissance différoit d'opinion avec la Prusse sur la manière dont celle-ci pourroit être amenée, elle n'en seroit pas moins satisfaite au cas que le Roi y parvînt par la voye qu'il se proposoit de suivre. Je convins avec Milord Elgin que quand Haugwitz me parlera sur cette matière et me rendra compte de sa conversation avec lui, je tâcherai de l'engager à faire une démarche en France sans avoir l'assurance qu'il désire avoir concernant nos colonies, puisqu'elle ne sauroit jamais nuire, et que si elle étoit de quelque fruit l'utilité seroit considérable, en quoi je me flatte de rencontrer les intentions de mon père, étant encore à remarquer que si le premier pas se fait, il est peut-être possible d'amener le second. The conference which I announced as due to take place on the eighth between Haugwitz and Elgin was indeed held, and Lord Elgin has already told me its result, of which I [?shall] give an account; while Count Haugwitz told me the day before yesterday at the King's ball that he would come to me one of these days to speak to me on this subject. And he made to Elgin the communication of the idea we had agreed on together, of making an approach to France to induce that power to consent to restore affairs in the Republic on the old footing, adding that, given the degree of influence he thought he had in Paris, he hoped that such a proposal would not be fruitless; but that, as the first question he expected on the part of France would be whether in that case England would give back the colonies to the Republic, he wished to have assurances beforehand so as to be able to handle this affair all the better in France. Lord Elgin told him he was not in a position to answer him [direct]ly on that, and that, before seeking new instructions in this respect, he wished to know whether, in case an overture made by the King in Paris were fruitless, the King would support it by arms; that he believed he ought to ask this, because it is in the spirit of his instructions, since in England it is not supposed possible to obtain anything unless one supports one's demand by arms, and that in this respect at least a demonstration [would be] necessary, for which, according to his latest orders, he could give assurance that the expenses would be amply repaid to Prussia; that, for the rest, if the King did indeed have an influence preponderant enough in Paris to be able to bring about there, by simple negotiation, the restoration of the affairs of Holland, the prior assurance of the restitution of the colonies was superfluous, and that it would be time to ask for it in England after France had declared itself. Haugwitz replied that the aim was solely to open a negotiation without having recourse to the way of arms, since in present circumstances the King could in no case take up arms for the restoration of affairs [in Holland]; whereupon Elgin declared he could not ask for orders contrary to the spirit of his latest instructions, but he nevertheless recommended Haugwitz to make approaches in France in our favour, England's principal aim being the restoration of the Republic; and if that power differed in opinion from Prussia on the manner in which this could be brought about, it would be no less satisfied in case the King achieved it by the way he proposed to follow. I agreed with My Lord Elgin that, when Haugwitz speaks to me on this matter and gives me an account of his conversation with him, I shall try to engage him to make an approach in France without having the assurance he wishes to have concerning our colonies, since it could never do harm, and if it bore any fruit the benefit would be considerable; in which I flatter myself that I meet my father's intentions, it being further to be remarked that, if the first step is taken, it is perhaps possible to bring about the second. A clear letter with words and parts of words in cipher. Where National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O’Neal Greenhow: the cipher original is naId 6925618, a photostat of burnt fragments (catalogue entry 646); the clear copy is naId 1634051, images 1–2 (catalogue entry 645). The cipher One symbol per letter, the system of the 1864 key sheet found on Greenhow’s body (NARA M1091, naId 62017285, image 0484). How it was deciphered The clerk’s copy gives every cipher passage in plain words, and a lighter hand wrote “h a r” under the first group on the original. Matched sign by sign, the 1864 key gives the copy’s letter for all 82 securely transcribed signs. What it says Jordan asks for Hardee’s and Scott’s Tactics, Mahan’s Field Fortification, eight yards of navy-blue flannel and shoulder straps for a lieutenant colonel: “These books are essential to me in my position”. Still open Three short stretches of the fragment (a line before “handed”, a central strip, the end of “for the rest to”) are too faint or torn; the copy has dashes there too. Credit The identification of the two items as one letter, the transcription and the key match by WAINUT (pull request #100, 27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents. The decipherment is the clerk’s copy of 1861.

NARA’s naId 6925618, “Copy of a Letter Fragment Partially Written in Cipher”, is a white-on-black photostat of burnt and torn fragments pasted on a sheet: clear words with groups of symbols, cross-written in places. The catalogue had it as a letter from Greenhow to an unknown contact, written at Washington. The photostat as NARA holds it, a negative: left block (the books), right block (“he will bring” to “by sending”). Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 6925618, image 1, via the National Archives Catalog. In the file “Letters from Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Jordan to Mrs. Greenhow and to My Dearest Rachel” (naId 1634051), images 1–2 are a fair copy in a clerk’s copperplate of a letter to “My Dearest Rachel”, all in clear, with dashes where the original is lost. Every clear phrase of the fragment (“to get for me”, “and if to be had conveniently / 8 yards navy flannel (blue)”, “for the rest to”, “me from Alex”, “essential to me in my / position as”, “by sending”) is in the copy, in the same order, so the fragment is the original of the copied letter, and the copy is its decipherment. Who made the copy, and when, the images do not show; a Federal clerk working on the seized papers is likely but not proved. Images 3–6 of the same file are a different clear letter and an envelope. The clear copy, image 2: “to get for me Hardee’s Tactics, or the new Copies of Scott’s Tactics, also — volumes of Mahans field fortifications …”. Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 1634051, image 2, via the National Archives Catalog.

The 1864 key sheet (see the mourning-paper letter , which deciphers with the same key) was applied unchanged to the fragment’s 22 cipher groups, 89 signs, transcribed on inverted and contrast-stretched crops. Of the 82 signs transcribed without doubt, all 82 give the letter the clear copy has at that place: HAR(dee’s), (Tacti)CS, (n)EW COP(ies), SCOTT, (Tact)ICS, (vol)UMES, (Ma)HANS FIELD FORTIFICATION, (Sh)OULDER, (Str)APS, LIE(utenant), CO(lonel), (b)RIN(g), ANY, CAN G(et), HIM, BOO(ks), LIEU(tenant), COLONEL, IN(fantry). The left block, inverted. From the top: “to get for me” and the group HAR with “h a r” written under it; CS; EW COP; SCOTT; ICS UMES; HANS FIELD; FORTIFICATION; the clear lines; OULDER; APS “for a” LIE. Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 6925618, image 1, via the National Archives Catalog; inverted and contrast-stretched here. Controls ( decode.py ): 20,000 random substitution keys average 3.1 of the 82 signs (best 36); the key shifted by 1, 2, 3 or 13 letters gives none; the true key with the groups set against the wrong words of the copy averages 5.5 (best 19); 22 of 22 groups come out whole, against at most 4 for a random key. The signs were transcribed knowing the copy’s text, but the key comes from a separate document of 1864 and each sign was matched to it by shape, so the bias is limited to the seven signs marked doubtful. Points of detail: the first sign of HAR’s group is an O-sign (J on the key) that is not explained; SCOTT and BOO write their doubled letters plainly, not by the sheet’s inverted-second-letter rule; the first sign of OULDER may be the key’s sh digraph.

The fragment with the copy’s words supplied in brackets (cipher in capitals): … to get for me HAR[dee’s Tacti]CS, [or the n]EW COP[ies of] SCOTT[’s Tact]ICS, [also … vol]UMES [of Ma]HANS FIELD FORTIFICATION[s], and if to be had conveniently 8 yards navy flannel (blue) [Indigo …]ing of [SH]OULDER [STR]APS for a LIE[utenant] CO[lonel. … handed …] he [will b]RIN[g] ANY you CAN G[et to] [H]IM, [and I will …] for the rest to […] me from Alex[andria …]. These BOO[ks are] essential to me in my position as LIEU[tenant] COLONEL of IN[fantry] and you will [do me a great favor] by sending [them by hand …]. Jordan, newly a lieutenant colonel, asks “Rachel” for the drill and engineering manuals of the day and for the cloth and insignia of his rank, to be sent by hand. On the first page of the copy he fears that an earlier letter did not reach her: he had no access to his cipher at the time, and a letter “in ordinary cha[racters]” “was intercepted”. The content is domestic. Its interest is the cipher: it shows the Jordan–Greenhow system in use in 1861 with the key found on Greenhow three years later. Jordan himself wrote on 29 October 1861 that he had arranged this cipher “last April”, hastily, under the alias Thomas John Rayford ( Official Records , Series II, vol. 2, pp. 564–565).

Three stretches of the fragment are not transcribed: line 12 before “handed”, the central strip, and the end of “for the rest to”. The signs are faint or torn, and the copy has dashes at two of them. The copy’s dashes: the original is torn at those places too, and the surviving cipher does not fill them. Seven signs are doubtful (marked in the transcription) and are left out of the count of 82. The date: after Jordan became a lieutenant colonel and before the seizure of 23 August 1861. The place is presumed to be Beauregard’s headquarters at Manassas. No printed text of the letter was found: not in the Official Records , Series II, vol. 2 (pp. 561–577), Pinkerton’s Spy of the Rebellion or Greenhow’s My Imprisonment . Fishel and Blackman could only be searched through the web.

Soviet radio telegrams intercepted at Constantinople and filed unread by the State Department (NARA M316 rolls 40–48). The file holds several systems. The small 4-figure table Kopp and Lutovinov used shows literal phrase repeats, but no group value was recovered and each hypothesis failed its control. 1209 1101 1313 8023 9023 1112 1201 Berlin → Moscow · figure table, values unknown · April–May 1921 · attempted, not deciphered The Kopp and Chicherin radiograms, 1921 to Georgy Chicherin American officials in Constantinople copied Soviet radio traffic and could not read it. Part of that file has now been deciphered, but the figure telegrams to Chicherin have not. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 2 November 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The documents Kopp's telegram of 16 April 1921 and Lutovinov's Nr 417 of 23 May, typed copies sent to Washington by Admiral Mark L. Bristol. Where NARA RG 59, Central Decimal File 861.00, microfilm M316 roll 41 frames 0876–0877, roll 42 frame 0953. The whole file is rolls 40–48. The cipher A 4-figure table with literal phrase repeats, so no additive is at work on it. Its group values are unknown. How it was tried Ciphertext-only annealing against Russian, with shuffled controls, plus a search for a periodic numerical key. Each hypothesis failed its control. Still open All of it. The British decrypts, the War Department copies and most of the printed Soviet documents have not been checked.

From March 1921 the US High Commission at Constantinople sent Washington envelopes of intercepted Moscow telegrams. A Russian radio operator working in the Embassy took them down. Bristol's despatch No. 153 of 20 April 1921 (861.00/8575) passes on the operator's opinion: the bulk of the Kopp–Chicherin traffic is in Russian, messages from Hilger and Staehler are in German, and the Bolsheviks “use old Russian code books” and sometimes apply a “Captain Murashenko” method, a numerical key added to or subtracted from the coded text. Bristol would not vouch for this. On 1 July he reported that anti-Bolsheviks had promised him the code, secured in Berlin, and that it never arrived. The OCR gives 1,478 runs of figures, 66,640 groups, retransmissions and non-Soviet traffic included, so treat those counts as provisional. Several unrelated systems share the file: Letter groups to Stomoniakov: a columnar transposition with a new key per telegram. Two are deciphered, each on its own page: Lejava's gold payment and Voikov's buying order . Karakhan to Kopp, 29 April: a different 4-figure table, unread. 5-figure traffic with a word before the figures (SWET, MISTERIA, PALLADA, FORUM, ANCHAR, SIRIUS), with clear counters every 25 groups: unread. Austrian traffic running from 0 to 19999 with no leading zeros, and German telegrams: unread.

Funkspruch Nr 417 of 23 May 1921, signed Lutowinoff. Most groups start 11, 12, 13 or a round 20 to 90. Image: NARA RG 59, 861.00, M316 roll 42, frame 0953, via the National Archives Catalog. Kopp's telegram of 16 April (M316-041-0876, 0877) and Lutovinov's of 23 May (042-0953) share one shape. The first pair of each group is almost always 01–09, 10–13, 15 or a round 20–90; the second is 01–31 or a round 40–90. They give 717 groups as transcribed, the two April frames from blurred carbons. Phrases recur literally, for instance 1206 1214 1206 1101 1226 9010 1117 twice running on frame 0876.

Chained consonant and vowel tables. Annealing the two pairs as letter tables scored about the same as shuffled controls (−5.42 against −5.54). From one group's second pair to the next group's first pair, mutual information is z = 2.2, against 22.9 inside a group. The second pair as a plain alphabet. It scored −3.69 per character, the same as its control and far from −2.11 for real Russian on that model. Each group as one letter. −2.43 to −2.50 against −2.40 to −2.54 for shuffled groups, and the text collapses into repeated letters. With 228 distinct groups in 715, nearly any mapping scores well. This table plus a periodic key on the clustered Berlin traffic. On Nr 461 a period of 14 scored z = 11.2, but the image shows 14 groups to a typed line. Stripping a key put only 9–15% of groups in the known vocabulary.

Statistics alone cannot confirm a reading of a table this size. Any of these could change that: HW 12 at The National Archives: GC&CS was decrypting Soviet traffic in 1921. Whether Berlin traffic was among it is unchecked. RG 457, 6707N, “Russian Coded Messages, 1921”, the War Department copies, not digitised. A printed text of one of these telegrams. Dokumenty vneshnei politiki SSSR vol. IV could not be fully searched: the site hosting it refused further access during this work.

A letter from Leicester’s fleet before Sluys (BL Harley MS 287 ff. 39–40), catalogued on DECODE with no recipient. The key to its three-grid pigpen alphabet was recovered from a few words glossed at the time on the same pages and the alphabetical order of the grids, and every run of f. 39v was deciphered: Parma had closed the channel with hoys and flyboats chained together. ⌟: ⌝ □ ⌝̣ ⌟: ⌝ □ ⌝̣ □ ⌞: ⌟ ⊐̣ … ther there was any bridge or not ⌟ = a · ⌟̣ = k · ⌟: = t · □ = e · □̣ = o · □: = y Before Sluys → Walsingham · three-grid pigpen inside clear English · 28 July 1587 Francis Needham to Walsingham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 to Francis Walsingham Go to the transcriptions ↓ British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 39–40 (DECODE R8479): Walsingham’s servant with Leicester’s relief fleet writes of the failure to relieve Sluys. The cipher is a pigpen alphabet. The long cipher passages of f. 39v had no decipherment. The key was recovered from a handful of words glossed at the time on the same pages and from the alphabetical order of the grids, and every run was deciphered; one word stays uncertain. The key is said to survive in BL Add MS 5935, which was not consulted. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letter Francis Needham, Walsingham’s servant, to Walsingham before Sluys, 28 July 1587, written on Leicester’s expedition to relieve the town. Where British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 39–40; DECODE R8479, catalogued as a partially decrypted letter of “Needham” to an unknown recipient in an unknown cipher of graphic signs. The cipher A pigpen of nine box shapes in three forms (plain, dot below, dot inside) carrying the alphabet a–i, k–s, t–z in order. How it was read A contemporary hand glossed a few cipher words on f. 39r. The glosses advise , enemyes , campe nor the towne and Burgrave gave half the alphabet, and the order of the grids gave the rest. What it says The besiegers had no intelligence of the enemy, did not know whether there was a bridge, and found the channel closed with hoys and flyboats fastened with chains. Still open One word of about six letters on f. 39v is unsure. Credit The clear text follows the same-day despatch calendared in CSP Foreign 1587 (pp. 206–8).

Harley MS 287 is a volume of Walsingham’s correspondence (the Cobham letters of 1588 on ff. 70–72 are deciphered in another write-up ). Folios 39–40 are one letter: f. 39r opens “It may please your honour. The sudden departure of the bark … before Sluce, was the cause that I was forced to break off”, f. 39v continues, f. 40r ends it with the date 1587, and the address leaf f. 40v is endorsed “28 July 1587. From Needham”. CSP Foreign vol. 21 pt 3 (1929) calendars Needham’s letter to Walsingham of the same day from Flushing (SP 84/16 f. 216): the council aboard Leicester’s ship before the haven of Sluys, the firework ship that could hardly be brought up to the bridge, the States’ captains who would not lend boats because “this commission must come from the States”, and the fall of the town. The Harley letter tells the same story in more words; the calendar does not list it. A note in the same volume (p. 237) says Needham wrote to Walsingham in the cipher of Thomas Wilkes, whose key is at the front of BL Add MS 5935 (p. 35 n. 4). That manuscript is not online and was not used here.

Nine box shapes, each written plain, with a dot beneath, or with a dot inside its angle. Taken in order, the shapes carry the alphabet straight through three grids: shape plain dot below dot inside ⌟ a k t ⊔ b l u, v ⌞ c m w ⊏ d n x □ e o y ⌜ f p z ⊓ g q — ⌝ h r — ⊐ i s — Words are divided and spelled as in the clear text ( wyth , chaynes , bootes ). No homophones, nulls or code names occur on f. 39v. The dots are the whole difficulty: a dot below sits under the lower left of its sign, the script slants to the right, and a dot inside ⌟ lies in its upper left, so the first transcription gave several t’s as k’s until the grid order showed the error. f. 39v: “campe nor the towne” glossed above its signs; beneath, the bare line whether there was any bridge or not, or whether there were any at the chanel . Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 39v, via DECODE R8479 (image 4).

Cipher in italics; clear words around it paraphrased where the clear text was not transcribed in full. “… we had want of intelligence these five days last past … [no] advise out of the enemyes campe nor the towne ” (the last four words glossed at the time). “and we were so far from knowing what was meet to be done at that time [that] we knewe not whether there was any bridge or not, or whether there were any at the chanel .” “… being above 100 of their files into the town walls, and that the chanel was b[…]ed with hoyes and flyboates fastened wyth chaynes, strengthned behind wyth flatt bootes .” f. 39v: “… into the towne walls. and that the chanel was b[…]ed with hoyes and flyboates fastened wyth chaynes, strengthned behind wyth flatt bootes .” Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 39v, via DECODE R8479 (image 4). This is the “bridge” of the calendared despatch: Parma had closed the haven of Sluys with a boom of boats chained together, and the English and Dutch could neither see it nor learn what it was. The rest of f. 39v, in clear, covers Sir Roger Williams’s sallies, the storm, the state of the town, Count Maurice, Colonel Morgan and Sir William Russell; the three words glossed near its foot (“Mr Burley”, “the Spaniard”, “were removed hence”) were deciphered at the time.

The four images were fetched from DECODE. The glossed words gave letters by alignment: advise = ⌟ ⊏ ⊔: ⊐ ⊐̣ □, enemyes = □ ⊏̣ □ ⌞̣ □: □ ⊐̣, the towne = ⌟: ⌝ □ ⌟: □̣ ⌞: ⊏̣ □, and Burgrave on f. 40r began ⊔ ⊔̣ ⌝̣ ⊓. The first bare line then gave want of intelligence , and once a, b, c, d, e, h, i and k–s, t–z were in hand the order was plainly alphabetical, which fixed f, g, p and q and corrected the mistranscribed dots. A solver (simulated annealing on quadgram statistics) was prepared in case the key could not be completed, and was not needed. The transcription is in targets/needham1587/cipher.txt and the key in decode.py .

Line G, the verb after “the chanel was”: ⊔ then four cramped signs (one blotted), then □ ⊏, so b ···· ed. Sense: closed or blocked. Grade M. All other cipher words: grade H (every sign decrypted with the key; they spell English in the letter’s own spelling). The key has not been checked against the Wilkes key in Add MS 5935. The clear text of ff. 39r–40r is summarised, not transcribed.

Two ciphered copies of the duc de Nevers’ letters to the marquis de Pisany from his 1593 embassy to Rome for Henri IV’s absolution. Tomokiyo’s numerical key no. 46, transcribed at full resolution and checked on a letter deciphered by the office, deciphers them, one completely and one in long stretches. His letters to Revol are in another cipher and have their own page. 88̈ 38̄ 29 42 74 32 69 66 95 79 15 82̄ 1̈ 19̄ 52 77 35 18 69 25 42 17 22 79 18 26 58 80 17 56̄ 51̄ 74 76 55 69 45̄ 58 80̄ · 50̄ 54 73 17 25 74 55 1 46 83 12 99̈ 80̄ 5̄ 1 42 99̈ 51̄ 76̄ 79 18 53̄ 90 17 36 77 25 12 83 Nevers, Edolo → Pisany · numerical cipher of two-digit figures with bars and dots (no. 46) · 1593 · known key applied, decoded, not read Nevers to Pisany, 1593: two letters in the numerical key no. 46 from Duke of Nevers Go to the transcriptions ↓ Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46, a known key, gives a value to every figure of Nevers’s two letters to Pisany of autumn 1593, but the register copies carry wrong figures, and neither letter yet builds sentences throughout: both are decoded, not read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 17 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source, earlier solution) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Seven letters of the Duke of Nevers from the road to Rome, autumn 1593, to Revol and Pisany, while he sought absolution for the newly converted Henri IV from Clement VIII. Where BnF fr. 3985 and fr. 3986; the catalogue lists them as “avec chiffre” and treated them as one key with one passage deciphered. The cipher Two keys. The Pisany letters use the numerical cipher Tomokiyo catalogued as no. 46: a two-digit alphabet with homophones, barred and plain figures for words, double-dotted figures for names and the digit 1 as a null. The Revol letters use the symbol cipher no. 60. How it was read The key was transcribed from the full-resolution table and checked against the office’s own decipherment of a Gondi letter in the same key. It gives a value for every figure of both Pisany letters. What it says The 8 September letter is deciphered completely: the Pope is not to be contented and one should not go. The 14 October letter, after Possevino said at Poschiavo that Nevers would not be received, is read in long stretches. Still open The Revol letters: 27 August is in clear throughout, 9 October carries two and a half lines of symbols, and three were not reached on the image. They need the symbol key matched to the copyist’s hand.

The catalogue took seven ciphered copies of Nevers’s letters as one office’s key. They are in two: the five to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60 ( their own page ), the two to Pisany in no. 46, below. Item Date and place To Where on the image Cipher fr. 3985 no. 116 Nevers, 8 Sept 1593 Pisany f. 209 (canvas 419) no. 46, decoded, not read fr. 3986 no. 81 “Ville” [Edolo], 14 Oct 1593 Pisany f. 168 (canvas 332) no. 46, decoded, not read Both volumes are microfilm digitisations on Gallica with every canvas labelled NP; the folio is close to half the canvas number, and the 1400 px canvases do not resolve two-digit figures, so the pages were fetched at full IIIF resolution (about 4,900 px wide). Tomokiyo’s Henri IV article states the division of keys: Gondi and Nevers used the symbol cipher no. 60 with the King and Revol from July 1593, and the numerical no. 46 with Vivonne (Pisany). The catalogue entry had not taken that in.

Below it, three word lists. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 87, via Gallica (btv1b525085665, canvas 169). Tomokiyo’s published image of the key is 225 pixels wide; the Gallica image of the sheet is 7,677. The table has a barred series from 99 down to 2 for common words (80̄ de , 56̄ je , 51̄ luy , 53̄ la , 11̄ que , 9̄ quil , 38̄ ne , 73̄ est , 5̄ recherche ), a plain series on the figures the alphabet leaves free (24 sa , 28 sans , 29 se , 87 si , 45 tout , 62 vous , and the provinces), and a double-dotted series of names (99 Pape, 98 Roy, 88 Duc de Nevers, 70 Cardinal Gondi, 89 Duc de Mantoue, 54 Revol, 34 De Pizany, 1 Ambassadeur). In the letters the digit 1, and once 0, is dropped inside a group as a null, the device the sister key no. 45 prescribes in words. The conventions were checked against a letter the office deciphered interlinearly in the same key, Girolamo Gondi to Pisany of 22 September 1593 (fr. 3986 ff. 64–65v): personne, rencontre, congregation, absoudre, sainct, siege, ladicte, Romme all come out figure for figure.

The first two passages. Above: “Car j’estois sur ce mesme faict” followed by figures; below: “Car” and the passage about the Duke. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3985 f. 209, via Gallica (btv1b90606498, canvas 419). Three passages, 122 figure groups, all in the key. Decoded, not read: passage 2 holds as a sentence, but passages 1 and 3 rest on figures the copyist wrote wrong. Passage 1’s figures were looked at again on the Gallica IIIF image on 23 October 2026 and are as transcribed, so these are slips in the copy, not in the transcription. The partial reading is texts/f209_reading.md . “Car j’estois sur ce mesme faict” l’on dissuadoit [Pape] de rechercher [Pape] luy don[n]es[t] l’absolutio[n] . The copy has the Pope’s sign twice; one of them is probably the King’s (98̈) in sense. Tomokiyo deciphered this passage with the figure 14 for 74 and the name as Beaulieu; the figures are 74 and, in the next passage, 54 Revol. “Car” [Duc de Nevers] alléguoit qu’il n’estoyt besoin qu’il a[l]la[s]t sans cela, parce qu’il ne feroit rien , then in clear “Je suys attendant des nouvelles de” [Revol] “à qui j’ay escript”. Nevers is named by his sign in his own letter; the 61 in allast is a slip for 65. “Je suys d’opinion que” l’on n’a [11] volonté d[14]e contanter le Pape, que l’on n’[y a]ille poynt , and in clear “Et suys bien ayse que soyez de mesme volonté”. Several figures in this passage are the copyist’s (11 where the u of volonté is expected, 14 inside de , 57 83 84 where y a i is expected). The third passage: “Je suys d’opinion que … Et suys bien ayse que soyez de mesme volonté.” Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3985 f. 209, via Gallica (btv1b90606498, canvas 419).

The seven-line block after “ce qu’il en dit et”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3986 f. 168, via Gallica (btv1b9060631k, canvas 332). Seven full lines of figures, a short run and one more line: 269 groups, 268 in the key. No decipherment, original or edition of this letter is known. On 22 October 2026 the figures were re-read on the IIIF image (4,948 px): fourteen corrections, mostly bars set on the wrong figure in the first pass and groups wrongly divided ( texts/f168_corrections.tsv ). The reading ( texts/f168_reading.md , English f168_en.md ) now holds in about half its sentences: [le Duc de Nevers] ne sera receu come [Ambassadeur] pour pluseurs resons. Je luy ay demandé come [...] [le Pape] voloit que j’y alase; el[le] m’a dit n’avoir autre charge, ne me declarans que j’y alle ou non. Ce qu’il faict tenir segret, et le [faire] savoir a [Cardinal Gondi] [...]. Lines 4, 5 and the last line keep holes where the copyist’s figures are corrupt (24 for a , 27̄ for 29̄, dropped figures), legible but wrong, so the letter stays decoded, not read. Tomokiyo’s fragment stopped at “Je luy ay demandé”. Only a second witness, Pisany’s original, which has not been located, could restore the corrupt groups.
Nevers’s letters of the same months to Louis de Revol, secretary of state, are in the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60, a different cipher, with its own page .

A letter wholly in a homophonic cipher of graphic signs, image 2 of DECODE R1854, a record catalogued as one letter of unknown sender. The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone with a solver on a Latin model and checked sign by sign on the image: 1,757 of 1,802 signs read. Δ 17 16 w 13 g + T N 17 · A 17 16 w quod am actus … quod Rome → Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, Mantua · homophonic cipher of graphic signs, Latin · 9 August 1428 A Gonzaga agent in Rome to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 9 August 1428 to Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga Go to the full text ↓ A letter wholly in signs, about a marriage for the Gonzaga, deciphered with a key recovered from the ciphertext alone. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter An unnamed Gonzaga agent, signing with a lozenge mark, to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, lord of Mantua, Rome, 9 August 1428. All 37 lines are in cipher. Where Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Archivio Gonzaga. DECODE R1854, image 2: the record has five images, catalogued as one letter of unknown sender and recipient. The cipher A homophonic substitution in graphic signs and digits: about forty letter signs, a dozen nulls, signs for con , et and -rum , and two word codes. How it was deciphered A solver (simulated annealing on a Latin language model) recovered the key from the ciphertext alone; every sign was then checked on the image. What it says A countess agrees to her daughter’s match with a Gonzaga son, but her subjects object that Mantua is too far and “Carolus est nimis iuvenis ad talia”. Still open One word code used once, and about 45 signs in doubtful spans. DECODE R1854 holds four letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, each in a different cipher, and each has its own page: Pandolfo Malatesta, 22 April 1428 (not solved), an informant at Forlì, 6 November 1428 and Francesco de’ Cattanei, February 1430 . They were written up together until 14 October 2026.

DECODE R1854 “Mantova enciphered letters” has five images (I8411–I8415), catalogued as “unknown” with graphic signs. Each sheet has an archivist’s note at the top: “1428 · 22 ap(ri)le Roma” (stamped 23), “1428 · 9 Ag.to Roma” (24), “1428 · 6 novembre Forlì” (26), and so on. This page is image 2. The images are not in the public domain, so none is reproduced here. The companion record R1853 “Mantova keys” is the Gonzaga chancery register of ciphers, begun about 1401. Its first folio lists “Zifra cum Malatesta d(omi)ni Pandulfi”, “Zifra nova cum fratribus de Malatestis” and two keys “cum Karolo de Malatestis”, and later folios have keys dated 1406–1419. All are simple substitutions in letters and digits, and none gives sense on this letter. The other Mantua records on DECODE (R7858–R7888, Archivio Gonzaga E.I.2 busta 423) are sixteenth- and seventeenth-century keys.

The whole letter is in cipher: 37 lines of graphic signs and digits, dated in clear “Rome die viiii augusti”. It uses about forty letter signs, a dozen nulls, syllable signs for con , et and -rum , and two word codes, one of them twice in “in domo [·] Senensis” and “cum prefato [·]”, that is, the cardinal of Siena. The opening, as deciphered: Heri Iohannes de Orlandis, quam primum me vidit, dixit michi quod ser Victorius eomet die venit ad ipsum dicens dominam comitissam velle facere id totum quod placet et Iohanni predicto. Verum quia ipse incipiebat tunc prandere, dixit se ad eum reversurum et dicturum latius de ista materia. Postea cum heri sero plures essemus congregati in domo [cardinalis] Senensis pro quodam actu scolastico et cenaturi cum prefato [cardinali] … Ser Vittorio goes on to report the countess’s answer: as far as she is concerned she agrees to the match of her daughter, but her subjects are not content, “quia dominatio vestra nimium distat, si ibi contingeret aliquod sinistrum; et quod Carolus est nimis iuvenis ad talia”. The bridegroom under discussion is Gianfrancesco’s son Carlo, then eleven. The cousins of domina Palma and Antonio Colonna, the pope’s nephew, appear as parties to the negotiation. Line 28, read on 5 October 2026 from the re-fetched image: persuaserat matri et filie ut vellent vendere terras ipsas . The full text, with the doubtful spans marked, is in reading_p2.md .

This your L. shall reyde not spoken of my selfe, but this is a great parte of their greif, and all most everie mans speche, and preached in pulpet in playner wordes then I lyste to wryte. f. 277r, ll. 16–18. …to be sorte wth your L. it thinke utterlye undon , what so ever be come of us . The two images of R4931 are byte-identical to two of R4930's, so the "key" record was checked first and found to hold no key. Boyd's abstract, made from Sussex's clear copy, was lined up with the cipher runs. The runs were transcribed into symbol tokens, and a solver (simulated annealing) fitted the key against an English n-gram model (en-1640s), keeping the word divisions. With no crib fixed, it already produced "murtherers and traitors", "regent", "whome … nor conscience they thinke them selves … unto". With the crib words fixed as known plaintext, about 70% of the text came out. The rest would not converge, because several signs that look alike on the page (plain, curly and barred x; 3 against a tailed ʒ) carry different values. A sweep of the DECODE records from the same volume then found R4932, the decipherment, one leaf on. Every value recovered earlier agrees with it.

Three words of the clerk's first gloss line are faint or odd: "wyl reke ther owne", "handes", "fortefy" (C). The cipher under them is not otherwise confirmed, and the sense of that opening phrase stays doubtful in the original decipherment too. The bracketed [in], [to], [be], [with], [for] are words the clerk left out of the gloss (M). Everything else is deciphered and agrees with the key values (H).

A letter to the King of Aragon in plain Catalan, cut into chunks and written down the columns of each block, listed on DECODE as a cipher of unknown type. Xavier de Salas explained the transposition and printed a complete decipherment in 1931. His rule was checked on the archive’s image and reproduces his text. Senyor jous / pus compli / escriua ja / auem fet / tot son densa / met ho en / present segen / als p(ro)mens auie q(ue)zacom / dament se / senyor sab / asi en Bar / nostra p(er) tal / conseil p(er)q(ue) / e tan uostre / de p(er)piya hic escrit de so q(ue) / los afers / ets so q(ue)l nob / chinona / q(ue) mils ajen / senyor nola / afers maraue / an escrit als Barcelona → the King of Aragon · columnar transposition of word chunks · 2 May, reign of Ferdinand I A Catalan letter in transposition, Barcelona 2 May [1413–16] to Ferdinand I of Aragon Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Reserva 12 (formerly Cartes Reials, Alfons IV, caixa 2, núm. 357) · one paper strip, 21 lines, endorsed “2 mayo” · DECODE R10170, “ca. 1420, non-decrypted, cipher type unknown” A letter in plain Catalan, written as a transposition: chunks of words laid down the columns of each block. Xavier de Salas explained the system and printed a complete decipherment in 1931, in an article the DECODE record itself cites. His rule was checked on the archive’s image and reproduces his text; nothing was deciphered here that was not already in print. It is the oldest item on DECODE with a public image, and the only pre-1450 one. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter A letter in plain Catalan to the King of Aragon from a royal financial officer in Barcelona, dated “ha ii de mag” with no year. It is cut into chunks of one to four syllables by slashes. Where Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Reserva 12, a single paper strip; DECODE R10170 gives a palaeographic date of about 1420, the symbol set as “graphic signs, alphabet, numerical”, and no decipherment. The cipher A simple transposition: read down the columns of a block, chunk by chunk, with a marginal dot marking the last line of each block. The writer’s clear postscript promises the King it will not be tiresome once he sees the trick. How it was read Salas deciphered it by eye and printed the full text in 1931. Here the first block (lines 1–5) was transcribed from the DECODE image without the printed text; the rule gives Salas’s opening word for word. What it says About nine hundred words: the King should leave the city and hold the corts, the mood in Catalonia has turned in his favour, and the writer defends his accounts against suspicion. Still open The writer’s name and the year. Salas placed it between the autumn of 1413 and 2 April 1416. Credit X. de Salas, Estudis Universitaris Catalans XVI (1931).

ACA Reserva 12 is a single strip of paper about three times as wide as it is high, written edge to edge in a round chancery cursive of the early fifteenth century, with slashes every few words and a dot in the left margin every five or six lines. Below the text, in the same hand, is a dateline ( en Barchinona ha ii de mag ), and to the right two short notes in clear. A later hand has endorsed the strip “2 mayo”. The address on the back, which Salas printed, is Sacre Regie Aragonum Majestati . The strip as Salas reproduced it in 1931 ( Estudis Universitaris Catalans XVI, fig. 7). The dots at the left margin mark the blocks; the dateline and the two clear notes are below. Image: X. de Salas, Estudis Universitaris Catalans XVI (1931), fig. 7, via ARCA, Biblioteca de Catalunya. Taken along the lines, the text is a string of Catalan word fragments without sense: Senyor jous / pus compli / escriua ja / auem fet / tot son densa / met ho en / present segen … That is what put it on DECODE as a cipher. The record gives the symbol set as “graphic signs, alphabet, numerical”, the language as Spanish, the cipher type as unknown and gives no decipherment, and under References it lists Salas.

In 1931 Salas gave the rule in one sentence. The letter runs from top to bottom, by columns: along a line until the first slash, then down to the next line, and so on to the last line of the block, which the marginal dot marks; then back to the first line for its second chunk. If the lines are 1, 2, 3 … and the chunks a, b, c …, the order is 1a, 2a, 3a, 4a, 1b, 2b, 3b, 4b. The writer enciphered by writing the letter down the columns of a block and then went on to the next block. The first lines of the strip, from the archive’s image. Down the first column: Senyor jous · auie q(ue)zacom · escrit de so q(ue) · asi ses feit . Image: Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Reserva 12, via DECODE R10170. The check made here is the first block, lines 1 to 5, transcribed from the DECODE image without reference to the printed text, then set against Salas: Line Chunk a Chunk b Chunk c 1 Senyor jous pus compli escriua ja 2 auie q(ue)zacom dament se senyor sab 3 escrit de so q(ue) los afers ets so q(ue)l nob 4 asi ses feit me son acor le en Rog(er) de Palars 5 mas p(er) tal com dat que us e jo Down the columns: Senyor, jo us auie quezacom escrit de so que asi s’és feit, mas per tal com pus complidament sé los afers me són acordat que us escriua. Ja, senyor, sabets so quel noble en Roger de Palars e jo … That is Salas’s opening word for word. The chunks break words wherever the column happens to end ( compli/dament , acor/dat , nob/le ), which is what makes the lines look enciphered. The writer said as much himself, in clear, at the foot of the strip: No us anugets de legir, car con lest ho ajats prazer n’aurets e no playarets l’afany , do not be put off reading it, for once you have read it you will be pleased and will not regret the effort. He asks for the reply under the King’s ring seal, per tal que pus sacretament ho puxats fer . Salas remarked on the ingenuousness of a note that warns the reader there is a difficulty and then leaves the slashes and the dots in place.

The strip carries a day and no year. Salas dated the hand to about 1420, which is the date DECODE prints, but placed the content earlier: the writer reminds the King that not long ago people se tenien per agrauiats con contra lur conseil herets anat ab mà armada , held themselves aggrieved that against their advice he had marched in arms, which Salas took as Ferdinand I’s campaign against the count of Urgell in 1413. That makes the last months of 1413 the earliest date and Ferdinand’s death on 2 April 1416 the latest, since the letter is to the king who did the marching. The archive filed it under Alfonso, Ferdinand’s successor, which is where DECODE’s date comes from. Salas left the year open, and it is left open here. The wider setting fits Ferdinand’s last years: the King in Valencia, unwell, the corts in suspense, and Barcelona and Perpinyà being sounded for support.

The writer is a royal financial officer stationed in Barcelona who keeps accounts ( mos comtes ) and closes them every six months; he writes on behalf of himself and of the noble Roger de Pallars. Salas’s text runs to about nine hundred words. In outline: Barcelona and Perpinyà. He and Roger de Pallars have done what they could in Barcelona and await the King’s letter of credence daily, so that the consellers have grounds to put the matter to the council. The pròmens of Perpinyà have written to the consellers to learn their intentions and offer to do whatever is needed. A council was held that day on the Perpinyà request, and those who were well disposed before are doubly so now. Leave the city. The King should take counsel for his person and get out of the trouble he is in; once he is out of it, he will see such a stir in Catalonia that the whole world will marvel, but while he stays where he is nothing can be set in motion. The writer has already advised, through A. de Canet, that the King should hold and continue the corts as soon as his credence arrives. The mood has turned. Not long ago people were aggrieved that the King had marched in arms against their advice; now they grieve for him, take his part and speak sharply against València. Tomorrow he and Roger de Pallars meet the bishop of Vic; Pallars then goes to Claramunt to speak with Ramon d’Anglesola, who has been at Lleida; the viscount of Illa is gathering the barons and knights of Roussillon to join those of Catalonia. Let the King be steadfast and keep his affairs secret, que tot uostre fet hi ua . His own office. Just de Miravet has brought word from the King that his post is safe. But a royal letter has come to Berenguer de Relat ordering that his accounts not be released, as if he were the most suspect man in the world; the originals stay in the archive, so there is nothing to fear. Those so anxious for the patrimony should have the past treasurers’ accounts examined, which have never been closed, whereas he closes his every six months and is still harassed. His accounts are closed to Christmas, save for the purchaser’s vouchers, which he has not been able to get for eight months through the fault of the clerk of receipts. He asks the King to look into it and to make an example of whoever is found at fault. The close, in Salas’s text … e de so senyor me farets gran honor e mercè. Dada en Barchinona ha ii de mag. Así, senyor, uos he escrit de part en Roger de Palas e de mi septat so que toque a mon hofissi. No us anugets de legir car con lest ho ajats prazer n’aurets e no playarets l’afany, e aje nostre resposta sagelade ab l’aneil nostre per tal que pus sacretament ho puxats fer. Sacre Regie Aragonum Majestati.

The oldest ciphered letter deciphered in this project is from 1497. The oldest ciphertext with no earlier known decipherment that anyone has broken in recent research is from 1449. DECODE has some six hundred records dated before 1497, nearly all of them keys, and this strip is the oldest one with an image that can be fetched without a login. It was the third of four pre-1450 candidates, and the memo that ranked them already noted that it looked like abbreviated Catalan. It came off the list within an hour: the References field of the record named the 1931 article, the Biblioteca de Catalunya’s ARCA portal has the volume, and the article has the text. The lesson is the same as with Sástago 1495–96, which DECODE lists with no decipherment although Parisi printed it in 2004. A record’s references should be checked before its status. The remaining candidates are Queen María’s letter to Alfonso V of 5 August 1435 (ACA Cancilleria reg. 3225 f. 59r, forty signs in four runs), the four pages of Luis Fernández from Rome in April 1424 (RAH 9/31), and the Heidelberg alchemical cipher of 1426 with its key on the first leaf.

Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Reserva 12. DECODE record R10170 , image public. Xavier de Salas Bosch, “Una lletra xifrada en català”, Estudis Universitaris Catalans XVI (1931), pp. 374–377 and fig. 7. Digitised by the Biblioteca de Catalunya: ARCA, vol. XVI (the article is at images 384–389 of the volume). A. Lange and E.-A. Soudart, Traité de cryptographie (Paris, 1925), the nomenclature Salas used. Salas’s article and transcription, the candidates memo and the notes are in the repository ( research/oldest/ ). The archive’s image is not committed. The decipherment is Salas’s; the check of the rule on the image is this project’s.

Siena’s orator to Charles V writes from Innsbruck on 4 January 1547 (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 15, DECODE R4803), with eleven short passages in a Greek-like homophonic alphabet and Latin-letter code words. George Lasry, with CTTS and Claude Opus 5.5, gave values to 75 of the 240 cipher signs by crib dragging; the rest and the code words are open.
