Decoded, not read: only a few clauses come through whole. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Contributed by George Lasry (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Mario Bandini, Sienese orator at the imperial court, to the Signori of Siena, Innsbruck (“Eltspruch”), 4 January 1546 Sienese style, that is 1547. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, no. 15; DECODE R4803, catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher About 65 signs: a homophonic alphabet of Greek-like and invented signs, probable nulls, no word dividers, and Latin-letter code words (buf, abs, som, Za) each followed by a bar with three dots. How it was tried George Lasry transcribed the passages in CTTS and, with Claude Opus 5.5, guessed and dragged cribs inside the clear context. What it says Only fragments: the cipher speaks of an occasion to be used and of discord among the factions; a minister warns that a fire would be kindled in a coded place. Still open 165 of the 240 cipher signs and the four code words, so the passages are decoded, not read. Checked again on 23 October 2026: all eight DECODE images of R4803 (the eighth is a clear postscript) and the neighbouring records R4802 and R4804 carry no decipherment, and no printed text was found. About 30 sign classes have no value in 240 signs, too few for a rebuild from the ciphertext alone; Lasry’s own CTTS transcription is needed for the next step. Credit George Lasry, with CTTS and Claude Opus 5.5: transcription and partial decipherment, sent by email to Daniel Bourdeau on 17 October 2026. This page reports his result. The two other sixteenth-century Sienese pieces of George Lasry’s report, no. 17 (Tantucci, 1528) and R4794 (the unnumbered artillery slip) , are different ciphers with their own pages; their key figures were compared sign by sign with this one and every shared shape has another value.

240 cipher signs and three Latin-letter code tokens, in eight lines of the second page and six of the sixth, set as eleven short passages in the clear Italian. Bandini protests that he did not come to Germany to quarrel with Piergiovanni Salvestri, dismisses the “calumnies” that Siena is displeased at the Emperor’s victory, and reports that a minister (Granvelle?) refused the thousand he brought and asked for Sienese vases “all’antica”. Page 6, lines 1–6: the minister’s words, in cipher, then in clear Latin “essent principes qui vellent persolvere centum milia coronatorum”. Image: George Lasry, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 report (17 Oct 2026), crop of ASSi Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 15 p. 6 (DECODE R4803). George Lasry’s partial key for no. 15, with the code words and the signs still unknown. Image: George Lasry, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 report (17 Oct 2026), signs cut from ASSi Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 15 (DECODE R4803).

SS.e Ill.me so’ prudenti et dunq[ue] anco da guardar [buf] [?] di ?ci?r? i?ae?u adosso se[Za] su? e?i? — De le calunnie che V. SS.e Ill.me mi significa P6, lines 1–6. reservandosi tutto a concludere con S. M.ta Ces.a / [abs] sc?it ?uno mi disse n?cn ?i ?rh? perche si entrasse in ???ione che si accenderebbe ?? fuoco in [abs] ?t?s c?n? soggiunse: essent principes qui vellent persolvere centum milia coronatorum ut Senenses viderent hunc errorem ut haberent occasionem turbandi ??t o? pe? iculo? queste His translation of P6: “reserving everything to be concluded with His Imperial Majesty. [abs] … he told me …, so that one should enter into … [confus]ion(?), which would kindle … fire in [abs] …; he added: there would be princes who would be willing to pay out a hundred thousand crowns, so that the Sienese might see this error, so as to have an occasion of disturbing … peril(?).” The date: the Emperor’s recent “victory and glory” is the Schmalkaldic campaign of autumn 1546, which fixes 4 January 1546 in the Sienese year (beginning 25 March) as 1547. Siena was then a republic under imperial protection, split between its Monti; in 1547 Charles V put it under Don Diego Hurtado de Mendoza.

165 of the 240 cipher signs; about 30 signs have no value, and several transcription classes are probably variants of one sign. The code words buf (three times), abs (three times), som and Za, and the persons or places behind them; “His Excellency” who spoke in Latin (Granvelle?). The filed key “Cifra con m. The Signori have suspended the settlement of the affairs of the order of the Nove until the Emperor's full resolution; Bandini has always wished every family and every order to hold its due place in the city, the sooner the better, but leaves it to their prudence. Here the cipher begins: it speaks of an occasion that must be used and of discord among them (the factions), of someone who brought matters [report page 30] back into the hands of a coded party, and of what the Signori must also guard against; the code words buf, abs, som and Za stand for the persons or places concerned. In clear again he dismisses the 'calumnies' that Siena is displeased at the Emperor's victory and glory, citing the city's obedience, down to sending the relegated exiles wherever His Majesty ordered. On P6 a minister ('S. Ex.tia', apparently Granvelle), reserving everything for the Emperor's decision, told him in words put into cipher that if Siena entered into [confusion?] a fire would be kindled in a coded place, and added in Latin that there were princes ready to pay a hundred thousand crowns so that the Sienese should see their error and give them an occasion to stir up trouble. The same man refused outright the thousand (ducats?) Bandini brought him, saying it would be talked of ten years hence and that he already knew of it from elsewhere; Bandini will try again and awaits orders. The minister also asked for Sienese vases 'all'antica', to be sent through the ambassador Figueroa at Genoa to Lyon and on to Burgundy, and Bandini promised a hundred fine pieces. The bearer is Mattio delle Poste; Alessandro Pieri(?), who has been unwell, will follow shortly. Historical context and dating Siena was a republic under imperial protection, split between its Monti (Nove, Popolo, Riformatori, Gentiluomini). Charles V's chief minister Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, a Burgundian, had imposed a settlement among them in 1541; new disorders in 1545–46 brought the exile of faction leaders (the 'relegati' of the clear text) and, in 1547, the Emperor's decision to put Siena under Don Diego Hurtado de Mendoza with a Spanish garrison, the prelude to the revolt of 1552 [Hook, Siena: A City and its History, 1979; Cantagalli, La guerra di Siena, 1962]. Bandini wrote from Innsbruck, on the Brenner road to the Emperor's winter quarters in Swabia, just after Charles V had dispersed the Schmalkaldic League's army (November 1546) [Brandi, The Emperor Charles V, 1939]. The 'victory and glory of His Majesty' in the letter is that campaign, which fixes the Sienese date 1546 (year beginning 25 March) as 1547. Open points. The code words buf (three times), abs (three times), som and Za and the persons or places behind them, 'His Excellency' who spoke in Latin (Granvelle?), the party that 'brought matters back into the hands' of someone, and Piergiovanni Salvestri's backers are unidentified. English translation Revised to match the current Italian edition; uncertain identities remain bracketed. Memorandum for Iacobo Spinelo, who is going to the Marche. First, the said Iacobo shall tell [Tartaglia?] that the King wishes him, together with Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], with diligence, vigour and every precaution, to ensure that [Paolo Orsini?] can neither return to nor get back out of the Marche. Although the King wrote to [Tartaglia?] that he should not undertake this business personally, the King has now changed his orders and counsel: he wants him to go in person, take the passes of Ascoli, and have the passes of the Tronto, Arquata, Monte del Monaco and such other neighbouring places as he thinks fit well guarded. He is to spread the word that he has gone to these passes and places for fear that the troops in the Marche might get out, come and damage the said lands and other places belonging to the King, and in order to have the works on the Tronto completed. He shall also tell [Tartaglia?] to finish getting ready without delay, so that, if the King wants him, with [Name3], [Sforza?] and Rodolfo's men, to attack [Paolo Orsini?] or lay siege to him, they can do so immediately. He shall advise [Tartaglia?] that he will likewise go and speak to Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], and that they must all act in concert: if [Paolo Orsini?] tries to cross by the passes on that side, then at the request of Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], they can all fall on him together and pursue him; likewise if he comes to cross by [Tartaglia?]'s passes. They must coordinate well and keep good spies so that nothing can fail, for the whole affair depends on this. Orders shall be given to the infantry for whatever this business requires and for completing the works on the Tronto. They are to come to a secret understanding with the Malatesta on this matter and on no others, and report whether they could defeat him on the march [or break his escort]. Likewise, he shall deliver the same message, as appropriate, to Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], telling them to guard the passes and places on that side, while [Tartaglia?] guards those on this side. They shall let it be said that [Name3] and [Sforza?] have gone there both because [Paolo Orsini?] has taken their companions from them and is their enemy, and so that neither [Paolo Orsini?], Messer Ludovico nor the Malatesta can harm the King's allies and loyal subjects. Likewise, Iacobo shall tell or write to [Sforza?] that, at the request of Rodolfo and [Name3], he must meet and join forces with them as requested. Nonetheless, he shall attend to recovering and retaking the castles in the district of [Name5] occupied by the exiles, with the 140 lances that Dominico de [Name4] has left there by the King's command for the business of those castles. Likewise, until [Tartaglia?] has gone to the aforesaid passes and places, he is not to let [Name6?] leave those parts. Likewise, Iacobo shall not leave the Marche, but remain there to urge on those named above, see and hear what is being done, report frequently to the King the news as it occurs, and carry out whatever the King writes to him. He shall keep going from one to the other and back to urge them on. Memorandum for Messer Francisco Gactule of Naples, who is going to Tartaglia. First, as soon as [Tartaglia?] has gone to the passes of Ascoli and the Tronto, Francisco shall order and tell [Name6?], on the King's behalf, to come immediately with his entire company, infantry, baggage train and everything to camp at the Maccione de le Rose, in the King's presence. For the King, with the counsel of [Name6?] and the other captains who are here, wishes to decide what he is to do, ride out and take the field. He must therefore be at the Maccione de le Rose by the fourth day of May at the latest. Likewise, Messer Francisco carries money to give to [Name6?], so that he can set out and come to His Majesty, as stated above. He shall tell [Name6?] that although the King is not obliged to give him money at present, and he is obliged to come to the King, the King nevertheless sends him 1,000 ducats through Messer Francisco, so that [Name6?] can come more easily and quickly with his entire company, baggage, infantry and gear. He shall therefore give him the money and arrange with [Name6?] that he comes to His Majesty with his whole company, baggage, infantry and gear by the fourth day of May at the latest, [as?] stated above. And he shall obtain [Name6?]'s promise under his own seal that he will come as stated.

Two documents, one cipher; proposed spring 1413 setting. Siena Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, no. 20 (DECODE R4808) is a captain’s complaint addressed to a king from Perugia on 30 March, without a written year. No. 23 (R4811) contains two royal memoranda for Iacobo Spinelo and Francisco Gactule. Its 4 May date is an arrival deadline, not an issue date. The best current historical hypothesis is Ladislaus of Naples’s campaign of spring 1413, with the memoranda probably written before 4 May. The year and correspondents remain inferred. Contents. The letter’s writer says an enemy has taken fully 200 horses and threatens retaliation despite the risk of royal punishment, while promising not to harm the Church’s lands, people or livestock. The first memorandum coordinates the guarding of passes near Ascoli, the Tronto, Arquata and Montemonaco to contain a hostile captain in the Marche, with intelligence gathering and limited, secret cooperation with the Malatesta. It also orders the recovery of castles using 140 lances. The second arranges a royal muster at “Maccione de le Rose”, a payment of 1,000 ducats, and a promise under seal. Why 1413. The Fermo chronicle describes an unusually close parallel in April 1413: forces at Forca di Presta and Sforza’s troops around Caldarola and Sarnano were placed to prevent Paolo Orsini from leaving the Marche at the King of Naples’s request. Orsini’s departure and pursuit are recorded on 10 May. This supports the campaign setting and fat = [Paolo Orsini?] , but supplies no verbatim decipherment. [ Cronache della città di Fermo, printed pp. 39–40 ] Probable participants. Minuti recounts Sforza’s grievance against Orsini, his service to Ladislaus, and his return to Perugia in February 1413 before pursuing Orsini in the Marche. This makes Muzio Attendolo Sforza a plausible writer of no. 20, although its subscription remains unread. Rodolfo is probably Rodolfo III da Varano; “messer Ludovico” probably Ludovico Migliorati. These contextual proposals do not replace the names actually recovered. [ Minuti, Vita di Muzzo Attendolo Sforza, pp. 163–169 ] Key comparison and dating safeguard. Meister’s printed Viviani nomenclator, dated 25 July 1412, has a circle-and-cross Sforza sign comparable to o+ . This supports [Sforza?] ; the Lucca alphabets differ, so they are not the recovered key. Meister’s 1421 date belongs explicitly to Siena piece no. 1, not nos. 20 or 23. The local “Siena1421” name therefore cannot date this pair. [ Meister, Die Anfänge der modernen diplomatischen Geheimschrift (1902), pp. 51, 55–57 ] Place and remaining limits. “Maccione de le Rose” probably denotes the Mazzone delle Rose muster ground. Later royal records independently attest a camp there, including near Ponte Annecchino in 1450; they support the place identification, not the date of these letters. [ I registri privilegiorum di Alfonso il Magnanimo, register 2905, nos. 11–16; register 2914, no. 27 ] The supplied research report surveys 44 key records, 43 with images, and reports no matching key; R4783 could not be inspected (it has no image on DECODE, confirmed 18 October 2026). It also reports no external copy of these plaintexts. These are bounded search results. The heading certainly names Tartaglia, but # = [Tartaglia?] remains tentative: # and the repeated e = [Name6?] may name different people. Name3–Name6, the place [Eucebio?], one difficult clause and the subscription remain unresolved. No priority or “oldest deciphered cipher” claim is made.

The unresolved dessut clause, [essereme?], [Eucebio?], [prout?], erasures, closing and subscription remain explicit. No new identity is treated as established. The seven reference signs occupy 41 positions; all remain open at the identity level. George Lasry supplied and reviewed the CTTS material and directed recovery with GPT-6 Astra. On 17 October 2026 George Lasry sent a consolidated report on all the cipher pieces of Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2, grouped by key. Its section on nos. 20 and 23 is filed verbatim in the repository ( targets/siena2023/lasry_report.md ). It states that both sheets are deciphered in full: about 4,260 symbols, one key with a nomenclator. It dates no. 20 to 30 March 1413 and no. 23 to mid-April 1413, from the contents and the Fermo chronicle’s record of the cordon round Orsini about 16 April. Its readings agree with the editions above in the passages compared; where the editions write [Name6?], the report writes ?. The key of nos. 20 and 23 as drawn in the report: 60 signs cut from the manuscript, each with its number of occurrences; homophones stand under their letter. No. 20 (R4808), [Muzio Attendolo Sforza?] to King Ladislaus, Perugia, 30 March [1413] (George Lasry) A captain in the king's pay, most probably Muzio Attendolo Sforza, to King Ladislaus of Naples, Perugia, 30 March 1413: an enemy, 'quel traditore de [Paolo Orsini?]', has taken fully 200 horses, and the writer threatens retaliation despite the risk of royal punishment, while promising not to harm the Church's lands, people or livestock. Decryption and translation are George Lasry's (PR #41 edition and his report of 17 Oct 2026); project_attempt/no20.txt is this project's independent 24 Sept transcription, on which his reading was checked. WHAT IT IS - 17 written lines. m.00 = clear salutation + 7 cipher signs; m.01-m.14 = continuous cipher, full width; m.15 = 41 cipher signs, then the clear dating clause on the same line; m.16 = one clear word at the left margin. - No interlinear glosses, no deletions noticed, no word separators, no dots between groups. CLEAR TEXT (as read; abbreviations expanded in round brackets) - Opening (m.00): "Sacra Regia Maie(sta)s(?) Serenissime princeps ac metuendissime d(omi)ne an(te?) terre pedu(m) oscula," - "Maie" carries a superscript "tas"/"tts" and a following s-like mark (Maiestas); "dne" has a macron. NOTE: the word before "terre" reads "an" with a long overstroke (an(te)?), NOT "post" as in the brief; one letter-form, but "a" + "n" are clear. A comma/virgula follows "oscula", then the cipher begins. - Closing (m.15, after the cipher): "Scriptum(?) Perusii(?) die penultimo mensis Martii" + one further word at the line end, unread (a capital like S/B + "r" + a looped final with a long descender; possibly an abbreviation of the year or of the subscription). "Scriptum": S + c + a-like letter + u/r + p with a stroke through the descender (Scriptu(m)/Scripta?). "Perusii": p + r-shaped (per-?) + u + long s + y = P(er)usy = Perusii (Perugia), reading fairly likely. "die penultimo mensis Martii" certain ("Marty" with a y-ending). - m.16, left margin under the first cipher signs of m.15: "Ind" with a looped I and a crossed/abbreviated d (Ind(ictione)? or start of a subscription), nothing else on that line. SIGN LEGEND (names used in the transcription; "^x" = superscript x written ABOVE the preceding sign) Letter-like signs a a (closed bowl, short tail); almost always in "f a" (27 of 37) b b: tall ascender (often looped) with a closed bowl at the foot. Most Serene Prince and most dread Lord, after kissing the ground at your feet. As Your Royal Majesty can and ought to know, and as I have written to you several times, that traitor [Paolo Orsini?] has all this time been striving to ruin me and take away my lands and my company. Up to now he has taken fully two hundred horses from me, and many times I have complained of it to Your Royal Majesty. You have always comforted me and promised to act with our Lord so that these things would cease; yet nothing has been done ⟨unresolved connection: dessut⟩ [Paolo Orsini?]. On the contrary, the said traitor has behaved worse from day to day. Thus, seeing him [to be my?] mortal enemy, I have resolved—even if I were certain that Your Royal Majesty would have my head cut off—to do to him, to the extent of my power, what he has wanted to do to me. I inform you that tomorrow, on the last day of this month, I shall leave this town and go to find that traitor, and do against him whatever I can, even if it puts me in danger. For I would rather see myself lose my property once than have it taken from me every day in this way. Of one thing I assure and inform you: I shall do no harm to the Church's lands and people, whether to persons or livestock. But as between him and me, consider me excused, for I am resolved to do the worst I can. For when I was in the territory of [Eucebio?], he set out with his company to come and find me, as Your Royal Majesty and all the world know. First, the said Iacobo shall tell [Tartaglia?] that the King wishes him, together with Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], with diligence, vigour and every precaution, to ensure that [Paolo Orsini?] can neither return to nor get back out of the Marche. He is to spread the word that he has gone to these passes and places for fear that the troops in the Marche might get out, come and damage the said lands and other places belonging to the King, and in order to have the works on the Tronto completed. He shall also tell [Tartaglia?] to finish getting ready without delay, so that, if the King wants him, with [Name3], [Sforza?] and Rodolfo's men, to attack [Paolo Orsini?] or lay siege to him, they can do so immediately. They must coordinate well and keep good spies so that nothing can fail, for the whole affair depends on this. Orders shall be given to the infantry for whatever this business requires and for completing the works on the Tronto. They are to come to a secret understanding with the Malatesta on this matter and on no others, and report whether they could defeat him on the march [or break his escort]. Likewise, he shall deliver the same message, as appropriate, to Rodolfo, [Name3] and [Sforza?], telling them to guard the passes and places on that side, while [Tartaglia?] guards those on this side. They shall let it be said that [Name3] and [Sforza?] have gone there both because [Paolo Orsini?] has taken their companions from them and is their enemy, and so that neither [Paolo Orsini?], Messer Ludovico nor the Malatesta can harm the King's allies and loyal subjects. Likewise, Iacobo shall tell or write to [Sforza?] that, at the request of Rodolfo and [Name3], he must meet and join forces with them as requested. He must therefore be at the Maccione de le Rose by the fourth day of May at the latest. The marginal text under Throckmorton’s letter of 10 July 1559 (BL Add MS 4136 f. 32, DECODE R2988), one of the two ciphers Tomokiyo lists as unidentified. Its 222 groups have the statistics of English words, so it is a word-sign code, and half its tokens are signs used once. It probably copies the 8 July despatches; without its key or their originals it cannot be deciphered. / u+d z+e+l’ t i’+v+e+r / s i⁶ u+h – y+y+d c+o+o+p’ u: n … groups of one to four dotted signs; “/” and “//” mark the clauses Paris · word-sign code (dotted letter-like signs) · probably 8 July 1559 The margin code on Throckmorton’s leaf, 1559 A half-page of dotted signs under Throckmorton’s letter of 10 July 1559: a code of word signs, half of them used once, which cannot be read without its key or the despatch it copies. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The text About twelve lines of small cursive signs below and beside the subscription of Throckmorton’s letter of 10 July 1559, with a date line “… 8 … 1559” and a three-line block keyed by a star to the letter. Where British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 32 (old f. 9), in the Forbes Papers; DECODE R2988 (catalogue item 97). Tomokiyo lists it as a cipher “yet unidentified”. The cipher Small letter-like signs whose value changes with the position of their dots, in groups of one to four signs: a word-sign code or shorthand, like the dotted-letter word codes of Thomas Smith (1563) and the Cecil–Norris table. How it was tried Transcribed sign by sign (about 405 signs in 222 groups) and measured against English; tested as mirrored and inverted script; the known keys of the volume and the period tried. Why it resists Each group is a word, and 113 of the 222 tokens are signs used only once. A sign seen once carries no evidence of its own value, so no method that works from the ciphertext alone can reach half of the text. What would finish it Its key, or the originals of the 8 July 1559 despatches it probably copies (TNA SP 70/5; CSP Foreign I nos. 947, 950) as a crib. Other ciphers Throckmorton’s letter above it is in his Cipher 1, deciphered in part on its own page ; John Wood’s 1568 line on the next leaf has its own page . f. 32, lower half: the marginal text, its date line “… 8 … 1559” and the starred block. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 32 (lower half), via DECODE R2988.

Transcribed sign by sign ( margin_transcription.txt , first pass): about 405 signs in 222 groups, about 29 base shapes (22 frequent) and about 80 shape-and-dot combinations. Groups average 1.9 signs; 106 are single signs. One boxed group occurs four times and is probably a name. Written left to right, with “/” and “//” as clause marks; not Hebrew, not mirrored or inverted Latin. What it probably is. The date line reads “… 8 … 1559”, and the letter above it says Throckmorton wrote twice on the 8th. The margin is likely his copy of the 8 July despatches (CSP Foreign I nos. 947, 950: Lord Grey’s ransom, the French King’s fever, forces for Scotland, Ruy Gomez, Arran at Geneva, Anne du Bourg), sent again with the letter of the 10th. Lord Grey, who recurs in both abstracts, is the best candidate for the boxed group. The calendar gives only abstracts, and the originals (SP 70/5) are only in the subscription State Papers Online.

Taking each group as a word: 222 tokens give 141 types and 113 once-only types. The same measure on 222-word stretches of Bain’s calendar gives a median of 140 and 107 ( margin_stats.py ). Letter-for-letter English would give groups of about 4.3 signs with few single letters. The signs change value with the position of their dots, like the dotted-letter word codes of the period. 51% of the tokens are signs used once, which the ciphertext alone cannot determine, so no ciphertext-only method can reach half of the text, let alone the 95% the project asks of a full reading. The key leaves bound in the same volume (ff. 173–185, DECODE R9258–R9262) hold Throckmorton’s and Smith’s letter ciphers, not this code; Tomokiyo’s Ciphers 1–3, Smith’s 1563 cipher, the Cecil–Norris table and the Moray–Wood signs give nothing on it.

Kryptos K4, the Beale papers, Voynich, Debosnys, the Kaliningrad bottle, D’Agapeyeff, Dorabella and seventeen more: real ciphers with no accepted reading, ranked, each tagged with the reason it holds out (open, needs a source, too short to prove, probably no message, unbreakable, undecided) and where it stands on 5 November 2026. Lost scripts are left out. 97 characters · 1,188 glyphs · 520 numbers 87 symbols · 392 digits · 135 letters twenty-five ciphers, none with an accepted reading A survey · November 2026 Top 25 unsolved ciphers Real ciphers with ciphertext in hand and no accepted reading, ranked, from Kryptos K4 to a ten-letter inscription, each tagged with the reason it holds out. Lost scripts are left out. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 · every entry checked against the repository notes and the open web on 5 November 2026 The short version. Nothing on this list has an accepted reading. Five entries are genuinely open: a workable amount of ciphertext and a method that could still be recovered. Five more need a source nobody has: a transcription, a codebook, a book, or a better scan. Nine are too short for any reading to be proved, and several of those have been attacked to exhaustion. Two probably hold no message, one is unbreakable without its key material, and three are undecided. The page ranks interest, not difficulty: ranked by tractability, Debosnys, Kaliningrad and the diplomatic codes of 1917–21 would come first.

Three things count, in this order. The thing must be a cipher , with a message hidden from readers who did not hold the key, which rules out every lost script (see below). There must be enough ciphertext on paper for a solution, if one turned up, to be proved against the text. And the story must be worth a reader’s time. The first two are checkable and the third is a judgement, so the order inside each band is mine. The tag on each row says why the cipher is still unsolved: tag what it means open A genuine cipher of workable length where the method is plausibly recoverable. Effort can still pay. needs a source The ciphertext is real and long enough, but a transcription, a key, a codebook or a better scan is missing. Nothing more can be done from the text alone. unprovable Real encipherment, but so short, or with so much room in the key, that many readings fit and none can be demonstrated. probably no message Our tests, and most of the literature, point to a text that was constructed, botched or never enciphered. unbreakable Without the original key material the answer is not in the ciphertext. undecided Two live explanations, or a disputed claim, and no test yet separates them.

# Cipher Why it holds out Where it stands, 5 November 2026 1 Kryptos K4 CIA, Langley, 1990 97 characters open The method is unbroken. Kobek and Byrne recovered the plaintext from Sanborn’s papers in 2025, which they say is not a cryptographic solve, and the archive sold in November 2025 for $962,500. The plaintext is unpublished. 2 The Beale papers, B1 and B3 Virginia, pamphlet of 1885 520 and 618 numbers probably no message Only B2 decodes (with the Declaration of Independence). Lost scripts: Linear A, the Phaistos disc, the Indus script and Rohonc. A cipher hides a message; these were written to be read by people who are gone. Zodiac Z340, read in December 2020. The Shanghai gold bars: 21 of 26 letters occur exactly ten times, which says they were constructed, not enciphered ( gold bars ). Not ciphers at all: the Rilke cryptogram (typewriter keys, Morse practice), Codex Seraphinianus (asemic by its author’s statement), the YOG’TZE case (closed as an accident), and the Riverbanks Ripper (an April Fools’ joke of 2017). Read since Schmeh’s list: Rivest’s timelock (2019), Bonus 22 (2018), the crypt cryptograms (2019), the silk dress cryptogram (2023), Ferdinand III’s letters (2017).

Several readings have been announced in 2026 and none is accepted. A claimed reading counts when someone else can run it and when the same method, run on a matched control with no message in it, returns nothing readable. Urquhart’s distich, Zodiac Z13 and Z32, the Voynich preprints and the Beale “breakthrough” have not been shown to pass that test. A different kind of claim is real but not a solve: Kryptos K4’s plaintext surfaced from an archive, and the cipher that produced it is still unexplained.

Archivio Segreto Vaticano, Segr. Stato Spagna 1A/2, ff. 70r–73v. Set as MysteryTwister ’s Vatican Challenge Part 5 by George Lasry in 2019; its key was recovered by Simon Klee in September 2026. This project’s own attempt did not obtain the text and misidentified the system; it is kept below as a record. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 September 2026 · updated 6 November 2026 · independent review and earlier attempt: Daniel Bourdeau Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained Credits · Simon Klee (earlier solution) · George Lasry (transcription, pointer to a source) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter A letter from the Farnese chancery to a nuncio: four folios, 6549 code digits, with long passages left in clear. The clear passages mention the Diet of Speyer (February–April 1542), the peace negotiations between Charles V and Francis I, and the couriers Gioi da Montepulciano and Montepescali. Where Catalogued as Lett. Orig. e cifre del card. Farnese al nunzio , 4 Oct 1539–24 Nov 1548; a MysteryTwister challenge, with the manuscript images on DECODE records 91 and 92. The cipher Not an Antonio Elio polyphonic-syllabic cipher, as this page first argued. Each letter has one code of one or two digits, with a small layer of dotted syllable and title codes; 9 is the null. Why this attempt failed The earlier diagnosis took digit 4 for a null and the cipher for a syllabic codebook. Five model classes were tested here; Meister’s four printed keys were all rejected. Digit 4 is in fact o . How it was solved Simon Klee searched code assignments and one- versus two-digit boundaries together, submitted key and candidate plaintext on 15 September 2026, and the challenge team accepted it. Either half of the letter independently recovers the same eighteen letters and null. What it says The opening decrypts as Dopo la partita del Montepulciano . 6,358 of 6,562 digit tokens decrypt exactly, giving a 1,241-word candidate plaintext in Italian. Still open Damaged digits and supplied letters: 170 tokens fall on recorded departures and 34 remain in gaps.

Klee searched for the code assignments and the boundaries between one- and two-digit codes together. The decisive check is the split experiment: either half of the letter independently recovers the same eighteen letters and null, in all twelve half-text restarts. The same method recovers invented keys from clean and damaged synthetic texts; a shuffled copy of the real digits scores far worse. This is much stronger than one fluent output from one language model. The page then tests the model. A predicted u in Montepulciano points to a digit transcribed as 2 ; the manuscript shows the clerk’s hooked 1 , exactly the code for u/v . A systematic image review found five duplicated groups, fourteen omitted digits and two swapped pairs in the public transcription. Historical sources independently corroborate the public offer of papal aid at Speyer and the Gonzaga people and places in the closing report. After those corrections, 6,358 of 6,562 digit tokens decrypt exactly, including 365 nulls; 170 tokens are consumed by recorded departures and 34 remain in gaps. That supports the recovered key and the substance of the 1,241-word Italian plaintext. It does not turn every damaged passage into certainty, which is why “candidate plaintext” remains the right description of the edition. The recovered alphabet is 5=a 8=e 6=i 4=o 1=u/v 7=n 2=r 0=s 3=m 03=l 73=d 80=t 57=p 27=c 72=b 37=f 75=g 07=z ; 81=et and 9 is null. Dotted pairs supply ce/ci, qua/que/qui, non and three abbreviated titles. The opening decrypts as Dopo la partita del Montepulciano , “After Montepulciano’s departure”. Primary credit and research files: Simon Klee, “The Farnese letter” . Repository record: solution review and recovered key . Earlier investigation retained, conclusions superseded The remainder of this page records the failed September 2026 investigation for reproducibility. Its measurements and exclusions describe what was tried, but its claims that the key was out of reach, that 4 was a null, or that the design was an Antonio Elio polyphonic syllabary are retracted.

Four folios, 6549 code digits, with long passages left in clear. The clear passages date and place it beyond doubt: they mention la dieta di Spira , the Diet of Speyer which sat from February to April 1542; la materia della pace and la parte di Francia , the negotiations between Charles V and Francis I; a papal breve for quello di Osma ; and the couriers Gioi da Montepulciano and Montepescali . The fascicle is catalogued as Lett. Orig. e cifre del card. Farnese al nunzio, 4 oct 1539 – 24 nov 1548 . The courier's name is a tantalising detail. Aloys Meister printed, in 1906, a key headed “Cifra data a Monsig. Montepulciano” and dated between 1539 and 1542, and another headed “Cifra ultima con Mons. Poggio mandata per il Montepulciano” , the last cipher with Poggio, sent by way of Montepulciano. The right people, the right courier, the right years. Neither key fits, and that is checked below.

the null settled Digit 4 is a null, but not a word separator Conditioning on 4 in the middle drops the mutual information between its neighbours to 0.030, which is what Italian gives across a word boundary (0.028), where every other digit sits between 0.08 and 0.17. Meister's key of 1539–42 spells the convention out: “pongasi la nulla al fine di ogni parola” , put the null at the end of every word. This scribe did not. There are 482 nulls where the text needs about 1300 word ends, so the stretches between them average 12.6 digits, far too long to be words, which misled two earlier passes here. The chancery instruction quoted in section 04 resolves it: the null marks the end of a letter or syllable carrying an abbreviation, not the end of a word. the vowels three independent tests The vowel-bearing digits are {7, 0, 3} Italian ends about 97% of its words in a vowel, so word-final enrichment separates the classes. Over the 482 stretches: 1: 1.79 7: 1.76 3: 1.52 0: 1.49 against 6: 1.01 9: 0.64 2: 0.58 5: 0.25 8: 0.08 . Digit 8 ends a word at one twelfth of its overall rate. The frequency masses agree independently, to three decimals: {7,0,3,1} carries 0.476 of the text where all five Italian vowels carry 0.479. And a third line, new this session, agrees again: every string enriched immediately before a null ends in one of those digits. the word endings new Two units carry a third of all word endings Scanning every n-gram for enrichment before a null gives an extremely sharp answer. unit occurrences immediately before a null p 27 265 86 7.4 × 10 −33 80 349 82 4.2 × 10 −21 73 222 38 9.8 × 10 −7 37 73 17 1.7 × 10 −5 27 and 80 together end 35% of the marked words. For comparison, the commonest two-letter ending in real Italian takes under 5%. Word endings this concentrated are single codes, not letter pairs. structure new Two-digit units, and a real phase The stretches between nulls prefer even lengths, 278 against 202, chi-squared 12.0 on one degree of freedom. An earlier pass here looked at exactly this and recorded “no preference”; that was an error, and it cost two attacks. Inside those stretches the digit distribution at even offsets differs from the one at odd offsets: chi-squared 39.4 against a null of 8.3 ± 4.1 built by shuffling each segment, z = +7.6 . Digit 9 sits at even offsets 1.60 times as often as odd. Every doubled digit is suppressed, some severely: 00 occurs 6 times against 117 expected, 44 twice against 35, 99 twice against 21. Four hundred shuffles of the same digits produce a mean of 0.01 such suppressed pairs and never more than one.

the polyphonic single-digit model excluded by a matched control No key of that kind exists to find A constrained trigram search, with vowels restricted to {7,0,3,1} and consonants to {8,5,2,6,9}, gives 24 different keys in 24 runs, mean agreement 0.861 where chance in the same constrained space is 0.799. That alone would only mean the search failed. So the identical search was run on a synthetic ciphertext built to the same design: real Italian, same alphabet, same vowel split, same polyphony, same null density, same 6553 digits. agreement between runs recovers the key? synthetic, same design 0.90 yes, 0.97 the real ciphertext 0.86 (chance 0.80) no The method works at this polyphony, this length and this alphabet. The real text is therefore not a polyphonic single-digit substitution of Italian. the letter level excluded The consonant runs are three times too long If each digit stood for one letter, the alternation of vowel-digits and consonant-digits would have to match Italian's own. The share matches. The runs do not. cipher period Italian vowel share 0.475 0.464 mean vowel run 1.604 1.301 mean consonant run 1.769 1.504 consonant runs of 3 or more 0.183 0.059 And the three tests that fix the vowels disagree about the fourth member. Frequency mass picks {7,0,3, 1 }; a search over all subsets for the best match to Italian's run profile picks {0, 2 ,3,7}; the final-digit distribution picks {7,0,3, 6 }. All three agree on {7,0,3} and contradict each other beyond it. No single letter-level assignment satisfies all three, which is exactly what happens when the units are not letters. Meister's four printed keys all rejected Including the two named for the right courier Read directly from the 1906 page images rather than from OCR. Key 1, Cifra data a Monsig. Montepulciano , has Nulla 1 where this cipher's null is 4. Key 2, the Poggio cipher sent by Montepulciano, puts the vowels on 3 5 7 9 0, which the word-final evidence contradicts. Key 3, which shares the null 4, predicts digit 8 at 5.0% of the text where it is observed at 13.6% . Key 4 writes vowels as two-digit codes beginning with 1, which would make digit 1 about 40% of the text; it is 3.1%. Meister sampled these from Rome, Biblioteca Chigi M II 49, ff. 85–148 , some sixty folios of Vatican keys of 1539–1566, of which he printed a handful. The key to this letter is most likely in that manuscript, which is not digitised.

Antonio Elio (1506–1576), known in his own lifetime as Antonio delle Zifre , was cipher secretary to Paul III , the pope whose cardinal-nephew and Secretary of State, Alessandro Farnese, wrote this letter. He is credited with inventing the polyphonic cipher, and he trained the Argenti brothers who followed him. In 2025 Lasry, Simonetta and Biermann published a reconstruction of one of his designs. It has four properties: Syllabic. Most symbols encode consonant-vowel syllables, with a few for clusters or short words. Polyphonic. Every syllable symbol carries two meanings, and the second is chosen by a dot on the preceding symbol . The dots are applied inconsistently, so even a secretary holding the key is often guessing. Compound symbols. Some elements are encoded by pairs, so any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a pair . h and every doubled letter are dropped before encryption. Each of those makes a prediction, and this cryptogram satisfies all four. measured here Elio's design all ten doubled digits suppressed — 00 occurs 6 times against 117 expected doubled letters dropped before encryption dotted digits are 7, 2, 0 and the digit after a dot is 2/0/7/5 the dot sits on the antecedent and selects the alternate meaning word-final units are two digits, 27 and 80 , at p < 10 −20 consonant-vowel syllables as units unsupervised units come out 15% one digit, 32% two, 29% three; the even-length preference is real but only 58/42 any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a compound consonant runs three times too long for letters the level is syllables, not letters The doubling rule is not an inference. Meister prints the Farnese chancery’s own written instruction: “Scrivasi stretto et senza duplicare le consonanti quando occorrono dittioni che la ricerchino”: write tightly, and without doubling the consonants where the words call for them. The same instruction says other names may be abbreviated “con il segno della nulla in fine della lettera o sillaba” , with the null at the end of a letter or syllable. That reframes digit 4: it is an abbreviation and syllable marker, not a word separator , which is why the stretches between nulls average 12.6 digits and never did look like words.

Lasry, Megyesi and Kopal worked this exact corpus for Cryptologia in 2021. Two of their sentences govern everything here. On the one published key that names Poggio, the one whose title matches this letter’s own courier: “attempts to decipher the ciphertexts using that key did not produce any result.” And on the cipher itself: “The scheme appears to be a variable-length polyphonic cipher , which is a unique case in the Vatican collections … The ciphertexts in the second part (IA-2) seem to belong to another key.” Their phrase for the scheme, variable-length polyphonic , is what the run-length, phase and compression work on this page arrived at from the other direction, without having read it. The 2025 paper is blunter. “Ciphertext-only cryptanalysis for such a cipher would be extremely difficult and nearly impossible, even with modern computing, without prior knowledge of the principles of its complex design.” And with matching plaintext in hand, recovering the key of a sibling took three expert cryptanalysts two full days to make initial inroads, and many hours more to finish.

No edition, calendar or regesta prints this letter. The Spanish nunciature of the period has no published series at all: Monumenta Hispaniae Vaticana stops at 1486, Olarra’s index begins in 1556, Serrano covers 1566–72. Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland I/7 prints Poggio but jumps from December 1541 to July 1543, its editor noting that the 1542 correspondence survives only in fragments. Concilium Tridentinum IV prints Farnese to Poggio on 5 February and 4 June 1542 and has nothing from April; its two April letters go to the nuncio in France instead. Pastor prints exactly two Farnese–Poggio letters, February 1541 and August 1542. Three manuscripts would settle it, and none is digitised: Naples, Archivio di Stato, Carte Farnesiane 723 : a Farnese to Poggio letter of 12 April 1542 , three days before this one and in the same courier cycle. AAV, Lettere de’ Principi 14 A : the Farnese to Poggio register copies, running to 4 June 1542. This is where the printed editions took their texts. BAV, Chigi L III 65 : the originals, 348 folios. Calibrating from dated letters in the editions puts 23 November 1541 at f. 153 and 29 June 1542 at ff. 191–195, so 15 April 1542 should sit at roughly ff. 165–190 . These registers are repeatedly described as carrying contemporary interlinear decipherments. A clear copy may simply be sitting there.

Part 4 of the same challenge series is the Portugal cryptogram from the same Vatican collection, and its key has been recovered. Compare the two transcripts as they are distributed. transcript single spaces between digits double spaces Portugal IA-1 — Part 4, solved 7603 3210 Spain IA-2 — Part 5, this one 6412 6 The Portugal transcript carries the spacing of its page; the Spain transcript is one undivided stream. When this section was first written it read the difference as a transcriber’s omission that the images would repair. That was wrong. George Lasry, who set the challenge, confirmed on 16 September 2026 that the Part 5 documents carry no visual separators at all (no dots, commas or wider spaces between tokens), and that recognising the variable-length tokens is the point of the challenge and the reason it is rated Level X. The 400 dpi images, examined in section 10, bear him out. The asymmetry between Parts 4 and 5 is real, but it is in the manuscripts, not in the transcription, and no image can repair it.

If the text sat on a fixed two-digit grid it could be cut into units and attacked as a substitution over about a hundred symbols with three thousand tokens. That is tractable, and it is the one thing that would make this cryptogram breakable. So it was tested directly, in the three ways the null could behave. phasing chi-squared, even vs odd shuffle null z null counted, absolute index 6.8 9.0 ± 4.2 −0.53 null deleted, global index 4.3 8.0 ± 4.0 −0.93 null deleted, per cleartext run 4.3 8.0 ± 4.0 −0.93 All three sit below their shuffle nulls. There is no fixed two-digit grid anywhere in the text. The only phase signal is a local one that restarts at each null, and it is modest. That is the final piece, and it is exactly what Elio’s compound symbols predict: any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a pair. Without a segmentation there is no unit inventory; without a unit inventory there is no substitution to attack; and the polyphony doubles every unit’s meaning on top of that.

The earlier attempt concluded that the cipher is a variable-length syllabic code : mostly two-digit units, some of one digit, over vowel-bearing digits {7,0,3} and consonant-bearing {8,5,2,6,9}, with 27 and 80 as the dominant word-final units and 4 as an intermittent word null. The arithmetic is consistent: 6068 non-null digits at about two per unit is some 3000 units, at about 2.3 units per word some 1300 words of four to five letters, which is ordinary Italian for four folios. Against a shuffle of its own digits the text has 441 repeated 7-grams where the shuffle gives 5 , and 244 repeated 8-grams where the shuffle gives none. Unsupervised byte-pair encoding separates it from both controls: compression gain +1.6% for the cipher, −8.2% for genuine Italian pushed through a polyphonic single-digit cipher, −14.0% for a shuffle. It is a codebook, and it recurs because the same words recur. What would open it is the key from Chigi M II 49, or a matching plaintext in the Farnese correspondence of April 1542, or more ciphertext in the same key. Klee’s search later recovered the key without any of them. Five model classes have now been tested here, two of them against matched synthetic controls that the same code solves correctly. Working files in targets/vatican5/ : vc.py and vc_syn.py (the constrained search and its matched control), phase.py (parity and phase), escape.py (suppressed pairs), units2.py (unit inventory), bpe.py (unsupervised units with controls), cvtest.py (the vowel/consonant run test).

On 18 September 2026 the DECODE records behind the challenge were opened with a registered account: record 92, the eight 400 dpi page images of this letter with its transcription and address leaf, and record 91, the letter bound just before it in the same volume (ff. 62v–66v, catalogued as Spain IA-1). There is only one transcription DECODE’s transcription of record 92 is byte for byte the text MysteryTwister distributes. The images are the only new evidence. The address leaf confirms the transcription of the clear frame: Al Rev.mo mons. come fratello il vescovo di Tropea, Nuntio di N.S. (Poggio was bishop of Tropea), endorsed Roma 1542, dal Card.le Farnese ; the last page closes Da Roma alli XV di Aprile 1542 … Come fratello, Il Car. Farnese . No hidden decipherment Faint writing runs between the cipher lines of 70v. Mirrored, it reads dar notitia … circa la materia della … and per questa causa principali è stato mandato : the cleartext of 70r showing through the leaf. There is no interlinear decipherment on any page. An image-verified transcript Every cipher line of 70r–73r was checked against the images, digit by digit. The transcript proves sound, but not perfect: 151 digit positions change (2.3%), 62 by substitution, 39 by insertion, 22 by deletion. The largest single fault is on 71v, where the transcriber copied four groups twice ; on 72v and 73r the scribe struck digits through, and those are now marked. Of the 202 dots in the transcript nearly all sit over the digit given; about 20 missed dots were added, for 222. The commonest confusion is the scribe’s flat-topped 3 against his z-shaped 2 and barred 7. About 90 small dots also stand on the line between digits, all on 71r–73r. The digit before one is most often the null 4. At one per seventy digits they are far too sparse to divide words, as Lasry said, and look like clause punctuation. No structural statistic moves. Doubled digits, the dotted digits (7, then 2 and 0), the digits that follow a dot (7, 2, 0, 5), the vowel set and the unit inventory are what the earlier sessions measured. The sibling letter is another key this letter (IA-2) Spain IA-1 Portugal IA-1 (Part 4, solved) digits 6552 2956 10934 doubled digits, against chance 0.30 0.88 0.57 share of digit 1 3% 16% 16% IA-1, a December letter on the Diet of Nuremberg and Buda, repeats digits freely and leans on digits this letter hardly uses. Lasry, Megyesi and Kopal called IA-2 “another key” than IA-1; the numbers agree, and nothing transfers. Record 91’s four document images are cleartext Farnese letters of summer 1542, with no key sheet. Its key was found on 5 November 2026: Meister’s key no. 2, the Poggio cipher, read polyphonically. It is a different cipher, with its own page . A new exclusion: no renumbering of the Farnese keys fits A doubled digit stays doubled however a key is renumbered, so the rate of doubled digits belongs to the key’s design, not its numbering. Italian, written in the chancery’s own orthography (no h, no doubled letters), encoded with each printed key: encoding doubled digits against chance Meister key 1, data a Monsig. Montepulciano 9.7% 0.82 Meister key 2, ultima con Mons. Poggio 7.8% 0.63 any polyphonic single-digit key 6.4% 0.48 this letter 3.6% 0.30 Key 2 would put about 510 doubled digits into 6552; the letter has 233, some twelve standard deviations short. So neither printed Farnese key, under any relabelling of its digits , is this letter’s key. This one was built so that the same digit almost never has to be written twice. Only 7, 5 and 8 double at all, which is what a syllabary gives when most digits serve only as the first half of a unit or only as the second. DECODE holds nothing further The public catalogue has no other record from Paul III’s chancery: nothing under Poggio, Montepulciano, Tropea or Chigi, Farnese only from 1579, and no papal item among the records of 1538–1548. The four undated papal keys of the Camera Apostolica (records 23, 202–204) were fetched as a last check. They are the Avignon keys of Gabriele de Lavinde, about 1379: symbol alphabets and letter-pair nomenclators, 160 years too early. So the images did what Lasry said they would: they settle the dots and the doubtful digits, and nothing more. The routes in are the ones in section 09 (the key, the clear copy, or more of the Spagna 1A ciphertext), and all three need an order from the archive. Working files in targets/vatican5/ : IA-2_reread.txt (the image-verified transcript), decode/reread/ (the page-by-page readings with every disagreement listed), decode/build_reread.py . The images themselves are the Vatican’s and are not redistributed.

Four cipher letters of Afonso VI, countersigned by Castelo Melhor, to the general of the Alentejo army, written while Don John of Austria besieged and took Évora (ANTT, Luís de Miranda Pereira liv. 2). Brice Dudout recovered the substitution key from the ciphertext of the 26 May letter, froze it and tested it on the 13 May letter; second copies with other homophones and a sentence clear in one copy and enciphered in the other confirm it. The court sends cavalry and pay, plans to bring the King to Setúbal, and orders the relief of Évora at all risk, even at the cost of a battle. Catalogued as 1660–61. Contributed by Brice Dudout. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letters Four letters of Afonso VI, signed Rey and countersigned by the Count of Castelo Melhor, to Sancho Manuel de Vilhena, Count of Vila Flor, governor of arms of the Alentejo: 13 May, 15 May (a long letter and a short note) and 26 May 1663, while Don John of Austria besieged and took Évora. Where Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Luís de Miranda Pereira, liv. 2 (PT/TT/LMP/0002), on DigitArq: images 87; 53–57 and 59; 69 and 71; 37 and 39. Three of the four letters survive in two ciphered copies. Catalogue no. 391, which dated them 1660–61: they are of May 1663. The cipher A letter-for-letter substitution on Portuguese with a few homophones: numbers from 2 to 53 and letter-like symbols, separated by points. The greeting and the date stay in clear, and in the long letter whole paragraphs. How it was deciphered Brice Dudout recovered the key from the 26 May letter alone, froze it, and tested it on the 13 May letter, which had been transcribed without it. Second copies enciphered with other homophones, and a sentence clear in one copy and in cipher in the other, confirm it. What it says Cavalry on its way, money for the pay, and a plan for the King to come to Setúbal; then the order to relieve Évora “a todo o risco”, even at the cost of a battle, repeated on 26 May as the King’s final resolution. Still open One symbol used once (ʒ) and a struck-out name in the 13 May letter; about fifteen encipherer’s slips there corrected from the sense. Of the long 15 May letter, only a 174-symbol passage is transcribed in the repository. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée), working with Claude Opus 5.5: transcription, key, decipherment, Portuguese text, translation and notes. His write-up .

In spring 1663 Don John Joseph of Austria invaded the Alentejo. From Lisbon the court, governed by the Count of Castelo Melhor, escrivão da puridade , in the name of the young Afonso VI, wrote almost daily to the general of the Portuguese army, the Count of Vila Flor. Book 2 of the Luís de Miranda Pereira collection at the Torre do Tombo (864 images on DigitArq) keeps letters of that correspondence, among them four in cipher. Each is signed Rey , countersigned by Castelo Melhor and addressed P[ar]a o Conde de V[ila] Flor . date images symbols in the repository key subject 13 May 1663 87 636 K2 the cavalry sent as reinforcements 15 May 1663, letter 53, 54, 59 (copy 1); 55, 56, 57 (copy 2) 174, one passage of copy 2 K3 reinforcements, money, the King at Setúbal 15 May 1663, note 69 (second copy 71) 509 K1, K2 relieve Évora at all risk 26 May 1663 37 (second copy 39) 634 K1 the King’s final resolution Most letters were sent twice, the original and a via by another courier, and both copies are bound here, each enciphered separately with other homophones and other line breaks. The two copies of the long letter of 15 May are interleaved: their third leaves are swapped in the binding, so that copy 1 runs over images 53, 54 and 59 and copy 2 over 55, 56 and 57. The cipher itself proves it, since a word runs on across the leaves ( estam r|[ec]olhidos ). The catalogue entry (no. 391) dated the cipher letters 1660–61; every one of them is dated in clear in May 1663. The letter of 26 May 1663: Conde Amigo. Eu ElRey vos envio muito saudar como aquelle q[ue] amo in clear, then the cipher, Ƶ·3·31·17·50·Δ·31 Ƶ·3 10·5·ß·A·3·30 , despois de hontem . The sixth and seventh cipher lines carry he socorrer Evora em todo o cazo e a todo o risco . A substitution of single letters, on Portuguese, with no code words. The symbols are numbers and letter-like shapes written with points between them. Several are ordinary cursive letters standing for other letters, which makes a run look like garbled Portuguese: x is c , h is l , n is f , r is g , a is p , d is x . The repository transcribes the special shapes by the letter they resemble: Z for a barred z (Ƶ), D for a delta (Δ), B for a long-stemmed B (ß), F for a barred 7 (ꝼ), K for an overlined x (Ӿ). Key K1, as recovered from the 26 May letter (30 distinct symbols there): plain symbols plain symbols plain symbols a 4 h F, 10 p 17, a b 7 i 11, D q 21 c x l h, 25 r 6 d Z m 30 s 31 e 3 n 40, B t 24, A f n o 50, 5 u / v 22 g r, 8 x d, 27 z K The other letters use a few more homophones, set on the 13 May letter itself (K2): 9 = c, a looped 9 (g) = e, e = q, 2 = f, p = a, Q = u/v, S = b, 53 = d, u = m, & = e. The long letter of 15 May was deciphered with K3; the K2 and K3 files in the repository list the same forty values. No key has a symbol for j , k or y , or for the cedilla and the tilde, and u and v are not distinguished. Numbers of two or more figures are written in clear inside the cipher ( 203 cavallos , 56 , 55 ), and so are some dates, which is a trap: in the 13 May letter 10 and 9 are days of the month, although 10 and 9 are also the symbols for h and c .

One letter, no crib. The 26 May letter carries no decipherment, and no key survives in the volume. Brice Dudout transcribed it symbol by symbol (634 positions, one of them lost in a tear of the right margin) and recovered K1 from it alone, with Portuguese letter statistics and the words such a letter must contain: que , exercito , cartas , risco . The key was then frozen, its SHA-256 fingerprint recorded, before any test. A test fixed in advance. The 13 May letter, transcribed without the key (636 symbols), was decoded with the frozen K1 and scored with a Portuguese language model: −2.61 per character. The same letter with its symbols shuffled scored at best −4.52, and keys with permuted values at best −5.52 in 200 trials, while a Portuguese text enciphered with K1 with 3% of simulated errors scores −2.58. K1 covers 92.8% of the 13 May symbols; the extra homophones of K2 were then set on that letter. The other copies. The second copy of 26 May (image 39) and the second copy of the 15 May note (image 71) are enciphered with other homophones and other line breaks; each gives the same text, and between them they settle every doubtful symbol of the first copies. The frozen K1 decodes the note at −2.25 per character, against at best −4.72 for the controls. Of the long 15 May letter both copies were deciphered with K3: they agree with the established text at 98.7% and 99.0%, and with each other at 0.927, against at best 0.131 when one copy’s symbols are shuffled (20 trials). A sentence in clear. Copy 1 of the long letter writes one sentence in clear that copy 2 enciphers (image 57, lines 20–26). The key gives 164 of its 166 characters; the two differences are spelling ( quasi and quazi , thenente and tenente ): K3 on copy 2: a defensa e quazi no mesmo tempo tinha enviado o tenente de mestre de campo general luis ribeiro para que tomando as noticias convenientes encaminhe dali as carruagens e outros socorros pela parte mais segura copy 1, clear: E quasi no mesmo tempo tinha enviado o thenente de m[estr]e de campo g[ene]r[a]l Luis R[ibeir]o, para q[ue] tomando as noticias convenientes encaminhe dali as carruagens, e outros socorros p[e]la parte mais segura. In the cipher the slip is the encipherer’s: quazi is written with F ( h ) where K ( z ) was meant.

The project’s statistical check ( docs/_validate.py ) was run on the two letters deciphered with K2, 13 May and the 15 May note: 1,139 symbols of 37 kinds, scored with a Portuguese letter model. The reading scores −2.36 per letter. Random keys score −7.41 on average, 6.8 standard deviations lower, and a key fitted by the annealer to the same symbols in shuffled order reaches at best −3.64. The annealer run on the real text from random starting keys reaches −2.50, close to the reading, so the search does find this key. The verdict is pass : with about thirty occurrences per symbol, the letter statistics separate this key from any key fitted to noise.

Clear text roman, cipher in italic ; spelling of the cipher kept; word division, punctuation, capitals, u/v, i/j, cedillas and tildes editorial, since the cipher has no symbols for them; [x] an expanded abbreviation or restored letter; {x} an encipherer’s slip corrected; ‹x› unresolved 13 May 1663: the cavalry on its way Conde amigo. Eu ElRey vos envio muito saudar como aquelle q[ue] amo. A ultima carta que se recebeo vosa foi de {10} do corrente, e fico com cuidado de se nam hav{e}r recebido outra, e se entende pod[e]ria t{o}mar-se o correo. Despacho {es}te para vos avizar que Manoe[l] Freire de Andrade partio d{e} Coimbra em 9 deste á tarde com 203 cavallos, e escreve q[ue] nam faria outra detença mais q[u]e em montar alguns que hião desmontados; com elle deve hir tambem tudo o que faltava do socorro da Be{i}ra; conforme a isto pod{e}reis fazer conta de quando ahi poderá {c}hegar. Das companhias de cav[a]los desta cidade pasa amanhã a de Luis Lo[bo] ‹aal› de Agalega com 56 cavalos; no dia seguinte parte a do comisario Gonçalo da Costa, e no outro Diogo Luis Ribeiro e Jorge Furtado, e cada hum leva 55 cavalos pelo menos. Nam se oferece outra couza de q[ue] vos avizar mais que estar-se esperando {c}oreio com todo o cuidado. Escrita em L[isbo]a a 13 de Mayo de 1663. Rey. Written the day before Évora was invested. The last letter from Vila Flor received at court was of the 10th, and the court fears the courier has been taken. Manuel Freire de Andrade left Coimbra on the 9th with 203 horse and the rest of the Beira relief; of the Lisbon cavalry companies, one leaves tomorrow with 56 horse, then those of Gonçalo da Costa, Diogo Luís Ribeiro and Jorge Furtado, at least 55 horse each. 15 May 1663: the long letter Partly in clear and partly in cipher. The cipher carries everything the enemy should not learn: the Beira reinforcements reported by Pedro Jaques de Magalhães (1,801 foot in the terços of Manuel Ferreira Rebelo and Paulo de Andrade, 408 horse), Manuel Freire de Andrade’s 203 horse, three Lisbon cavalry companies embarking with 170 horse and Jorge Furtado following with 60; the King’s plan to make Setúbal a place of arms and to come himself to Setúbal or Palmela; 44,000 cruzados for the pay that left on Thursday and have taken shelter somewhere still unknown, with boots and other stores, money for the French and a thousand cruzados for the English, “e que tudo se tem entendido estar em Evora”; and the mestre de campo António Soares da Costa and an engineer sent to Montemor. In clear are the greeting, the doctrine that an army raised and paid by the kingdom exists to fight when it must, and the order to send a courier every day, “ainda que não haja couza de novo”. 15 May 1663: “a todo o risco” Conde amigo. Eu ElRey vos envio muito saudar como aquelle que amo. Demais do que vos digo em outra carta desta mesma data, tornando-sse a considerar a materia principal de que nella se trata, fui servido rezolver que, em cazo que o inimigo persevere no sitio de Evora e reduza aquela cidade a termos perigozos, ajunteis todas as forças dessa provincia, e com os socorros que das outras espera{i}s a procureis socorrer a todo o risco, ainda que vos exponhais a[o] ultimo transe de huma batalha, porque assim convem á defença do reino e a meu serviço, pella importancia da praça e conse[q]uencias que se seguirão d{o} sucesso que ella tiver; o que espero executareis com a rezoluçam e valor q{ue} he necessaria. Escrita em L[isbo]a a 15 de Mayo de 1663. Rey. A note added to the long letter the day after Évora was invested, wholly in cipher between the greeting and the date. The main question has been considered again: if the enemy keeps up the siege and puts the city in danger, Vila Flor is to gather all the forces of the province and the help expected from the others, and relieve it at all risk, “even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle”, for the defence of the kingdom requires it. 26 May 1663: the final resolution Conde Amigo. Eu ElRey vos envio muito saudar como aquelle q[ue] amo. Despois de hontem vos haver escrito as cartas cujo duplicado vai com esta, pareceo tornar-vos a dizer por ultima rezolução que o que convem a conservaçam de meus reinos he socorrer Evora em todo o cazo e a todo o risco, sem se duvidar desta rezoluçam; o modo e a forma haveis vós de dispor como vos parec{e}r. Esta minha carta mostrareis aos cabos desse exercito, de cujo valor e rezolução espero que todo este reino lhes deva sua conservação. Tambem me pareceo dizer-vos que logo, sem tardança, deveis logo mover esse exercito, tanto para animar essa gente como para entender o inimigo que he esta a minha rezoluçam; e dentro de dous dias partirá daqui dinheiro consideravel, que baste para paga do exercito e das carruagens; o q[u]e podeis fazer notorio a todos, [p]ara que o tenham entendido. Escrita em Lixb[o]a a 26 de Mayo de 1663. Rey. Written four days after Évora surrendered. The King tells Vila Flor again, “as my final resolution”, that the preservation of his kingdoms requires the relief of Évora in any event and at all risk; the manner is left to him. He is to show the letter to his commanders, move the army at once, both to hearten the men and to show the enemy the King’s resolve, and announce that within two days a considerable sum will leave Lisbon for the pay of the army and the wagons. The foot of the same letter: the last two cipher lines, the date in clear ( Em Lixb.a a 26 de Mayo de 1663 ), Rey , Castelo Melhor’s signature and the address P[ar]a o Conde de V[ila] Flor . The tear in the right margin took one symbol, restored as [p]. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Luís de Miranda Pereira liv. 2 (PT/TT/LMP/0002), image m0037, via DigitArq.

Don John appeared before Estremoz, the army’s base, on 11 May 1663; unable to attack it, he marched on Évora and invested it on the 14th. The 13 May letter was written while Lisbon did not yet know his target. Vila Flor’s council of war resolved to march to the city’s relief, and the army left Estremoz on 22 May, the day Évora surrendered (Ericeira, book VIII). The order was renewed on 26 May. On 8 June Vila Flor and Schomberg defeated Don John at Ameixial, and Évora was retaken in June. The letters fill in what Ericeira’s Historia de Portugal Restaurado only alludes to, “the King’s repeated orders and the urgent pressure of the Count of Castelo Melhor”. Several details agree with his narrative: the Beira terços of Manuel Ferreira Rebelo and Paulo de Andrade were with the army on 22 May, Manuel Freire de Andrade joined it with the Beira horse, and Ericeira counts eighty thousand cruzados sent from Lisbon among the funds of the Évora garrison when the siege began, which fits the 15 May letter’s belief that the pay convoy had taken shelter in the city. The plan to bring the King to Setúbal or Palmela was kept in cipher, and the contributor found no trace of the journey in Ericeira.

13 May, ʒ : a symbol used once, in Despacho {es}te , taken as es from the sense (grade I); it is the one position in the four letters without a value from the key. 13 May, Lo[bo] ‹aal› de Agalega : after Lo the encipherer struck out two symbols, probably bo (Luís Lobo is named in the long letter of 15 May); aal de Agalega is not explained. 13 May, slips : about fifteen symbols corrected from the sense (grade M): three times 30 ( m ) for 3 ( e ), in hav{e}r , d{e} Coimbra and pod{e}reis ; twice K ( z ) for c , in {c}hegar and {c}oreio ; A ( t ) for i in Be{i}ra ; letters left out. This letter survives in one copy, so the corrections rest on the sense alone. 15 May note : five slips of the first copy ( espera{i}s , a[o] , conse[q]uencias , d{o} , q{ue} ), all settled by the second copy. 26 May : one symbol lost in the tear, restored from the sense as [p] in [p]ara ; parecor written for parecer . 15 May, long letter : agardeço for agradeço in both copies, so the draft’s spelling; the engineer sent to Montemor, Adam Fr[ancis]co de Pontes in both copies, is not identified. Only the 174-symbol passage shown in section 03 is transcribed in the repository; the full transcriptions of the two copies (2,213 and 2,357 symbols, as the contributor counts them) and their decryptions are not, so the long letter’s text cannot yet be checked symbol by symbol here. The K2 homophones were set on the 13 May letter itself and are not tested independently of it; the test in section 03 is of K1. Prior work. Ericeira’s Historia de Portugal Restaurado , part II (1698), book VIII, and its 1751 edition do not quote the letters. The blog Guerra da Restauração , which publishes documents of the 1663 campaign, gives Vila Flor’s letter of 26 May, not the King’s. António Álvares da Cunha’s Campanha de Portugal pella provincia do Alentejo na primavera do anno de 1663 (Lisbon, 1663) is not digitised as far as the contributor found and has not been checked. Web searches in Portuguese and English found no edition (27 October 2026).

Translation 1663-05-13_translation.md # 13 May 1663: the cavalry sent as reinforcements: English translation Count, my friend. I the King send you warm greetings, as one whom I love. The last letter of yours received here was of the 10th of this month, and I am anxious at not having received another; it is thought the courier may have been taken. I send this one to let you know that Manuel Freire de Andrade left Coimbra on the 9th of this month, in the afternoon, with 203 horse, and writes that he will make no other halt than to mount some men who were going on foot; with him should also go everything that was lacking from the Beira relief; from this you can reckon when he may arrive there. Of the cavalry companies of this city, that of Luís Lobo (?) […] de Agalega leaves tomorrow with 56 horse; the next day that of commissary Gonçalo da Costa leaves, and the day after Diogo Luís Ribeiro and Jorge Furtado, each taking at least 55 horse. Nothing else occurs to tell you, except that the courier is awaited with the greatest anxiety. Written in Lisbon on 13 May 1663. The King. — The Count of Castelo Melhor. — To the Count of Vila Flor. Afonso VI to the Count of Vila Flor, 15 May 1663, the other letter: reinforcements, money, and the King at Setúbal This is the “other letter of this same date” to which the ciphered note of 15 May refers. Partly in clear and partly in cipher, it keeps for the cipher everything that would inform the enemy: the reinforcements on the way (Beira foot and horse, Lisbon companies), the King’s plan to set up a place of arms at Setúbal or Palmela, the pay money, the help sent to Montemor. Left in clear are the greeting, the doctrine (“an army is there to fight”) and the request for a courier every day.
