Conde Amigo. Eu ElRey vos envio muito saudar como aquelle q[ue] amo. Receberão-se as vossas cartas de 12 do corrente em q[ue] daes conta do que té aquelle tempo havia succedido, e tinheis alcançado do Inimigo, que me dera muito mayor cuidado, se vos não tivera no governo de minhas armas, e aos cabos que comvosco assistem, cujo valor vejo se communica a todos os soldados desse exercito, e ainda aos moradores de todos os lugares, conforme a informação q[ue] tenho, de como estão animados, o q[ue] me dá grande contentamento. Entendo que ja la tendes os terços auxiliares da Estremadura, excepto algumas companhias do de Torres Vedras que hão partido mais tarde; o do termo desta cidade se fica aprestando com toda a deligencia, e posto que não poderá chegar para a primeira ocazião que espero tenha, servirão para despois reforçar o exercito. Hoje se recebeo o avizo do mestre de campo general Pedro Jaques de Magalhães com data de 9 do corrente, com huma relação da infanteria e cavallaria que dis tinha partido té o primeiro de Mayo, que contem 1801 praças de infanteria nos dous terços do mestre de campo Manoel Ferreira Rebelo e Paulo de Andrade, e 408 praças de cavallaria, que conforme ao tempo em que refere partio devem de ser chegadas; e diz que esperava fosse de Almeida Manoel Freire de Andrade para levar tudo o mais que houvesse, o qual partio de Coimbra com 203 cavalos, que ali comprou em 9 do corrente, e parece chegará ahi muito brevemente. Desta cidade se embarcarão hoje as companhias de cavalos dos comissarios Gonçalo da Costa de Menezes, Luis Lobo e Diogo Luis Ribeiro com 170 cavalos bem montados, e amanhã parte Jorge Furtado com a sua, que constará de 60 cavalos, e vai com ordem de em Montemor tomarem as noticias necessarias para o caminho que hão de seguir. Tanto que vos chegarem estes socorros, se entende que vos achareis com poder bastante para pelejardes com o inimigo, se vos parecer, o que fica á vossa dispozição. O que daqui se vos pode dizer he, que assim para que {se a}junta exercito, e o Reino o sustenta com suas contribuições, he para o defenderem, pelejando quando he necessario, e do contrario se perderia a reputação das armas, e se desconsolarião os vassallos, e se seguirião outras consequencias muito perjudiciaes. Presentes vos são estas razões, e conheço de vós que as medireis com o tempo e ocazião que vos offerecer, para acertardes no que mais convenha. Para engrossar ao diante e conservar esse exercito, pareceo o meio mais eficaz passar eu a essa provincia; e assim ordeno se faça praça de armas na villa de Setuval, por se julgar parte mais acomodada por muitas razões, e ali mando juntar o que for possivel com toda a brevidade, e com a mesma passarei eu logo a assistir naquella villa ou na de Palmela, para socorrer como e aonde o tempo mostrar que he necessario; e no interim e sempre se vos hirá acudindo com a maior pontualidade que puder ser, particularmente com dinheiro para paga dos soldados: quarenta e quatro mil cruzados tinham partido daqui quinta feira, e se entende estão recolhidos em parte segura, mas ainda se não sabe ao certo aonde, e com elles huma partida de botas e outras couzas. Tambem mandei remeter dinheiro para os Francezes, e mil cruzados que faltarão para os Inglezes. E que tudo se tem entendido estar em Evora. Aquella cidade tenho por bastantemente prevenida, conforme o tempo deu lugar, e vos agardeço a deligencia com que o fizestes; espero em Deos que se defenderá té que chegueis a socorrê-la; e sendo ella da importancia e reputação que sabeis, não tenho para que vo-la encomendar. A Montemor me pareceo enviar o mestre de campo Antonio Soares da Costa e o engenheiro Adam Fr[ancis]co de Pontes para assistir ao que for necessario para sua defensa; e quazi no mesmo tempo tinha enviado o tenente de mestre de campo general Luis Ribeiro, para que tomando as noticias convenientes encaminhe dali as carruagens e outros socorros pela parte mais segura. Ao correio mor se ordenou mudasse as postas como apontais e as dobrasse. Encomendovos muito, que todos os dias infalivelmente me despacheis hum correyo pelo menos, com aviso do que for succedendo, ainda que não haja couza de novo, para me tirar do cuidado em que he força esteja do que passa dessa banda. Escrita em L[isbo]a a 15 de Mayo de 1663. — Rey. — [Conde de Castelo Melhor]. — P[ar]a o Conde de Villa Flor. Translation 1663-05-15a_translation.md # 15 May 1663, the other letter: reinforcements, money, and the King at Setúbal: English translation Count, my friend. I the King send you warm greetings, as one whom I love. Your letters of the 12th of this month have been received, in which you report what had happened up to that time and what you had learnt of the enemy; this would have caused me much greater anxiety had I not you at the head of my arms, and with you the commanders who assist you, whose valour I see passes to all the soldiers of that army and even to the inhabitants of every place, according to what I am told of their spirit; which gives me great satisfaction. I understand that you already have there the auxiliary terços of Estremadura, except some companies of the Torres Vedras one which left later; that of the district of this city [Lisbon] is being made ready with all diligence, and although it cannot arrive for the first occasion I hope you will have, it will serve afterwards to reinforce the army. Today the report of the mestre de campo general Pedro Jaques de Magalhães was received, dated the 9th of this month, with a return of the infantry and cavalry which, he says, had left by the 1st of May: 1,801 foot in the two terços of the mestres de campo Manuel Ferreira Rebelo and Paulo de Andrade, and 408 horse, which, given the time of their departure, must have arrived; he says he was waiting for Manuel Freire de Andrade to come from Almeida to bring all the rest; he left Coimbra with 203 horses, which he bought there on the 9th of this month, and should reach you very soon. From this city the cavalry companies of the commissaries Gonçalo da Costa de Meneses, Luís Lobo and Diogo Luís Ribeiro embark today with 170 well-mounted horse, and tomorrow Jorge Furtado leaves with his, which will be of 60 horse; they are ordered to take at Montemor the news they need for the road they are to follow. As soon as these reinforcements reach you, it is thought you will have strength enough to fight the enemy, if you see fit: that is left to your discretion. What can be told you from here is that, if an army is raised and the Kingdom maintains it with its contributions, it is so that it may defend it, fighting when it is necessary; otherwise the reputation of our arms would be lost, the vassals would be disheartened, and other very harmful consequences would follow. These reasons are present to you, and I know you well enough to know that you will weigh them against the time and the occasion that offer, so as to do what is best. To enlarge this army in future and maintain it, the most effective means seemed to be that I should go myself to that province; I therefore order that a place of arms be made in the town of Setúbal, judged the most suitable spot for many reasons, and I am having everything possible gathered there with all speed; with the same speed I shall go at once to reside in that town or in Palmela, to give help as and where time shows it is needed. In the meantime, and always, you will be supplied with the greatest punctuality possible, particularly with money for the soldiers’ pay: forty-four thousand cruzados left here on Thursday [10 May], and they are thought to be sheltered in a safe place, but it is not yet known exactly where; with them a consignment of boots and other things. I have also had money sent for the French, and a thousand cruzados that were lacking for the English. And it has been learnt that all of it is in Évora. That city I consider sufficiently provided, as far as time allowed, and I thank you for the diligence with which you did it; I hope in God that it will hold out until you come to relieve it; and as it is of the importance and reputation you know, I need not commend it to you. To Montemor I thought fit to send the mestre de campo António Soares da Costa and the engineer Adam Fr[ancis]co de Pontes, to help with whatever is needed for its defence; and almost at the same time the tenente de mestre de campo general Luís Ribeiro had been sent, so that, taking the appropriate news, he might forward from there the wagons and other supplies by the safest way. The correio-mor has been ordered to change the post relays as you suggest, and to double them. I strongly charge you to send me without fail every day at least one courier, with word of what is happening, even if there is nothing new, to free me from the anxiety in which I must needs be about what is going on on that side. Written in Lisbon on 15 May 1663. The King. — The Count of Castelo Melhor. — To the Count of Vila Flor. Afonso VI to the Count of Vila Flor, 15 May 1663: “at the risk of a battle” The day after Évora was invested, the King added to a long letter of the same date a note entirely in cipher apart from the greeting and the date. The main question had been “reconsidered”: if the enemy persisted and put the city in danger, Vila Flor was to gather all his forces and relieve it at all risk, “even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle”. Afonso VI to the Count of Vila Flor, 26 May 1663: "my final resolution" On 22 May 1663 Évora, one of the chief cities of the kingdom, surrendered to Don John Joseph of Austria. Four days later the court in Lisbon, governed by the Count of Castelo Melhor in the name of the young Afonso VI, wrote to the general of the Alentejo army, the Count of Vila Flor. The letter opens and closes in clear; the whole order is in cipher: relieve Évora “em todo o cazo e a todo o risco”, move the army without delay, show the letter to the commanders, and count on the pay money leaving in two days. Thirteen days later Vila Flor and Schomberg defeated Don John at Ameixial. Having written to you yesterday the letters whose duplicate goes with this one, it seemed good to me to tell you again, as my final resolution, that what is fitting for the preservation of my kingdoms is to relieve Évora in any event and at all risk, with no doubt to be cast on this resolution; the manner and the form you shall arrange as you see fit. You shall show this letter of mine to the commanders of that army, to whose valour and resolution I hope this whole kingdom will owe its preservation. It also seemed good to me to tell you that at once, without delay, you must move that army, both to put heart into those men and to make the enemy understand that this is my resolution; and within two days a considerable sum of money will leave here, enough for the pay of the army and for the wagons; which you may make known to all, so that they may take note of it. Waddall writes in a phonetic English about the elections to the second Protectorate Parliament: the City’s members (major-general Browne, aldermen Adams and Foot, Mr Jones), and a riot at Westminster between Colonel Grosvenor’s soldiers and Mr Latham’s party, “the solgers came in to cry for Gravenar, the setisans cried no sword men, no marsonary men”. Then the cipher, in a clear frame: “There is [6] of [3] sent to lie near [7] and six [6] of [243 226] are [3] to strengthen [3], and [8] is so far out of favour now, that [5] told me he had a greater mind to [3] him than [4]” (the bracketed numbers count the figures). The cipher words in Waddall’s clear frame, and his signature. Image: Thomas Birch, A Collection of the State Papers of John Thurloe (1742), vol. 5 p. 337, via the Internet Archive. This letter was one of four short pieces with no known decipherment in Birch’s volumes that Cryptiana lists together. They share only the printed source and each is in its own cipher: Beverning and Vande Perre to Boreel, 1653 , du Gard to White, 10 June 1656 and Brussels to Copinger, 12 August 1656 each have their own page.

Every royalist and Commonwealth key of 1653–60 that Cryptiana publishes (Marshall 1656–58, Barwick–Hyde 1659–60, Stamford 1655, Butler 1656, the Charles II key intercepted in 1655, Kingston 1658, Westrope 1655, the Hague agent and Blake) was applied and scored with an English quadgram model. The Marshall key covers 48 of the 50 groups and gives “Theare is b s g n g m of i l m sent to lie nere k g c i k m d”: noise. Cribs. The frame invites guesses (“horse”, “hang”), but with 27 distinct letter figures in 50 groups and homophones, each guess fits many assignments equally well, and none forces the rest.

The eight cipher words and the code pair 243 226 (50 groups): not read. Blocker: too short. The key would be among the ciphers of Charles II’s agents at Bruges in the Clarendon manuscripts, which are not online.
